en: New Commentary on Sengzhao’s Treatises: The Unhindered Blade, Volume One.

The Founder and Abbot of Dawa Shengyuguo Temple on Mount Wutai, the Master of Baima Temple, the Posthumously Honored Duke of Gui, and the True Awakened One who Transmits the Dharma of the Sea-Seal: Shi Yuandabai.
The Great Master’s Extended Lecture on the Śramaṇa, composed by Wencái.

In preparing to explain this commentary, I shall introduce it through two sections: first, an exposition of the treatise’s purport; second, a word-by-word explanation of the commentary’s meaning. Regarding the first:
In Sanskrit it is called *Abhidharma*; here it is translated as "Incomparable Dharma" (*Anuttara-dharma*), meaning that it expresses the most supreme wisdom.

It is also translated as "Dharma in Opposition" (*Pratidharma*). This "opposition" has two meanings: first, opposition in contemplation, wherein one contemplates the Four Noble Truths; second, opposition in orientation, wherein one is oriented toward *nirvāṇa*.

Through contemplation, one attains sainthood; through orientation, one attains cessation. The essence of that which performs this opposition is untainted, pure wisdom (*anāsrava-śuddha-prajñā*). That which is opposed [by it] is...
The Dharma of this [treatise] is none other than the Four Noble Truths and Nirvāṇa; it is the counterpart to that Dharma because wisdom (*prajñā*) is its primary subject. Question:

The Buddha taught that the Three Piṭakas are all subsumed within the Holy Teachings (*ārya-śāsana*). Why, then, do the compositions of eminent monks not fall under this category? Answer: Because they originate from the source.

This means that the fundamental basis for the meaning of this treatise was also spoken by the Buddha, though it is scattered throughout the *Vaipulya* section of the canon. The Master of the Treatise composed this work based upon those sūtras, rendering it extremely concise.
The essential point is that it subsumes the wisdom of the primary principles within the first [category], thereby attracting those of superior faculties who delight in brevity.
This is established solely on the basis of its being consistent with the Mahāyāna’s profound nature-reasoning and the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna);
thus, it may also be included within the noble teachings of the Abhidharma, as was the case for Katyāyanīputra during the Buddha’s lifetime.
Śāriputra and others composed the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, the *Saṃgītiparyāya-pāda-śāstra*, and so forth; as these are all subsumed within the Abhidharma Piṭaka, they are indeed śāstras.

However, while śāstras encompass both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, this treatise belongs exclusively to the Mahāyāna. Within the Mahāyāna, it encompasses both the provisional and the ultimate, yet here it is strictly the ultimate and not the provisional.

Among the five teachings, it is subsumed solely under the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) Final Teaching (*niṣṭha-deśanā*). Among the five schools, it belongs to the school of the Non-obstruction of Principle and Phenomena (*li-shi wuai zong*). Why is this?
This is because within all four treatises, the principle of the Middle Way—which is neither existent nor non-existent—is elucidated.
As it says below: "Do not abandon movement in search of stillness," and also: "The myriad things are themselves void," which likewise includes the sudden teaching. Furthermore, as it says below:

"The eyes face the Truth yet do not perceive it," and also: "In every encounter with phenomena, one encounters the Truth," this corresponds to the *Tathatā* (Suchness) section of the *Awakening of Faith*.

It is taught that the distinctions among all phenomena exist solely based on deluded thought; if one is free from mental conceptualization, then every phenomenon is true and every phenomenon is suchness (*tathatā*).

Since the Great Master Xianshou (Fazang) judged the Gate of Suchness (*tathatāmukha*) to be the definitive scope of the Sudden Teaching, this treatise—from its beginning to its end—reaches the profound depths of the One Vehicle and exhausts the subtle essence of the principles of nature.
It encompasses all existence as it envelops space, and reveals the provisional to manifest the ultimate.

The "Shi" (Reality) chapter expounds the principle of non-transmigration, clarifying the fundamental tenet through the metaphor of flowing water. The "Fa" (Manifestation) chapter issues discourses on the unreal, unfolding profound depths by relying upon the gates of the Truths (*satya*).
It explains the purport of *prajñā* as being without vision or cognition, exhausting the mysteries within mysteries;
it clarifies the mind of *nirvāṇa* as neither emerging nor abiding, reaching the pinnacle of wonders within wonders. Therefore, Huiyimin remarked that he bathed his mind in the Vaipulya sutras.
To fathom the abyss of his realization and to perceive the expanse of his profound, transcendent insight would not be an exaggeration.
As for his prose, it contains the brilliance of flowers and weaves together their petals; it strikes the notes of *shang* and *yu*. It arises from principle and is born of substance.

Neither the empty talk of Hui Shi nor the veneration of non-being by He Yan could even remotely resemble it. One might say it is truly refined, elegant, lush, and flourishing—the very mouth of discourse itself.

Thus, the meat was succulent and the fine grain fragrant; when cast upon the ground, it produced sounds like metal and jade. As for the lament of the "Leftover People" (Yimin): "The principles are subtle and the expressions are perilous;
the solo chant finds few echoes. This may indeed be called knowing how to speak of the Way.

Next, following the commentary, the explanation of the meaning of the treatise is divided into three parts. First, the explanation of the title of the treatise. Regarding the phrase "Zhao ji" (肇即) and so forth:

it means that the author of the treatise, by means of his wisdom that thoroughly penetrates the Dharma and his skillful eloquence in adapting to the capacities of beings, provisionally employs sounds, names, phrases, and sentences to reveal the principle of the Middle Way, thereby enabling sentient beings to obtain the benefit of the equality of the One Vehicle;
for this reason, he composed the treatise. As for the section "Person and Dharma" (Renfa) and below, it follows [the previous pattern].

The *Qingliang Chao* (Clear and Cool Commentary) comprehensively distinguishes the various modes by which the various sutras receive their names. Some are titled after persons, while others are named after dharmas;
they may be based on causes or fruits, and may be either compound or simple. This present work differs in that its title consists of two characters, namely "person and dharma.

From the passage beginning with "By means of the four [factors]," the reason for establishing the name is revealed. A detailed examination of the Liang Dynasty biographies shows that after Master Kumārajīva produced the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he...
The Master first composed the *Treatise on Non-Cognition*. Next, he composed two treatises, including the *Treatise on the Non-Reality of All Phenomena*.

It was only after Master Kumārajīva’s passing that he began composing the *Treatise on the Namelessness of Nirvāṇa*. This is the sequence. If it were not so now, one might seek the reason through inference:

it likely reflects the order of the thematic meanings when the author established the fundamental framework of the work. That is to say, he first demonstrated the principle of non-transmigration, and next...
To manifest the truth of the primary meaning (*paramārtha*), one relies on the divine mind of *prajñā* to illuminate the wondrous realm of *nirvāṇa*.

*Nirvāṇa* is the ultimate destination to which the three vehicles (*triyāna*) return; therefore, it is placed last. However, this is not the original intent of the author, but is merely arranged here according to the sequence.

Furthermore, as each [treatise] adheres to a specific principle, that which is followed is determined by the title of the discourse. This, however, pertains only to the provisional teachings (*neyārtha*). As for the true teaching (*nītārtha*)—
The principle that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, as discussed in the definitive sutras and śāstras, is the primary tenet of the "Treatise on Non-transmigration.
Even the exposition of the meaning of nirvāṇa is the central doctrine of the "Treatise on Namelessness. [The text] intends to synthesize these; it combines four into one.

One must not place four titles together within a single heading. As for the phrase "furthermore, it is composed as such," this refers to the fact that the *Zongben* (Fundamental Tenet) chapter was composed last;

it is placed at the beginning of the treatise to subsume the four [chapters] into one. Regarding the statement "both the tenet and the commentary pertain to it": the "tenet" (*zong*) is the *Zongben*, and the "commentary" (*shi*) refers to the four treatises.
These four merely elaborate upon the meaning contained within the tenet; the tenet itself provides a concise indication of the essential framework, just as in the *Awakening of Faith*.

Regarding the "Section on Establishing the Thesis" (*Siddhānta-vibhāga*): its explanation extensively sets forth the principles and meanings, as found in the "Section on Explanation" (*Vyākhyāna-vibhāga*).

As for the term "treatise" (*śāstra*), it is explained briefly in the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*. Fully stated, a treatise consists of established, definitive, and normative words and phrases that analyze and explain the profound principles of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
It is called a "treatise" (*śāstra*) based on this meaning of definitive judgment. Furthermore, a "treatise" is that which collects the discussions regarding the Dharma.

Furthermore, it is called a "treatise" (*śāstra*) because it establishes the roles of interlocutor and respondent to engage in a reciprocal exchange of inquiry and analysis to investigate correct principles.
"Reciprocal exchange" refers to question and answer; "inquiry" means to seek out [the meaning]; and "analysis" means to dissect [it].

This is exemplified by the successive rounds of question and answer—nine in each case—in the *Tattvārtha-śāstra* (The Treatise on Seeking Explanations) and the two treatises on Ignorance (*Ajñāna*) and Namelessness (*Anāman*). To "demonstrate for beings so they may cultivate awakening" is the fundamental purpose of composing a treatise.

Therefore, it is intended to cause sentient beings to awaken to principle and cultivate contemplation, to cease delusion and manifest the true, and to realize the real mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena;

it is not for the sake of textual scholarship or worldly affairs. As for the statement that "there are two kinds," according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (the "Later Treatise" by Nāgārjuna), the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa composed the *Awakening of Faith* based on one hundred sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Likewise, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also takes the six sūtras and other texts as its basis. Regarding the commentaries, they are as follows:

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is a commentary on the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* is an exposition of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and related texts; these are treatises that take the sūtras as their primary authority and synthesize their meanings.

Regarding the term "Da Qin" (大秦) in the sub-commentary (*shu*): this is the name for our own dynasty [the Tang], which succeeded the two Qin dynasties starting from the reign of Emperor Mu of the Eastern Jin.

They subsequently emerged. The Former Qin was of the Fu clan; the Later Qin was of the Yao clan. As both clans were of the Qin lineage, the court historians distinguished them by prefixing the terms "Former" and "Later.
These were not self-designations. Fu Jian was the son of Fu Hong. Hong had changed his surname to Fu and was a person of the Western Qiang.
When Hong was executed by Ma Qiu, a general of the Zhao state, Jian received his father’s mandate and took control of the Passes.
The interior was the seat of the Heavenly King’s throne; indeed, all the regions west of Jigu were designated as Guanzhong.

Fu Jian was the son of Donghai Wang Fu Xiong. When Fu Jian died, the Crown Prince Fusheng succeeded him. Fusheng was cruel and tyrannical, acting contrary to the Way; Jian killed him and established himself as ruler.
"In the final years" refers to the twenty-fifth year of the Jianyuan era. Jian led an army of eight million seven hundred thousand to launch a campaign.
He advanced to Shouchun, where he was defeated by the Jin general Xie Xuan. He returned to Chang’an, but Murong Chong and Yao Chang both rebelled against him.
Chong besieged Chang’an; when Fu Jian fought with all his might without success, he fled north to Mount Wujiang.
He was again besieged there by Yao Chang, who subsequently captured him and strangled him at a Buddhist temple in Xinping—present-day Bingzhou. Yao Chang was [the son of] Yao Zhong.
Yi was his son. He was also a person of the Western Qiang. He killed Jian and established himself. When Chang died, his son Xing ascended the throne and changed the era name to Hongshi.
This lasted for a total of nineteen years. Chang’an is the name of a commandery. Regarding the clan name of the Tathāgata, the *Śākyaputra-vaṃśa* (Shijia pu) quotes the Mahīśāsaka Vinaya, stating:
"In the past, there was a king named Ummā. He had four sons born of concubines; the first was named Zhāomù, the second..."
Cóngmù had three sons named Tiáofúxiàng (Taming the Elephant) and Nílóu (Nīla). They were intelligent, martial, and possessed great majesty and virtue.
The first queen had a son named Chángshēng (Long Life), who was stubborn, base, and ugly, and was despised by all people.

Fearing that the kingdom and its throne would fall to the four other sons, the queen used her charms to entice the king. The king was pleased and subsequently slandered the four sons, causing them to be banished from the country.
At that time, the mother of the four sons, along with their kinsmen, the Mallas, and the people, seeing that the four sons had been exiled despite being innocent, all desired to follow them.
The king also granted them permission to depart. Thereupon, they reached the north of the Snowy Mountains and obtained a vast and remote territory where they resided for several years.
Their virtue attracted followers like a marketplace, and they flourished into a powerful nation. Later, the king, longing to see them, summoned the four.
The son declined the offer and did not return. The King sighed and said, "My son is Śākya; therefore, he shall be named of the Śākya clan.
*Kula* (clan) is also synonymous with *gotra* (lineage). *Śākya* translates as "able" (*śakya*). From Nīla, there was a son named Upāriṣṭa. Upāriṣṭa’s son was named Gotama.
The son Śiśunāga was King Siṃhahanu, the master of the *Jñānaprasthāna*. This king had four sons; the first was called Śuddhodana, whose son was the Buddha.
From the time he acquired his clan name until the Buddha, there were six generations in total. As for Master Dao’an and others, they lived during the era of Emperor Wu of the Eastern Jin dynasty;
their deeds are recorded in the *Liang* annals. Those who left the household life prior to Master Dao’an all followed teachers.
Regarding surnames: those such as Zhu Fayi and others, who were disciples of Zhu Daqian, are examples.

Dao’an, considering that among the origins of the Great Master, none is more venerable than the Buddha, therefore adopted "Shi" (Śākya) as his clan name. At that time, some followed this practice while others did not.

In the twentieth year of the Jianyuan era, the Tripiṭaka master Dharmaratna translated the *Ekottarika Āgama*. In its twenty-first fascicle, it states briefly: [The passage from the *Ekottarika Āgama* follows here.]
Now, there are four great rivers that flow from the Anavatapta Spring; each follows its own direction into one of the four oceans, where they no longer retain their original names.

This is also the case here: when those of the Kṣatriya, Brāhmaṇa, Gṛhapati, or Vaiśya castes shave off their hair and beards in the presence of the Tathāgata to leave the household life and study the Path, they no longer have their original surnames, but are simply called Śramaṇas of the Śākya clan.
The disciple [Yuanze] found that his views were already in accord with the scriptures; thus, they became a permanent standard. "Xie" means to harmonize; "qi" means to reach.

The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) was composed by Dharma Master Huìjiǎo of Jiāxiáng Temple in Kuàijī during the Liáng dynasty. The Master [Sengzhao] is categorized under the section on "Exegesis.

The biography briefly states: He was a native of Jīngzhào. His family was poor, and he made his living as a copyist. While engaged in transcribing texts, he consequently read through the scriptures extensively.
[The] History [states] (as follows). Regarding "resting the spirit" (*qishen*) and so forth: "resting" (*qi*) means to dwell or settle. "Spirit" (*shen*) refers to the wondrous mind.

"Mystery" (*ming*) is equivalent to stillness. "Accumulations" (*lei*) refer to birth and death. "Not yet having exhausted the good" means not having reached ultimate perfection. I, too, have the honor of having read the books of Zhuangzi and Laozi;
they primarily take as their model the Way of Non-being (*xuwu*), Spontaneity (*ziran*), the Profound and Dark (*yaoming*), and the Obscure and Silent (*hunmo*). From this...

It descends as the harmonious primordial qi, giving birth to heaven and earth. It animates the spirits and the celestial lords; it is the utility for the production of all things. At times it appears as if not full.
The method for cultivating it must necessarily emulate the Dao: internally, one guards the valley-spirit and maintains stillness, blunting sharp edges and unraveling entanglements.
Externally, one harmonizes with light and becomes one with the dust, neither boasting nor relying on oneself. As Zhuangzi says, when Guangchengzi bestowed the Way upon the Yellow Emperor, he said:
"The essence of the Ultimate Way is profound and obscure; the pinnacle of the Ultimate Way is dark and silent."
This discusses the Way (*Dao*). Below, it clarifies the practice, saying: "Without looking and without listening, embrace the spirit (*shen*) in stillness.

Be necessarily pure and necessarily clean; do not weary your form, and do not agitate your essence (*jing*); only then can you attain longevity. It further says: "I guard the One (*yi*) to abide in its harmony;
therefore, though I have cultivated my person for twelve hundred years, my form has never decayed. The commentary explains: "Guarding the One" means—
This is to maintain the prior Way. To abide in harmony is to not compete with things. When one does not compete, life is preserved; when one maintains the One, the Way is perfected.
This is the essential purport of the *Zhuangzi*. Based on this, it does not yet accord with our school’s concept of unconditioned cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Even if one were to attain that state—devoid of cognition and awareness—it would merely result in sinking into the Great Void. As for the divine mind of Prajñā and the wondrous Nirvāṇa...

There is. Based on the primary and secondary [bodies], its sovereign characteristics and functions are perfectly luminous; stillness and illumination share a common source, and its power penetrates all without obstruction. How could that [other teaching] compare to this?

Therefore, the Master of the Treatise (Vasubandhu) censured it for not exhausting the excellence [of the Dharma]. This was not intended as an exaggeration. Thus, Chong said: "Do not take offense at my choice of words;
I am merely mocking Zhuangzi and Laozi, for they have not yet entered the ten-foot wall of the Tathāgata. As for the "Old Vimalakīrti," this refers to Zhi Qian of the late Han dynasty.
Regarding "translated": *Vaipulya* means "square, correct, and equal," which refers to the *Vaipulya* division [of the Mahāyāna]. The *Tripiṭaka* refers to the teachings of the Hīnayāna;
many masters, relying on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, refer to the Hīnayāna as the "Tripiṭaka Teaching.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* also states that one should not associate with those who study the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna. Guzang is present-day Xiliang. When the Master of the Treatise heard this, he bypassed two...
From a distance of a thousand *li*, he came to study under him; Kumārajīva also praised him as a vessel of great capacity and divine intelligence, remarking that his potential was inexhaustible.
As for the Xiyao Garden, it was originally an imperial park that was bestowed upon Master Kumārajīva to serve as a hall for translating scriptures.

The phrasing of the commentary is entirely based on the text of the biography; it is presented in full as in the biography itself. Regarding terms such as "zuò" (作), they are explained according to their specific meanings:

when a sage establishes a new system, it is called "zuò" (creation); when a worthy person follows the model of that system, it is called "shù" (narration). As the *Zhongyōng* says: "The father creates it; the son narrates it."

Confucius also said of himself that he "transmitted but did not create," and so forth. Now, while the Dharma Master’s discourse merely follows and transmits the meanings of the sūtras and śāstras, from the perspective of the literary composition itself, it may also be called a "creation."

Commentary: Regarding "that which is venerated" (*chóng*): "veneration" means to hold as one's central principle and ideal; it also implies honoring and reverence. It refers to both the subject and the object.

That which is the object of veneration is precisely this first chapter, the "Fundamental Principle. As for "the single mind of the true mark" (*shíxiàng zhī yīxīn*): Master Kumārajīva took the true mark as his fundamental principle;
therefore, all phenomena such as non-transmigration are the true mark. The true mark encompasses both principle (*lǐ*) and phenomena (*shì*).

Non-duality is the one mind. The Wu monk Jingyuan annotated this treatise, titled it the *Zhongwu ji* (Collected Works of Central Wu), and initially explained the meaning of the fundamental principle by establishing the one mind as the central tenet.
The commentary cited entirely from that text: "Although they differ," and so forth, because the one mind fully manifests all phenomena (*dharmas*), and every phenomenon is the mind;
through the discrimination of the deluded mind, there appears to be arising and ceasing. If one were to depart from the mind...
When mindfulness is present, there is no coming or going. How could it be that the characteristics of differentiation do not undergo transformation?
Next, that which currently appears as mental factors is not real; being unreal, their nature is inherently empty. Thus, they are neither existent dharmas nor non-existent dharmas.
Neither bound by the ultimate nor the conventional, emptiness and form are of one essence; encountering all things as one—this is the primary truth.

With Prajñā as the mind, there is no need for further interpretation or explanation. The principle of Nirvāṇa equalizes gods and humans, unifying identity and difference; it reflects the mind by encompassing the six directions of the universe.

Since coming and going constitute the very substance [of reality], the meaning of the "one mind" is likewise clear and beyond doubt. Thus, we know that all four treatises expound the meaning of the one mind.
Furthermore, the mind is the *tathāgatagarbha*, within which the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all enshrined; how much more so, then, the four dharmas?
If one speaks of dharmas apart from the mind, one is no different from a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*). As for the subsequent sections: for instance, the *Treatise on Non-Transmigration* [states...]

"Taking non-transmigration as the primary tenet," and so forth. "Not [the same as] a single mind" and below: a single mind is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), while the four are the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
By gathering the specific into the general, there is no general apart from the specific; by opening the general into the specific, there is no specific apart from the general.

Therefore, a single mind encompasses the four dharmas without omission, and the four dharmas manifest a single mind with their respective locations. Regarding the phrase "the meaning refers to the principles," and so forth, it is as follows in the four sections below.

Within these treatises, if one takes their meaning in a general sense, they all concern the principles inherent within the single mind-dharma. If one takes their meaning in a specific sense, it is as in the *Treatise on Non-transmigration*, which concerns only the principle of non-transmigration;
the other three [treatises] may be understood by analogy. In interpreting any principle or meaning, the essential requirement is to penetrate the nature of phenomena (*dharma*).
Since there is no distinction between the Dharma and its meaning, how can one speak of "refining the illumination"? Thus, Guifeng said:
"People of the present day who listen and study merely seek the literal meaning and do not investigate the essence of the Dharma; nor do they examine what kind of dharma this meaning belongs to.

Based on this, the following section clarifies [the matter] by means of the expressive words, as the fundamental meaning of the school provides a general framework for the four treatises (*catuḥ-śāstra*), though it possesses a unifying principle.

Regarding the function of the prefix (*upasarga*): while there is no actual substance to what is indicated by the prefix, the four treatises refute this [position]. It can be known that the Dharma is the fundamental basis. Below follows the commentary.

The first two [compounds] are *karmadhāraya* (attributive compounds), and the last one is *tatpuruṣa* (determinative compound). "Meaning" (*artha*) is the manifestor, and "Dharma" (*dharma*) is the manifested.
Regarding the "Chapter on Not Speaking": it values the meaning rather than the literary style. [Commentary:
Below these five names, there are versions of the *Prabhāsa* (Radiant Light) that lack chapter divisions; the *Prajñā-pāramitā-śāstra-saṃgraha-sūtra* likewise has versions without chapter divisions.

As for the other four names, their characteristics are already indicated within the sūtras and śāstras, so they need not be cited here for clarification. Although the meanings are equal, as follows below...
The brief explanation according to the names can be understood as follows: the first four [categories] refer to principle (li), while "the convergence of conditions" refers to phenomena (shi).

The reason they are explained in this sequential manner is that, within the treatise, the enumeration of the names does not place them at the beginning, nor does the explanation of their meanings place them at the end; therefore, this explanation has been formulated accordingly.

Regarding the point that "that which was previously non-existent is the condition," the subsequent treatise states: "That which has not yet arisen does not exist. Therefore, if one considers phenomena from the perspective of their arising through conditions, they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*);
thus, although they appear to exist now, their existence is itself empty. Because the nature of causes and conditions is distinct, each [phenomenon] likewise does not arise.
Since they do not arise even through combination, all dharmas are fundamentally non-existent (*mūla-abhāva*). The *Jiaochao* (Excerpts from the Sutra) states briefly:

"Just as all dharmas are fundamentally non-existent, the Tathāgata is also fundamentally non-existent," and so forth. Regarding "the markless" (*animitta*), this refers to the nature of fundamental non-existence, which is far removed from the differentiated marks of male and female faculties, sense objects, existence and non-existence, identity and difference, and so on; for whatever marks exist are all false and illusory.

Therefore, "these very things" refers to the fact that phenomena (*dharma*) are the phenomena of reality (*vastu-dharma*). These phenomena of reality have no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); their nature is solely the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
This "emptiness of this nature" means that within the true nature there are no marks of delusion, defilement, and so forth—this is what is called emptiness;

it is not an emptiness of chaotic confusion or nihilistic annihilation. Furthermore, "by means of these" means that one reveals the principle by relying on the phenomenon, just as one speaks of water by pointing to waves. Relying on...

A bracelet is spoken of as gold; principle follows from phenomena. There is no principle apart from phenomena, for phenomena arise spontaneously from conditions; thus it is said that "conditions assemble.

According to the principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), all dharmas are produced through the harmonious conjunction of causes and conditions. Alternatively, the term "assembly" (*hui*) may be understood as a synonym for "conjunction" (*he*).
Below the section on Du Shun, this is the general commentary on the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*.

Regarding the phrase "the meaning relies upon [the principle]," the word "manifest" (*xian*) indicates clarity; it means that one relies on the principle to manifest the meaning, and relies on the meaning to cognize the principle.

The present mention of "one meaning" (*yi yi*) refers to both a single essence and a single meaning. The remaining terminology is easily understood. From the phrase "In this context," [it follows] the Great Master Xianshou.

This is Master Fazang’s commentary on the *Awakening of Faith*, explaining the principle that [the ultimate] is neither identical to nor different from [the phenomenal]. "Root" refers to the principle of original non-existence and so forth; "branch" refers to the phenomena of conditional conjunction.
When there is only the branch and not the root, this is the gate where phenomena can obscure the principle: it is merely a conjunction of conditions rather than the true reality (*dharmatā*).
When there is only the root and not the branch, this is the gate where the principle subsumes the phenomenon: it is merely the true reality rather than a conjunction of conditions.

If one considers the beginning and the end as being subordinate, then because principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*) are of one substance and their boundaries cannot be divided—just as water in its entirety is the waves, or as when a vessel is lifted it is but solid gold—who could establish a limit between them?
Even if the King of Geese possessed the power to separate milk from water, he could not distinguish between the waves and the water;
this is even more so [in the case of principle and phenomena]. Nevertheless, among these three meanings, the essential point lies in the third, not the preceding ones.

The two meanings also cannot establish the third meaning; therefore, I shall clarify this fully. If one were to equate them, it should be understood that this would be reconciled as the central tenet of the *Apochong-ron* (Treatise on the Non-transmigration of Dharmas).
Commentary: "To investigate" means to investigate the reason why five names share a single meaning. Commentary:
"Whether form or mind" means that form and mind encompass all phenomena, both defiled and pure. All such phenomena arise through the convergence of causes and conditions.
A cause lacks the power to produce [an effect] alone; it possesses the principle of producing [an effect] through shared power. Conditions are likewise.

This refers to the sense that there is the meaning of "arising" as explained according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Therefore, the second fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* translated during the Tang dynasty states:

"It is only in accordance with worldly convention that one speaks of arising and ceasing. By relying on this convention, one enters the supreme ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), such as the true nature of emptiness and so forth."
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the cause of causes and so forth," the cause of a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is the direct productive cause in relation to its conditions.

For example, a grain sprout arises from a grain seed, and visual consciousness arises from the seed of consciousness, and so on. As for "the cause of cause and effect," this clarifies the cause that produces phenomena in relation to the effect;
all causal conditions are such causes. Regarding the passage beginning with "Because there is no... [it] explains that what has not yet arisen does not exist.
This means that since all phenomena arise only through the convergence of conditions, one should know that phenomena which have not yet converged are fundamentally non-existent.

Because such phenomena have never existed, there is no basis for them; this refers to their lack of logical consistency. Regarding the subsequent phrase "and so forth," let us first investigate through inferential cognition (*anumāna*):
since all phenomena arise from the convergence of their own conditions, at the time when the four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) undergo transition and cessation and the conditions disperse—
"Phenomena (*dharma*) are destined to perish and fade away. Therefore, Aśvajit said: "All phenomena arise from conditions; when conditions cease, phenomena likewise pass away. Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "truly [not existent]" (*zhen wei*): since phenomena arise from conditions and cannot originate of themselves, whether they arise or perish, it all depends upon conditions.
The characteristic of dependent origination is not truly existent. If phenomena were truly existent, they would not depend upon conditions, nor would they [arise or perish].
"Already arisen, yet there is nothing that shall perish. This refers to the text from the *Wu zhen kong lun* (Treatise on the Non-True Emptiness) and the fourth fascicle of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "The end reveals the root," etc.: phenomena that currently exist through dependent origination are the "end"; the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature is the "root.

As for the phrase "how could one wait," it means that union and separation occur simultaneously; because the nature of causes and conditions is empty, within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is neither conjunction nor...
Dissipated. Thus, its nature is primordial. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that the nature of all phenomena is originally empty and quiescent.
"Qīngliáng" (Cooling) was the title bestowed by Emperor Dēzōng of the Táng dynasty. Therefore, the epitaph for Master Pèi says:
"He was able to cool the Emperor’s mind with the Holy Dharma," and consequently, he was granted the title of National Teacher Qīngliáng. Beholding his resolute conduct, he stood out as preeminent.

Leaving the crowd behind, he served as a teacher to emperors and kings; he was truly a sage. Master Dahui Zonggao called him the "Holy Teacher" (*shengshi*), just as the Eye of the True Dharma describes him.
The passage cited here is from the *Xuantan chao* (Notes on Hanging Discourses).

Commentary: "Below 'True Emptiness' (zhēnkōng)" means that phenomena have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); they take only true emptiness as their nature. It is like waves taking water as their nature.

Commentary: "And so forth" means that within this emptiness of nature, there is no form (*rūpa*), nor sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so on.
All phenomena, whether mundane or supramundane, arise from causes and conditions; they possess neither marks nor are they markless.
To be free from these various marks is what is called the "true mark" (bhūtalakṣaṇa).

[Commentary: Regarding the section "The collection of conditions" (*pratyayasāmagrī*) below: Question—In the *Śāstra*, it only explains that the true mark is non-existent in itself; why then does the *Vivaraṇa* rely upon dependent origination?

[Question: To resolve this doubt, [the author] replies: "It is because of a single principle," as previously stated in the section on "Original Non-existence" (*benwu*). The phrase "such as a mirror" and so forth uses metaphors to reveal the Dharma.
Images in a mirror and echoes in a valley also arise dependent upon conditions; their nature and characteristics are fundamentally empty.

The term "pushing away and refuting" means to investigate, reject, and disparage [them]. The passage beginning with "How could it wait... is also from the *Wu zhen kong* (Non-True Emptiness) chapter of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 18.
It says: "The nature of all dharmas is eternally empty of itself; it is not empty because of observing it through wisdom and skillful means," and so forth.

This distinguishes [the Mahayana] from the lower [vehicle]. That is to say, the followers of the Small Vehicle do not recognize the principle of the emptiness of essence; they rely on the analytical discernment of wisdom to break down material phenomena (rūpa-dharma) down to the limit of the infinitesimal atom (*paramāṇu*) before finally perceiving the principle of emptiness.
In the Mahayana, one realizes that matter and mind are produced by causes and conditions, and are thus both existent and empty.

Regarding the "enumeration of names" and so forth: this refers to the meaning of enumerating and explaining names within the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*. Although the explanations occur sequentially, the phenomena (*dharma*) themselves must exist simultaneously.
Because there are five names, they are not one; because they refer to the same meaning, they are not different.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "in various sūtras and śāstras," the seventh fascicle of the *Prabhāvatī* (The Radiant Light) states: "That which belongs to the twelve links of dependent origination has no agent;
that which belongs to the six pāramitās also has no agent. For this reason, all dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent.

This means that, below the terms "existence" and "non-existence," [dharmas] exist because they arise through conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*), yet they are non-existent because their nature is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). These two occur simultaneously.
Therefore, it is both existent and non-existent; because they mutually negate one another, it is neither existent nor non-existent.

These four propositions are fully detailed in the subsequent treatise, though I fear that citing the full text here would be too prolix. Furthermore, regarding the refutation of these views, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on Great Wisdom), fascicle 65, states:
"There are those who say that all phenomena have four characteristics: first, they assert existence; second, they assert non-existence; third, they assert both existence and non-existence; fourth..."
This refers to that which is neither existent nor non-existent. Within this context, erroneous recollection and attachment to these four dharmas is called the "false path.
Because of correct recollection within this context, one does not attach to these four; this is called the "right path. Regarding the "refutation of slander":

to reckon that all dharmas are existent is to fall into the slander of superimposition (*samāropa*); therefore, it is refuted by saying they are "not existent. To reckon that all dharmas are non-existent is to fall into the slander of denial (*apavāda*).
Therefore, it is refuted by saying "it is not non-existent. Furthermore, those who reckon that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent fall into the slander of conceptual proliferation;

therefore, it is refuted by saying "it is not neither existent nor non-existent. Moreover, those who reckon that all phenomena are both existent and non-existent fall into the slander of contradiction;

therefore, it is refuted by saying "it is not both existent and non-existent. It is because of the third alternative that this reckoning arises, namely, upon hearing the previous statement "not neither existent."
The calculation [of the opponent] says: "Non- is not 'is. 'Is' is said when there is existence. Hearing the previous statement, "Non- is not non-existence," the calculation says:

"Non- is not 'is. 'Non-' is said when there is non-existence. Now it is said: "Because you calculate that there is neither existence nor non-existence, I refute it by saying: 'Non- is not non-existence.'"

It is not that it is not non-existent. Who would say that "not non-existent" means it is existent? "Not non-existent" means it is non-existent; therefore, it is said to be neither existent nor non-existent.

This explanation, including the phrasing of the sentences, is largely the same as, yet slightly different from, the *Qixinlun shu* (Commentary on the Awakening of Faith), for the purpose of conforming to the four types of false attachment (*catur-apavāda*).

If the principle can be made to accord, then it is acceptable. The reason for citing this phrase below is to clarify the rejection of the two views and so forth, as will be understood from the discussion below.
However, upon careful examination of the four treatises, they are all extracted from within this very sentence.
The meaning of each word in the Dharma is infinite. Thus, the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* states:
"What I have spoken is speech of meaning, not of words; what sentient beings speak is speech of words, not of meaning. How true these words are!

Commentary: The first section, "Regarding the Following," refers to the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* (Treatise on the Buddha-nature) composed by Vasubandhu. It explains the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* and establishes the doctrine of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and Buddha-nature.

"All views" refers to those of annihilationism, eternalism, identity, difference, and so forth; the preceding four positions also constitute four views because they arise from [the conceptualization of] existence and non-existence.
These are predominantly found among the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). All that has been cited is entirely from the treatise itself. As for the text...
This is easy to see; I shall now explain it according to the difficulties. Regarding the phrase "all things are without cause" and so forth:

this refers to not knowing that the causes cultivated in a previous life induce the fruits of the present life, and that the causes established in the present life again summon retribution in the future. To "negate" (撥) means to reject or cast aside; it is a term for disbelief.
This is identical to the "spontaneous existence" (*zìrán*) of Zhuangzi and Laozi. Thus, when Zhuangzi discussed the wind, he said: "It rises up in a whirling gust from the north."
When one enters the Southern Sea from the sea, who maintains this? Who fans and breathes upon it? This refers to "naturalness" (*ziran*).

As for those with "annihilationist views" (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), they believe that there are only the present five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and other such phenomena, and that there is no further continuity of retribution in future lives.

This is similar to the Confucian school, which calculates only the existence of a single lifetime and does not speak of other worlds. As the *Shun Dian* says: "The Emperor then passed away. [End of] Exegesis.
The term "zu" (殂) means "to depart. It signifies that the *ātmā* (魂) of Yao departed for heaven. The term "luo" (落) signifies that the *bhūta* (魄) of Yao descended to earth.
Thus, Li Sishen of the Tang dynasty stated in his discourse: "Upon death, one returns to and merges with heaven and earth; there is no continuation, nor does anything remain.
Following this, if one explains it by correlating the two lines as opposites: because there is the persistence of birth, there arises the nihilism of the heterodox. However, this heterodox nihilism—

Both views are non-views. Therefore, they are explained according to the *Buddhatva-śāstra*. In the passage from the Sūtra below, it can be understood that [the ultimate] converges upon being neither existent nor non-existent.

The Commentary states: "Phenomena are dependent" means that "dependent" (*yin*) implies "waiting for" (*dai*). This commentary explains this by drawing upon the meanings of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra*. Regarding the *Laṅkā*: [...]
Gā said: "Mahāmati, it is the same with the horns of a rabbit. In relation to the horns of an ox, one says those [rabbit] horns do not exist.

Regarding the *Ghanavyūha*, this refers to the verse at the beginning of the second fascicle of that sutra; the subsequent citation of the *Ghanavyūha* also follows the verse immediately preceding it, which is easy to understand.
"How magnificent! and so forth, concludes the praise for its skillful means. In each of the three previous instances, he explained that things are neither existent nor non-existent. Each...
There is scriptural authority. This means that it exhaustively explores the subtle mysteries of the Buddhist scriptures.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Explaining through the perspective of contemplative practice (*guanxing*)," the intended meaning is as follows: Once the two types of grasping (*erzhi*) have been eliminated and the two types of views (*erjian*) have likewise vanished, the Dharma is neither existent nor non-existent, and correct understanding (*zhengjie*) manifests before one.
By relying on this understanding to cultivate practice, one may realize the true reality (*shixiang*). Having understanding without practice is likened to having eyes but no feet.
Those without feet cannot reach the place of jewels even when gazing at it from afar. Thus, the "Chapter on the Inquiry into Wisdom" (*Prajñāparipṛcchā*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"It is like a person who prepares a delicious meal but starves himself and does not eat; likewise, one who hears much but does not practice the Dharma is the same.

If there is practice without understanding, it is like a blind man traveling to a distant land—he cannot avoid the peril of falling into pits and ravines. Therefore, the Master of the Treatise demonstrates contemplation at this point.

It is practice (*caryā*). How do we know this? Because the *Śāstra* says: "Observing phenomena, one does not dwell in non-existence; observing existence, one does not grasp at marks. What else could this be but practice?
However, the intent of the *Śāstra* is subtle and hidden, not revealing its face; those who explain it with superficial minds have strayed far from it.
As for "the Dharma is equal," although the Dharma pervades all things, here it is discussed in terms of practice and thus pertains to the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*).
This concerns the Dharma. According to the commentaries, the Dharma encompasses both good and evil: good that accords with principle, such as the three trainings and the six perfections;
and evil that opposes principle, such as the five heinous crimes and the ten non-virtues. Here, these good and evil dharmas are explained in contrast to one another.

If it were said that all phenomena arise through conditions and their nature is fundamentally empty, then the actions of good and evil would necessarily have no results. Yet, when we observe the Dharma, although it is without [intrinsic existence],...
One does not grasp at non-existence. Although evil is empty, it must be severed; although goodness is empty, it must be cultivated.
Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "There is no self, no agent, and no experiencer; yet the karma of good and evil does not perish. This refers to contemplating emptiness without grasping.
When the mind has no attachments, one perceives the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) within all phenomena. Regarding the passage "not grasping at marks," the general meaning is as follows:

if the mind gives rise to attachment toward phenomena, then even though one cultivates the practices of the three trainings, such as *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the mind of arising and ceasing will be unable to forget its marks.
How, then, could one accord with the Truth? Regarding the phrase "it is because [one does not]," this means not grasping at existence; thus, one acts within existence all day long.
It has never dwelled in signs; in establishing merit and virtue and promoting the good without omission, it accords perfectly with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 15, states: "The true mark of the Buddha-dharma is neither existent nor non-existent, neither accepted nor clung to.

The commentary explains: "Whether accepting or clinging, this does not accord with reality. 'Mi' means 'not. The remaining terms are understandable. Regarding the word "zhong" (middle) herein, I shall now briefly explain it.

This is explained as follows: The first phrase is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). To contemplate without retaining emptiness is "stopping by realizing the true nature" (*tattva-śamatha*).

This is called "below. The second phrase is the contemplation of existence; not grasping at the marks of existence is "stopping that accords with conditions through skillful means" (*upāya-anu-pratyaya-śamatha*).

If one takes both phrases as the middle way between stopping and contemplating: contemplating non-existence without retaining non-existence is "existence within non-existence"; contemplating existence without grasping its marks is "non-existence within existence. This is called...

To view existence and non-existence as equal and to depart from the conceptualization of the two extremes is *śamatha* (calm abiding). This is explained in detail in works such as the *Tiantai Zhiguan* and the *Huayan Jiaozhi*.
In the twentieth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the three great principles of concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are correlated with these:

concentration corresponds to *śamatha*, wisdom corresponds to *vipaśyanā* (insight), and the equality of concentration and wisdom is called equanimity. This equanimity is precisely the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* of the Middle Way herein. However...

This treatise encompasses both the mind and its objects. While *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, as well as meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), pertain to the mind, their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are particularly numerous, and their realization of principle is profound and subtle;
thus, those who cultivate the mind must not fail to study them. These are explained in detail in the thirty-third and thirty-first chapters of that sutra.
To present the general outline here, it says: "Good son, the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages possess great power of wisdom and samādhi."
Their power is slight; for this reason, they cannot clearly perceive the Buddha-nature. Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas possess great power of samādhi but little power of wisdom;

by these causes and conditions, they do not see the Buddha-nature. Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have equilibrium between concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), they clearly perceive the Buddha-nature with perfect clarity and without obstruction.
Furthermore, it is said: *śamatha* is called "quiescence," which is concentration (*samādhi*). *Vipaśyanā*...
*Vipaśyanā* means right view; it is wisdom (*prajñā*). *Upekṣā* means equanimity; it is relinquishment (*tyāga*).

Relinquishment is the Middle Way of calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*). The phrase "the three meanings above are equal" explains the name [of the teaching] as being neither existent nor non-existent. Question:
Both of the preceding two interpretations are free from these two faults. What is their distinction? The answer is: the first is free from the two views of eternalism and nihilism;

these two arise because the two views of existence and non-existence regarding causes are activated. Thus, the third chapter of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "To hold that things definitely exist is to cling to eternalism;

to hold that they definitely do not exist is to cling to nihilism," and so forth. The second [interpretation] merely eliminates the two extreme views of existence and non-existence; therefore, it does not...
The same. A detailed discussion will clarify this; it is not a forced or artificial interpretation.

Commentary: Regarding "sages" (*ārya*), according to the *Awakening of Faith*, those who have already abandoned the grasping and conceptualization of names and perceive even a small portion of the Dharmakāya are also called sages.
In the teachings of Xianshou, the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) translated during the Liang dynasty is cited, stating that from the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) onward...

They are called "sages" (ārya). According to the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school, one is only designated a sage upon attaining non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) at the time of ascending to the first stage (*bhūmi*).
The treatise states that sages encompass both cause and fruit; however, those below the stages are included here according to the *Awakening of Faith* (Śraddhotpāda-śāstra).
This *Xinxin Fen* (Chapter on Cultivating Faith) is explained according to sentient beings who have not yet entered the stage of the "determined group" (*niyata-rāśi*).

In that treatise, those from the Ten Abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) upward are considered to have entered the determined group, while those within the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) are considered the undetermined group (*aniyata-rāśi*).

This [undetermined group] itself possesses five practices, the fifth of which is named the Gate of Calm Abiding and Contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā-mukha*). Therefore, that treatise states: "If one cultivates..."
Regarding "stopping" (*śamatha*): it means dwelling in a quiet place, sitting upright with a correct mind, and eliminating all thoughts as they arise through mindfulness.

It continues until it says that through long cultivation and thorough maturation, the mind attains stability; gradually becoming sharp and intense, one enters in accordance with the *tathatā-samādhi* (samādhi of suchness) and so forth.
This refers to a practitioner of the Nature School (*Xingzong*) who, although fully possessed of the fetters of afflictions...

If a person has, in previous lives, cultivated the power of hearing and seeing within this school, they will certainly be intelligent and sagacious in this life, becoming a vessel for the complete understanding [of the Dharma].
They may also apply their minds to and practice within these modes of non-abiding conduct.
Question: Why does the treatise cite "sages"? Answer: The present citation of "equals" refers to the general model and standard pattern.

Commentary: "Etc. refers to what follows below. It means that the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) is one; yet when the three vehicles observe it, each obtains a distinct fruit according to their respective capacities.
For instance, when the śrāvakas observe it, they obtain the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, and so forth.

The reason for this is that those who might not understand could see the differences between the small and great [vehicles] among the three vehicles and conclude that the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) itself is also different. This point will become clear of its own accord in the *Nirvāṇa-śāstra*. It is not [the case that the reality differs].

This is a detailed explanation that fails to understand what follows below; it is an interpretation based on the doctrine of the Nature School (Xingzong) regarding newly perfumed seeds (*navasaṃskāra*). The *Dàcǎo* (Great Commentary), fascicle five, states:

"It is said that because sentient beings encounter conditions and undergo perfuming, there are five [categories] due to the existence of the seeds of the three vehicles, as well as those of indefinite lineage and those without nature."
Why is this? If one associates exclusively with śrāvakas, one becomes fixed in the nature of a śrāvaka; if one associates with pratyekabuddhas, one becomes fixed in the nature of a pratyekabuddha;
and if one associates with bodhisattvas, one becomes fixed in the nature of a bodhisattva. If one associates with all three vehicles, one becomes a person of indeterminate nature.
If one does not associate with any of the three vehicles at all, one becomes one who lacks the [spiritual] nature, making them extremely difficult to transform and teach. Therefore...
Know that through the process of perfuming (*vāsanā*), five types of natures are formed; as for their primordial existence, there is no duality.

[Commentary: Regarding "right and wrong" and so forth: for example, when practicing the contemplation of the Pure Land, even if one simultaneously practices the contemplation of Tuṣita Heaven, it is considered wrong.

This is because the mind’s engagement with mixed conceptions harms one's rebirth [in the Pure Land]. Now, taking the true reality (*dharmatā*) as the right contemplation, then all phenomenal appearances...
These characteristics are all erroneous. As for the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is the *Prajñā-śāstra*. Its fifth fascicle states:
"Furthermore, with the exception of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, everything remaining is entirely termed 'Māra'. The text is extensive, so I have not cited it in full.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "There are two explanations regarding this," etc.: among the three vehicles, the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) are those who study the dharma-emptiness through the *prajñāpāramitā* and other teachings.

Because these two vehicles cultivate contemplations of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and so forth, they have not yet reached the principle of the true mark of intrinsic emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā-tathatā*).
Consequently, they remain stuck within the four inversions of the phenomenal level and are unable to realize the path and fruit of their own vehicle. This refers to the minor fruits as well.
One must see emptiness; then the two [aspects] can be known. "Now, below this" refers to those for whom the Tripitaka Teaching is intended.
Those who do not penetrate the emptiness of phenomena are called "foolish-dharma" practitioners. The rest is understandable. Regarding the *Great Commentary* (*Dàshū*) and so forth:

in its analysis of the teachings, that commentary states that the lay practitioner Liu Qiu of the Song dynasty and the Dharma Master Huiguan of Daochang Monastery established five periods within the gradual teaching.

Regarding this teaching: first is the teaching with characteristics (*sanimitta-śāsana*), which means that one attains the Way by contemplating existence. The *Qingliang shu* (Commentary of Qingliang) states:

"This contradicts the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* itself. That treatise says: "I now [abide] therein. The intent of the commentary is that even the "Dull-Witted" (*hīnayāna*) school contemplates the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) and thereby realizes it.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the emptiness of beings" and so forth: within the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), there is neither self nor phenomena. Yet sentient beings delusively conceptualize and cling to them as existing.

The followers of the Lesser Vehicle merely realize that there is no self within the aggregates (*skandha*); they perceive only a partial truth. If one realizes that both persons and phenomena are empty, [one perceives the complete truth].

The emptiness of nature (prakṛti-śūnyatā) manifests in its entirety. This distinction between the single and the dual depends on the person; it is not that the emptiness of nature itself differs. [Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "that which is pursued" (*suo qu*), "pursued" means to incline toward. Regarding the phrase "the vessel has," this explains the difference between the Great and the Small Vehicles. There are five pairs of categories in total.

The vessel of the Mahāyāna is vast, meaning that it gives rise to the great resolve and practices the great deeds, among other things. The vessel of the Hīnayāna is narrow; it can be known that its resolve, practices, and so forth are all inferior.

The *prajñā* of the Hīnayāna, which realizes the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), is shallow; the *prajñā* of the Mahāyāna, which realizes the twofold emptiness (*ubhaya-śūnyatā*), is profound.

The sheep and deer carts of the Hīnayāna are capable only of carrying oneself; the ox carts of the Mahāyāna possess the power to carry both self and others, bearing heavy burdens and traveling great distances.
"Remote. If the great arises from the small, it is called "detouring"; if it does not arise from the small, it is called "direct.

The Hīnayāna merely realizes the principle of solitary emptiness, whereas the Mahāyāna deeply realizes the twofold emptiness. This is a brief explanation. If we consider this in terms of the two types of grasping and the two obstacles:
To extract and detail every point from the various scriptural teachings would indeed be tedious and cumbersome.

Regarding the phrase "dual citation" (*shuangdie*) and so forth: these two names appear in all the sūtras; it is not necessary to cite them specifically. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (translated by Kumārajīva), it says:

"Mahā" means "Great" in the language of Qin; "Prajñā" means "Wisdom" (*hui*) in the language of Qin. However, this "wisdom" (*hui*) refers to "insight-wisdom" (*zhìhuì*), which is not the same as the technical definition of dharmas (*fǎxiàng*).
In the causal stage it is called *prajñā* (wisdom), while in the resultant stage it is called *jñāna* (knowledge). Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "What is wisdom? and answers:
"Because *prajñāpāramitā* encompasses all forms of wisdom. Furthermore, in the forty-third [chapter], it is translated as "wisdom. Regarding *upāya*:
the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* states that *upāyakauśalya* is the complete Sanskrit term. In a single thought-moment...
[The character] "Below" (*ge*) explains the great meaning. Within a single thought-moment, the provisional and the real flow together as two, illuminating the non-dual realm of the two truths;
it is only the wisdom of the Middle Way that constitutes "Great Wisdom. It should properly be called "Great Wisdom," but for the sake of metrical fluency, it is termed "Great Wisdom" (*da-hui*).
By this reasoning, even the wisdom of the dual emptiness is not yet "great," because it illuminates the conventional and the ultimate separately.
If one can encompass both in a single thought-moment, how much more so for the two vehicles' realization of the emptiness of persons? Therefore, the Commentary says this. "Ying" means excellence;
it also means emergence. The rest may be understood.

Commentary: Following the first two phrases, some versions read, "the true mark of all phenomena" (*dharmāṇāṃ bhūtalakṣaṇam*). This is a significant error regarding the correct principle. Although "true mark" is a general term, it is *prajñā* that provides a detailed discussion;
its meaning refers to the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), as stated below: "The gate of *prajñā* contemplates emptiness," and so forth.
The true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) encompasses both principle (li) and wisdom (zhi). Now, wisdom is taken as the subject that perceives, and principle as the object perceived.

Because one perceives the principle of the true mark of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, prajñā is established. As the subsequent treatise states: "Although the myriad dharmas are real, they cannot be attained without illumination."

The internal and external aspects mutually contribute to the accomplishment of their illuminating function, which is equal [to that of the Buddha]. If the true mark (*dharmatā*) is itself *prajñā*, then whom would one further seek to realize?
Furthermore, this also contrasts with the subsequent passage on skillful means (*upāya*), as their force differs; this may be investigated in detail.

Regarding the latter two phrases, because a single thought-moment possesses both [wisdom and compassion], the contemplation of emptiness does not take the form of a realization. It is not that wisdom precedes compassion.

Subsequently, he further cites [scriptures] to ensure they do not stagnate in quiescence. Regarding "those who have emerged from the Two Vehicles": because they weary of and abandon the realm with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) to enter the realm without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*), they sink forever and do not arise again.

Therefore, the sub-commentary below cryptically cites both the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, both of which clarify that the followers of the Two Vehicles are addicted to extinction (*nirodha*).
The third chapter of the *Laṅkāvatāra* states: "Intoxicated by the wine of samādhi, they abide in the outflow-free (*anāsrava*)."
The realm. That is not the ultimate destination, yet it is also not a state from which one falls back. Because they have attained the body of samādhi, they remain unawakened for as long as an eon.
It is like a person who is intoxicated; only after the wine has worn off do they regain their senses. The śrāvakas are also like this: after awakening, they shall attain Buddhahood.
The "Chapter on the Appearance" states: "O Son of the Buddha, the Great King of Medicine Tree of the Tathāgata’s wisdom excludes only two places."
It is able to bring about growth and benefit, specifically for those of the Two Vehicles who have fallen into the vast and deep pit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
as explained in detail below in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*.
Commentary: Furthermore, at the beginning [of the text], one should carefully examine the intent of the sūtras and śāstras. There are two kinds of skillful means (*upāya*):
first, the departure from signs; second, the transformation of sentient beings. This refers to taking great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) for the benefit of others as the skillful means.

Regarding the latter two [points] below, it means that while dwelling within the realm of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and extensively practicing transformation and benefit, one is not defiled by sensory desires. This is because, through the wisdom of compassion itself and objectless loving-kindness (*apraṇihita-maitrī*), one realizes...

The realm of sentient beings is empty; though they are delivered, there is no one delivered. Thus, defilement is not perceived. If taking the departure from marks (*animitta*) as a skillful means (*upāya*), it may also be said that compassion and wisdom serve as mutual skillful means.
Regarding the section following "Pure Name," the scriptural text is quite extensive; it is summarized here as follows:

Adorning the Buddha-lands and bringing sentient beings to maturity with a mind of craving and views, while self-disciplining within the states of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
...and thus remains subdued. This is called "bondage by wisdom lacking skillful means. The commentary explains:

here, taking the planting of the roots of all virtues as wisdom, one cultivates them within a mind of craving and views; because one cannot transcend conceptual construction, it becomes bondage. As the Sūtra says:

"One does not adorn the Buddha-lands with a mind of craving and views," which is called "liberation through wisdom accompanied by skillful means" (and so forth). Furthermore, one contemplates the body as impermanent.

Suffering, emptiness, and non-self are called wisdom (*prajñā*). Although the body possesses illness and one remains constantly within *saṃsāra*, to benefit all beings without weariness is called skillful means (*upāya*), and so forth.
The commentary states: the former is called skillful means because it is free from signs; this is called skillful means because it involves the transformation of beings (*nirmāṇa*).
The treatise takes up this transformation of beings. Regarding "lacking wisdom," "love" refers to compassionate love (*karuṇā-preman*). As for "view"...
This refers to attachment. It means regarding the realm of sentient beings as oneself or as one's kin;
seeing those who can be transformed, one does not become weary of transforming them alone, but rather becomes entangled by the net of views. "Sinking" refers to being submerged;

because the realm of birth and death is like a forest, one fails to understand that dharmas are without conditions or objects, and thus this results in compassion characterized by signs (*nimitta*). "Desire" refers to craving; it is called so because it defiles and sullies the pure mind.
The five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). These five objects are the spheres desired by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding the commentary’s statement that "Nirvāṇa is emptiness": this is said because it is contrasted with saṃsāra, which is taken as existence.

However, there are many gateways to emptiness, and they differ according to their respective schools. Here, following the intent of the treatise, it is stated thus. Below the latter four lines, the first two lines establish what precedes.
It is unstained by worldly entanglements. The latter two phrases establish the former capacity for non-manifestation and non-verification.

As for the dual fusion of the two wisdoms, it is because the non-dual essence is possessed within a single thought-moment. Regarding the non-duality of emptiness and existence: that which is dependently originated and devoid of intrinsic nature is itself nirvāṇa.
The arising of non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāva*) is itself birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). There are only two distinct meanings, yet no dual substance. Thus, the *Dharmadhātunirviśeṣa-śāstra* states:
"One should know that the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*), when purified, is the Dharmakāya; the Dharmakāya is Nirvāṇa; and Nirvāṇa is the Tathāgata.
Regarding the term "momentary" (*piērán*): the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as a "brief glance. Here, we take it to mean a single thought-moment or a short duration of time.

The meaning is as follows: when a Bodhisattva perceives form, he does not perceive it as anything other than emptiness. This is like a skilled butcher who, looking at an ox, sees no whole ox before his eyes.

The subsequent phrase, which is the reverse of this, explains the statement regarding "not being weary of existence" and so forth; it is like when one contemplates emptiness, emptiness itself is form.
Since one does not depart from form, how could one ever momentarily stagnate in emptiness? "Fu" (符) means to accord with; "zi" (資) means to rely upon, to draw support from, or to assist.
For those who practice the Dharma of the Nature School (Xingzong), when first studying this teaching, they must cultivate compassion and impartiality to achieve the practice of non-abiding.
If one adheres exclusively to a single practice, one immediately sinks into the level of the ordinary and the small; this can be understood through analogy.

From the perspective of the gate of principle (li), if one does not cultivate spiritual practice (lixing), there is no means to cut through the dense forest of birth and death or to roam the wondrous garden of nirvana.

If one does not cultivate phenomenal practice (shixing), there is no means to adorn the pure Buddha-lands or to exhaustively transform sentient beings who are steeped in defilement. Regarding the gate of principle, it refers to the wisdom of principle (li-liang) and the wisdom of phenomena (shi-liang).
The explanation of the meanings of *saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa* is as before.

In the commentary, the phrase "recollection" (*smṛti*) explains two senses of recollection: first, recollection that is endowed with wisdom is called "wisdom-recollection"; it is not that recollection itself is wisdom.
Second, even the most minimal single thought-moment—meaning the sudden arising of a thought—is also called a "single thought-moment. This refers to the wisdom of phenomena (*vastu-jñāna*).

It is called *quán* (expediency). It shifts and transforms along with things, following whatever is appropriate. Therefore, *quán* possesses distinctions such as contrariety and conformity, concealment and manifestation, as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
For instance, killing a Brahmin of false views is contrary to the norm, yet it is *quán*; it is *quán*.

In the *Mahākaruṇā-sāgara-megha Sūtra*, the rishi did not eat the rabbit that offered its own flesh to him; instead, he entered the fire and died. This is conforming to the norm; it is the constant. Confucianists regard this as *quán*.

This is to oppose the conventional text while conforming to the Way. For example, as Mencius said: "Men and women do not touch one another when giving or receiving; this is the constant rule of ritual (*li*).

To rescue a sister-in-law drowning by reaching out one's hand is the discretionary application of righteousness (*yi*). In the Inner Teaching, observing the precepts and maintaining faith so as not to transgress even unto death is the constant rule.

The benefits realized through the precepts of the Mahāyāna are immediately manifested; this is expedient means (*upāya*). Now, it is said that when engaging in activities for the benefit of sentient beings, one should be appropriate to both the Small and Great Vehicles, and appropriate to both the manifest and the esoteric.

Because its myriad transformations and thousandfold changes cannot be standardized by a single rule, it is called "expedient wisdom" (*upāya-jñāna*). "Ultimate wisdom" (*prajñā-jñāna*) is termed "reality."
Because one illuminates the principle of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) and is free from false discrimination, the wisdom is praised as "sublime.

This is because within a single thought-moment, the two wisdoms are not in conflict, simultaneously observing the profound principles of the two truths (satyadvaya). This cannot be described by words;
it can only be emulated by those who apply their efforts over a long period. Therefore, the text below encourages one to "reflect well."
Commentary: Regarding "Huàfàn" (Chinese-Sanskrit): "Huà" refers to China, that is, this world of Zhōushén Dàxià. "Miè" (extinction) and "jìn" (exhaustion) are similar in meaning.
The exhaustion of accumulated burdens is called the Truth of Extinction (*nirodha-satya*). This means it is a profound truth and is also real; that is, suffering is truly suffering, and so forth.

Commentary: Regarding "binding afflictions" (*saṃyojana*), this specifically refers to the various delusions; both the seeds and the manifest states of the two types of grasping—self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*)—are collectively the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

Furthermore, it also includes all karmic actions that increase the cycle of birth and death, which are termed "origination. Regarding "resolving principles" (*li-lie*): "principle" (*li*) means "to govern" (*zhi*).

Commentary: Regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*): the affliction of the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) form and mind is called suffering. These three—first, afflictions (*kleśa*); second, karmic bonds (*karman*); and third, birth and death (*saṃsāra*)—are gathered together within a single body; therefore, it is said to be "mixed. The three obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) will be explained below. Now, regarding the phrase "in terms of the path of counteraction" (*pratipakṣa-mārga*), "counteraction" means cultivation and purification. Because these three have been completely eliminated through such counteraction, [the text says this]. As for the section beginning "if explained separately," [it follows as]: The Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) consists of the two types of karma and afflictions. Karma refers to the various actions performed by body, speech, and mind. Afflictions refer to the various mental states that disturb the mind. The Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is the extinction of the aforementioned suffering and origination. It is of two kinds: first, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is the permanent severance of the seeds of afflictions through the power of wisdom; second, non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is the permanent non-arising of phenomena due to the lack of necessary conditions. The Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) refers to the various paths of cultivation that can eliminate the aforementioned suffering and origination. It is of two kinds: first, the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*), which is the path of cultivation that can eliminate the defilements of the Desire Realm; second, the supramundane path (*lokottara-mārga*), which is the path of cultivation that can eliminate the defilements of the Form and Formless Realms. The Truth of the Fruit (*phala-satya*) refers to the various fruits of the path that are attained when the aforementioned suffering and origination are extinguished. It is of four kinds: first, the fruit of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna-phala*); second, the fruit of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*); third, the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmi-phala*); and fourth, the fruit of Arhatship (*arhat-phala*). The first three are called "fruits with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa-phala*), because although the afflictions have been severed, the remaining aggregates still exist. The last one is called the "fruit without remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa-phala*), because both the afflictions and the aggregates have been exhausted. Furthermore, there are two kinds of fruits: first, the fruit of liberation (*vimukti-phala*), which is the fruit of the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) attained through the power of the supramundane path; second, the fruit of mastery (*vaśitā-phala*), which is the fruit of the exhaustion of the outflows attained through the power of the mundane path. This is what is meant by the "Truth of the Fruit. The above is a general explanation of the Four Noble Truths.
