This is according to the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*. The treatise is extensive; here it is summarized:

"An ordinary person at the stage of the ten faiths, becoming aware that an evil thought has arisen in the preceding moment, is thus able to arrest the succeeding thought so that it does not arise. This is the power of the stage of faith to extinguish [afflictions]. Regarding the phrase "delusions exist below":

fundamental delusions arise from being confused about the principle (*li*). As the treatise states: "Because one does not know, as they truly are, that the dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is one. (Guifeng’s summary).

The Sub-commentary (*Chao*) explains: "No" means "non-existent. "Awakening" (*jue*) means "clarity," which refers to fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). "Branches and tips" refers to that which arises from delusion regarding phenomena.
However, this is a general outline of the commentary; the *Śāstra* states in full: "Furthermore, based on non-awakening, three kinds of marks arise."

It is associated with and inseparable from that non-awakening (*abodha*). The three characteristics are the characteristic of activity (*karmalakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of evolution (*pravṛttilakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of manifestation (*nirbhāsalakṣaṇa*).

Non-awakening refers to ignorance (*avidyā*) among these three characteristics; this delusion is precisely the non-awakening of the secondary branches. These three characteristics are called the "three subtleties.

As for the "four grossnesses," they are: first, the characteristic of cognition (*jñānalakṣaṇa*); second, the characteristic of continuity (*anubandhalakṣaṇa*); third, the characteristic of grasping (*upādānalakṣaṇa*); and fourth, the characteristic of calculating names and forms (*nāmarūpaparikalpanālakṣaṇa*).

The characteristics [of these two types of birth and death] are explained as in that [preceding passage]. Regarding "birth and death are also of two kinds": birth and death within the realms (*dhātu*) is called "segmented" (*paricchinna*).

"Segment" (*pari*) refers to a limit; because it is either extended or brief, it possesses a fixed boundary. "Segmented" (*chinna*) refers to a physical portion; because it is either long or short, it possesses a definite measure.
Thus, the birth and death of the six destinies all belong to the segmented type. Birth and death outside the realms is termed "transformation" (*pariṇāma*).

"Transformation" (*pariṇāma*) means "to turn. It refers to turning the coarse body into a subtle substance. "Change" (*anyathībhāva*) means "to alter. It refers to altering a short lifespan into a long one.

Thus, the birth and death of all three vehicles involve both transformation and change. A detailed explanation is found elsewhere. The passage from "from the stage prior to the grounds" (*bhūmi-pūrva*) onwards is from the section on the characteristics of arising and ceasing in that same treatise.
The treatise states: "The coarsest among the coarse is the realm of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). The commentary on that passage states:

The three stages of the virtuous (trayaḥ kalyāṇa-pudgalāḥ) are called "inner ordinary beings" (*antar-prthagjana*) because they are able to awaken to this defilement. The essence of defilement is precisely the attachment to grasping and the conceptualization of a self based on names.

Furthermore, the lower treatise states: "Those who do not understand the meaning of the single dharma-realm [proceed] from the stage of faith-correspondence through observation, training, and abandonment," and so forth, up to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
The commentary (*ṭīkā*) also provides a general outline, indicating that within the path of seeing, the portion of the attachment to dharmas (*dharma-grāha*) is abandoned.

The characteristic of a distinct continuity (*pṛthag-saṃtāna-lakṣaṇa*) refers to that which has emerged from [the previous stage] and continues until the fulfillment of the mind of the seventh ground (*saptamī-bhūmi*), wherein the cognitive aspect of innate clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha-sahaja-jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) is severed.
These two types of afflictions are both termed "the subtle within the coarse" and are also called the afflictions of the *vastu-vijñāna* (phenomenal consciousness).

When these afflictions are completely severed, the *paricchinna-śarīra* (segmented existence) ceases. Regarding "from the eighth ground, etc.": the ultimate point of the ten grounds is called the "exhaustion of the grounds. This means:

In the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), the characteristic of manifestation (*nimitta*) is severed; upon entering the ninth stage, the characteristic of vision (*darśana*) is severed; and in the tenth stage, reaching the culmination at the Buddha-stage, the characteristic of karma (*karma-nimitta*) is finally severed.

At that time, the suffering of afflicted conduct (*kliṣṭa-pratipatti-duḥkha*) and the death-rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāma-vaśitā-saṃsāra*) are exhausted. These two [latter characteristics] are the coarse aspects within the subtle [characteristics].
The sphere of objects known by Bodhisattvas is the most subtle within the subtle; this is the sphere of the Buddhas. The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the commentary on "Nirvāṇa, etc.": if there were a separate location, there would have to be a limit; that which has a limit is impermanent. Regarding "the Lesser Vehicle" and below: "worlds" (śe) refers to the three periods of time;
these temporal worlds are the various characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). "Intervals" (jiàn) refers to the intermediate spaces, namely the three realms (*tridhātu*).

The outflowing (āsrava) states fall within this interval; the four characteristics (lakṣaṇa) undergo transition and cessation, and one revolves through the three periods of time (tryadhvan). This explanation encompasses all phenomena, both sentient and insentient.
If one speaks solely in terms of the primary retribution (vipākaphala), the initial activity of the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) is called birth, and their dispersal and extinction is called death;
nirvāṇa is known as that which transcends the world, for the followers of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) loathe worldly birth and death and aspire to transcendence.
Nirvāṇa. Therefore, the Mahāyāna can be understood. As for the phrase "how could they be different," it refers to the regions within and outside the realm (*dhātu*).
Regarding the passage "the nature of delusion... and so forth: because the nature of delusion and the nature of wisdom are non-dual, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states:

"When a Bodhisattva has not yet attained Buddhahood, he takes bodhi as affliction (*kleśa*); when a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, he takes affliction as bodhi. The characteristics of affliction must...
It is severed. Its nature is non-dual, which is precisely *prajñā*. Therefore, it is said that "delusions are exhausted," and so forth. Regarding "karma can [bind] below":
because karma can bind one to its fruit and thus lacks autonomy, it is called "non-liberation. When karma has passed away and retribution has vanished, there is a complete absence of bondage;
this is termed "liberation. Thus, liberation (*vimukti*) has the meaning of autonomy. Regarding "suffering can [obstruct] below": the suffering of the two kinds of birth-and-death can obstruct [it].
The Dharma-body is true bliss. Once the two types of death have been extinguished, the bliss of the Dharma-body manifests spontaneously;

this is precisely taking the absence of suffering as bliss, for there is no separate bliss apart from it. Therefore, in these cases, the three obstacles and the three virtues are described as being in direct opposition to one another.
By transforming defilement into purity, we know that the three defilements (*trimala*) are the interpretive gateways to the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

Since they are explained and indicated by relying on the gates of defilement, if the three defilements did not exist, the self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the three virtues could not be spoken of either. How, then, could there be a further state of ultimate exhaustion?
Furthermore, following the section on the three virtues, this is also explained according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The second fascicle of that sutra asks: "What is called the secret..."
The secret treasury is like the letter *i*. If its three dots were aligned horizontally, they would not form the *i*; if they were vertical, they likewise would not form it.
Only when the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara are arranged thus do they constitute the *i*. If the three dots were separate from one another, they could not form it either. I am also like this:
the dharma of liberation is not itself nirvāṇa, nor is the body of the Tathāgata itself nirvāṇa.
*Nirvāṇa*. Great *prajñā* is also not *nirvāṇa*. These three dharmas being distinct from one another is also not *nirvāṇa*. I now abide [in this state].
Because these three dharmas are for the sake of sentient beings, it is called "entering *nirvāṇa*," like the worldly letter *i*.
The commentary states: The *Chao lüe* (Abridged Commentary) says: "When combined, they form a single body; when separate, each occupies its own place. This vertically clarifies these three.
It is said: "Transcendence" (*yōng*) means that the Dharma-body is originally present; subsequently, one cultivates *prajñā*, and finally attains liberation, and so forth.

As for the four virtues, they are permanence (*nitya*), bliss (*sukha*), self (*ātman*), and purity (*śubha*). These will be explained in detail in the main treatise. Regarding the phrase "fully endowed with the meaning of the Ganges sands," it does not refer merely to the three or four virtues.
Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* states briefly: "That is to say, its own substance possesses the meaning of the great light of wisdom," and so on.

Since we have realized that present things do not depart, how could one calculate that present things migrate? Therefore, past things abide solely in the state of being past;
they cannot come to the present. Present things likewise possess the nature of emptiness this very day;
how could they reach the past? The principle of non-migration has been set forth thus far; even if the web of doubt were a thousandfold thick, it may now be dispelled.
All at once it was shattered and torn asunder. Do not resent that this public proclamation is too plain.

Regarding the passage "The *shū* [commentary] explains through antiquity and so forth": this expresses the underlying intent to clarify the principle, which is likewise manifest and easy to understand. Yao and Shun were two of the Five Emperors.
The lords of benevolence and righteousness have been praised by people down to the present day; therefore, this is cited here. Regarding the term "middle" (*madhya*) in this context:

"ancient" (*gata*) refers to the past, and "present" (*pratyutpanna*) refers to the present. By using the past and present as analogies for the future, one sees that future phenomena likewise abide within the future and do not reach the present.
Nevertheless, the time of the three periods is also a conceptual construction of the deluded discriminations of sentient beings.

It is manifested through [dependent] appearances; based on these objects, it is taught that they fundamentally lack substantial reality. Thus, the first fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* in ten fascicles states:
The Buddha addressed the King of Laṅkā: "What you call the 'past' is a mark of conceptual discrimination; the same applies to the conceptual discriminations of the 'future' and the 'present.'"
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "by means of 'now' and so forth," the force of the meaning is no different from what preceded; it is simply that the mutual perspectives differ.

One merely changes "the direction" (xiàng) to "now" (jīn), and changes "now" to "the direction. Where "coming" (lái) should be used, one uses "going" (qù); however, the character "going" should not be changed to "coming."
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "explaining the equality," this means that there is no present, nor is a past established; the same applies to the future.
As previously stated, all categories of duality—such as high and low—are mutually conditioned and mutually produced, and thus lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

In the section on "ordinary perception," the contrast between delusion and awakening is explained: ordinary perception fails to recognize that the phenomena perceived are merely manifestations of the mind itself. Because...
Arising through conditions, they are like illusions, dreams, shadows, and echoes. Within these illusions and dreams, one speaks of birth and speaks of cessation;

yet this merely serves to stir the mind of deluded discrimination regarding empty appearances. The awakened one understands that what arises from conditions is empty in nature, appearing solely as manifestations of the mind, where coming and going are without marks.
This is like two people in the same boat crossing a ravine: one perceives the shore moving while the other realizes it is the boat that is traveling; thus they differ in their views.
As for "non-mutability," who gains and who loses? One is not turned by it. In the seventh fascicle of the *Lü* (Record) previously cited below, it says:

"The deluded take that which is impermanent, non-abiding, and subject to momentary arising and ceasing to be 'transmigration. The wise, however, realize that its nature is empty and devoid of cognition;
seeing that every thought-moment is without birth, they call this 'non-transmigration. It further states: 'If one can see that dharmas are the mind...'"
Following conditions, one realizes the nature [of reality]. Not a single dharma enters from without; not a single dharma arises from within;
not a single dharma exists through combination; not a single dharma is accomplished spontaneously. Thus, one does not perceive even the slightest mark of abiding;
how much less could one observe the coming and going of the myriad dharmas? This is the thorough and ultimate clarification of the fundamental principle (and so forth). It is truly profound.

How wondrous, how truly wondrous! You should reflect inwardly and savor this. You must not look down upon the treatises and discuss mere phenomena, for you do not yet know that phenomena are themselves the principle of emptiness-nature.
To seek them solely within phenomena—claiming that the preceding sense-object is not the succeeding one, or that the preceding step is not the succeeding one—is the height of error.
Commentary: "Nanhua" refers to the book of Zhuangzi, also titled the *Nanhua Jing*. This is specifically from the chapter "Tian Zifang. As the text is extensive, it is summarized here:

"Qiu, by this day, I have passed away; my life has reached its end," and so forth. In the commentary, "cu" (徂) means "to go. It signifies that worldly conditions shift and flow, passing away day by day.
Regarding the meaning of "crossing arms" (*jiaobi*), various interpretations differ; the commentary follows the explanation of Guo Xiang.

The former interpretations may be seen as such; however, upon examining the teachings of Zhuangzi in detail, one finds that when Confucius and Yan Hui discussed the Way, its principles were profound and far-reaching, and there was also something resembling the doctrine of non-transmigration (*akṣaya*). It is regrettable that while the person has passed away, the book alone remains;
though we savor its dregs, we do not fully perceive its true essence. Those with the mental capacity to do so may yet chew upon it. — Dongpo’s "Red Cliff" (Chibi).
The *Fu* also says: Suzi said, "My guest, do you know of water and the moon? That which passes away is like this [river], yet it has never truly gone;
that which waxes and wanes is like that [moon], yet in the end there is neither decrease nor increase.
If one observes them from the perspective of their change, then even heaven and earth cannot endure for a single moment. But if one observes them from the perspective of what does not change..."
Then both things and the self are inexhaustible.
[Commentary: This concludes the preceding section. "Trace" (*zhèn*) refers to the initial manifestation. [Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "successively citing," the commentary provides a general indication. "It also applies to things": time is also a thing. *Xuānlán* (the whirlwind).
Regarding this, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Chih-lun), fascicle 11, states: "At the end of a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*), the Vairambha wind arises, blowing Mount Sumeru like withered grass.
The Great Commentary (*Ta-shu*) states: "It is also called *Svalaṇa*; these are merely variations in the weight of the Sanskrit pronunciation. It is the wind that raises clouds;

it is the wind of the north, and it is also the wind at the time of the destruction kalpa (*saṃvartakalpa*). The rest may be understood accordingly. As for the "white horse" (*baimu*), it refers to the shadow of the sun within a window opening.
It refers to flying dust. It drifts and rushes with great speed. The ancients also used it as a metaphor for the brevity of time;
as Du Fu’s poem says: "Worldly life is hurried on by the white colt. This is the traditional interpretation of the *Zhuangzi*. Furthermore, according to Yanzhai’s commentary:
"Wandering silk" (*you si*) refers to that which occasionally brushes against one's face in the air—it is invisible to the eye.

However, the motes of dust flying through a window crack appear extremely straight. Thus, the *Guchui shi* (Verses on the Drums and Pipes) says: "The sunlight within the window flies like wild horses.
This refers to their rapid movement; "shì" means the swift motion of horses. Regarding "the sun, moon, and so forth," the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "Midnight, sunset, and midday..."

The sun rises over the four continents simultaneously; that is to say, when it is midnight here in Jambudvīpa, it is sunset in Aparagoyānī in the west, midday in Uttarakuru in the north, and sunrise in Pūrvavideha in the east, and so forth. Thus, one day and night encompass the four continents.
The meaning of the remaining text is no different from what precedes.
Commentary: Regarding "emotional calculations" (*qingji*) and so forth: "dan" means emptiness; it means falsehood. Regarding "penetrating observation" (*daguan*) and so forth:

"da" means awakening; it also means to pass through. "Guan" means to see clearly; it also refers to what the Chan school calls "possessing the eye. "Ti" (body/substance) means to comprehend or to investigate. Regarding "the textual intent is already complete":
above, the intent was elaborated based on the text, and the principle has also been fully established. From this point downward, there is a comprehensive synthesis.
The inner and outer scriptures are intended to show that though the paths differ, they lead to the same destination.

[Commentary: "Lurking obstacles" contains the purport of his question. "The Brahmajāla Sūtra" refers to the preface of that sūtra. Regarding "various sūtras," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 23, states:
"Human life does not stop; it passes as swiftly as water flowing over a mountain. Though one exists today, tomorrow is difficult to guarantee."
Baoshou says: "What is meant by 'indulging the mind so that it dwells in unwholesome dharmas'? [The text] states, 'Vigorous physical form does not remain, like a galloping horse,' and so forth.

Regarding the first two phrases and so on: as stated in the second fascicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "By means of the Buddha’s gateway of teaching, one emerges from the suffering of the triple world."

This means that by hearing the teaching of the Four Noble Truths, one awakens to the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), cultivates the path of impermanence and so forth, and realizes the fruit of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and so on.

Among these, the essential point lies in the practice of impermanence and the other [aspects of the four truths]. A detailed explanation would be too prolix. Regarding the "conditions" (*pratyaya*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 18, states:
"There are two kinds of Pratyekabuddhas: first, the Solitary Realizer (*pratyekabuddha*); second, the One Awakened through Conditions (*nidānabuddha*). The Solitary Realizer..."
These are those who attain the Way in this present life; because they have awakened by themselves and did not hear it from another, they are called Pratyekabuddhas (Solitary Realizers).
Due to causes and conditions from previous lives, such a person produces wisdom alone without hearing it from another. It is like a king who goes out to play in a garden;
at dawn, he sees that the forest trees are lush with flowers and fruit, most delightful to behold. Having eaten, the king lies down to rest.
The king’s various queens and court ladies all gathered together to pluck flowers, thereby destroying the trees of the grove. When the king awoke, he saw that the grove had been ravaged;
thereupon he attained self-awakening, realizing that all things in the world are likewise impermanent and subject to decay. Having reflected thus, the mind of the untainted Path arose within him.
He severed all fetters and afflictions, attained the Way of a Pratyekabuddha, and became endowed with the six supernormal powers and other such qualities.

The commentary states: In this treatise, "realizing that objects of perception are detached" means realizing the truth. That is to say, by realizing that all phenomena arising through dependent origination are impermanent, one becomes detached from all fetters and afflictions (*saṃyojana-kleśa*) and attains untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*);
this is called "realizing the truth. While it differs slightly from the *Prajñāpāramitā* regarding causes and conditions, they are identical in their cultivation of impermanence.
A detailed explanation is provided elsewhere.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "penetrating the preceding," the former [section] also implicitly refutes [objections], and this [section] also implicitly resolves them. "Yan" (研) means to exhaustively investigate; "fu" (復) means to examine closely.
As for the expression "the provisional is the ultimate meaning," it is like discussing impermanence while secretly revealing the meaning of permanence, and so forth.

This is because permanence and impermanence arise in mutual dependence and are not separate from one another. Those with biased views understand according to their words, but upon hearing of the East, they become confused about the West. Only those with perfect vision...

"Hearing one, they know two. Regarding "Nirvāṇa" below: the ninth fascicle of the *Sūtra* states briefly that *saindhava*—which in the Western Regions is called *saindhava* and refers to four different things—is used as a name for salt, a vessel, water, and a horse. All of these are termed *saindhava*.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "this principle, etc.," one may comprehend this principle through a subtle and wondrous wisdom;

it must not be sought by following consciousness to cling to the sentiments of names, phrases, and phenomenal characteristics. In the fifth fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* (translated during the Tang dynasty), it says briefly:
"At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One, as it is said in the sūtras regarding the past and the future...'"
"The Buddhas of the present are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. How should this be understood? Is it to be accepted literally, or is there another meaning?
The Buddha told Mahāmati, "Do not accept it literally," and so forth, as explained at length.
Master Sheng was a disciple of Zhu Fatai and also studied under Master Kumārajīva. Initially, the Tripiṭaka Master Faxian produced the six-fascicle *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Its second...
In the sixth fascicle, it is stated that those who possess the icchantika nature cannot attain Buddhahood. When Master Sheng reached this point in his lecture, he offered this critique:

"Now, all beings who receive their physical form from the two polarities (Heaven and Earth) possess the primary cause for nirvana. How could it be that the class of sentient beings known as icchantikas alone cannot attain Buddhahood?

It must be that they have simply not yet been fully delivered by this sutra. At that time, Master Zhi adhered strictly to the literal text, while Master Sheng maintained the underlying principle; their debate continued for a considerable time.

The Sangha mostly followed Zhi [Dao]. Ultimately, he was dismissed by Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty. After Huiyuan was born at Huqiu, he later went to Mount Lu, where he obtained the newly translated Mahāyāna sūtras.

Master Sengsheng both lectured upon and interpreted them; whenever they reached the statement that even icchantikas possess Buddha-nature, the other masters would lower their heads and wring their hands in shame.
Initially, when Master Sengsheng was dismissed, he endured humiliation and lived on in death’s shadow, awaiting this sacred scripture. This scripture...

Upon his arrival, he testified that [the account] was not erroneous. As soon as the recitation of the sutra was finished, he entrusted it to the assembly, saying: "I have lived for the sake of this sutra;
I have endured until death for a long time (and so forth). You must propagate it well. Then, seeing his whisk falling to the ground in a flurry, he passed away.
At that time, he was titled the Bodhisattva Who Was Willing to Die. Regarding "rare sounds," the Master of Old (Laozi) said, "The Great Sound has rare sounds.

Now it is said that Master Sengsheng’s discourse on principle, which defies conventional scriptures, is a peerless song for all ages. Regarding "to serve as a standard," this means it may be taken as a model or rule.

However, the phrase "only [those who are] equal" serves as a warning; there are those in the world who crave fame, whose reckless simplicity leads them to overstep their bounds and give rise to groundless fabrications.
Those who carve out a fine composition are truly like a woman mimicking another’s frown or an owl imitating the speech of a parrot. As the ancients said:
"To deviate from a single word of the sutra is to speak as a demon."

The Commentary states: "Since they are equally [valued]" refers back to what preceded in order to clarify [the point]. "Defense" (*fáng*) means a dyke or barrier. Regarding these two explanations and so forth, according to the *Lüchāo* (Brief Digest), this accords with the intent of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

There are two kinds of inversions (*viparyāsa*): first, the four fundamental inversions of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), meaning that ordinary beings reckon the impermanent body to be permanent, and so forth;
therefore, when the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he preached impermanence and the other [truths] to shatter them.
Second, the four inversions at the end of the Two Vehicles. Those of the Two Vehicles cultivate the aforementioned practices of impermanence and so forth in order to transcend the triple world;

however, they have not yet realized the principle of the Dharma-body’s permanence and bliss. Therefore, this sutra uses the wondrous existence of Buddha-nature and the four virtues of Nirvana to refute these views, as explained extensively in that sutra.
Regarding the statement in the second fascicle that [the Tathāgata] is "not subject to transition" and so forth, this refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The commentary states: "All things are ineffable.

Regarding the phrase "dual citation below," this refers to the citation from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (the *Chengju jing*), which is cited there by way of its meaning. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 51, states:
"Because all dharmas have the characteristic of immovability, these dharmas have no place of coming, no place of going, and no place of abiding. This is what is meant in the commentary.
Dividing these, each realization of the preceding meaning is exceedingly clear. Regarding the phrase "all are antidotes" and so forth, this refers to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

That treatise contains four types [of *siddhānta*], while the commentary briefly indicates two. When the sūtras speak of the principle of the Middle Way and Buddha-nature, it is termed the *paramārtha-siddhānta*.
Commentary: As for the phrase "if [it appears in] the sūtras," etc., the sūtras and śāstras merely refute the emotional attachments to permanence or impermanence.

The reality of all phenomena does not necessarily conform to whether it is retained or discarded according to the words. Therefore, although the words of the sūtras and śāstras each represent a particular perspective, their underlying intent has never failed to be complete.

Commentary: Regarding the first two phrases and so forth, this section of the commentary provides a detailed explanation of the treatise to demonstrate that it is neither redundant nor repetitive; each part possesses its own specific meaning.

Nevertheless, the essential purport does not differ from what preceded. As for the subsequent portion: previously, it was shown that the Two Vehicles received teachings on impermanence and thereby realized the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle.
Now, however, we merely clarify that the teachings they received inherently contain both the provisional and the ultimate, rather than further clarifying the persons who practiced them.
This is why the commentary indicates it as such. However, when considering the intent of the treatise, the teaching encompasses both the provisional and the real.

Because those of the Two Vehicles perceive only the provisional and are oblivious to the real, they remain merely at the "transformed city" (the *parinirvāṇa* of the śrāvakas) without reaching the "Jeweled Place.
It is only upon reaching the *Lotus Sūtra* that the gate of skillful means is opened and the aspect of ultimate reality is revealed.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "this assembly" and so forth, "Nei-pian" (Inner Chapters) is the title of the work by Master Taizong. He possessed the Tripitaka;

he hid the boat in the ravine, hid the mountain in the marsh, and hid the world under heaven within the world itself. As the text is extensive, I do not cite it here in full. "Gu" means firm or secure.

In this commentary, I provide a direct explanation to facilitate easy understanding. "Parable" (*yuyan*) refers to employing figurative language rather than describing actual events. That book employs...

There are many such statements; they cannot be shown in full detail. Regarding the four *brahmins*, as is customary, from "newly and newly descending" (*xīnxīn xià*) onwards, the commentary by Zhu Wen-gong Xi has been used in its entirety.
Commentary: Regarding "the two canons" and so forth, this refers to using skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to attract followers of other schools and lead them to believe in the internal Dharma.
Commentary: Regarding "Confucius" and so forth, this refers to the teachings that conform to worldly conventions. One whose wisdom transcends the common person is called a sage (*ṛṣi*).

This is not like the internal school [of Buddhism], where one is considered a sage because their wisdom is in profound accord with ultimate reality (*tattva*). Thus, Mencius said: "The qilin among walking beasts, the phoenix..."
A bird compared to [the height of] Mount Tai; an anthill compared to Mount Tai; a puddle in a rut compared to the rivers and seas—these are all categories of comparison.
The Sage’s relation to the people is likewise a category of comparison. He emerged from his class and rose above the multitude;
since the birth of mankind, none has been more eminent than Confucius. Zhuang Zhou composed thirty-two chapters of writings; he took Huang-Lao as his progenitor and followed his teachings.

However, because he disparaged benevolence and righteousness and held ritual and music in contempt, the Confucians rejected him as being outside the Classics and ranked him at the head of the various heterodox masters.
That which people find difficult to exhaustively grasp is the realm reached by the sages and the subtle essence of the sagely scriptures—things that ordinary sentiments have not yet fully recognized.
As the ancients said: "To view the great through the small is to fail to exhaust it."

Commentary: This passage below states that, for the time being, one year constitutes a single transformation. If one seeks this in detail—as in the second fascicle of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, where King Prasenajit says:
"Is it not only the years that change, but also the months that transform? Not only do the months transform, but they are further shifted by the days.
Upon deep reflection and careful observation, from moment to moment and within every thought-instant, nothing can remain stationary"—the same applies to the physical form.
The lower [stages] likewise change anew with every passing month, year, and even moment. Regarding the transition from youth to old age, let us take a hundred years as an illustration;
in reality, there is difference in every thought-moment (*kṣaṇa*). If this is so, then the essence differs at every thought-moment;

yet, because one clings to it as being one, a twofold delusion is formed. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says, "Delusion within delusion," which refers to a doubling of the delusion regarding appearances. If one knows this...

Below, the meaning of non-transmigration is presented: since [dharmas] also undergo transformation and differentiation from moment to moment, how could each distinct portion abide and yet reach another?
Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "This Dharma abides in the station of Dharma; the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding.

This is because all dharmas, being dependently originated, are devoid of both essence and function; they are simultaneously existence and emptiness, the various stages of existence, and the ultimate reality of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
This is the state [of reality]. Therefore, it undergoes transition yet remains unchanging. A verse from the "Chapter on the Inquiry into Wisdom" (*Jñānaprasthāna*) states:

"All phenomena lack functional activity and possess no intrinsic nature. It further says: "For example, like the waters in a river, which flow in a rushing torrent toward their destination, each unaware of the others;
so too are all phenomena. Because both essence and function are empty, they are mutually unaware of one another.

Commentary: "This [uses] 'equality,' etc. This demonstrates skill in the treatise’s exposition. As previously cited, internal teachings were used to clarify internal matters such as those of the Śrāvakas;
here, external scriptures are cited to provide proof through the external affairs of the Brahmins.

How could one who is not skilled in composition be able to understand the marvelous ingenuity of this treatise? The remainder of the text is self-evident. To take a wife is called *na-hun* (marriage).
To marry is to value the continuation of one's lineage. To be like the ancients who made no distinction between all dharmas is not skillful regarding the conventional (saṃvṛti).
If one were such an ancient, then differing positions would be conflated; this is not skillful regarding the ultimate (paramārtha).
Thus, the white-haired brahmin is the "new self" of today, while the ruddy-faced brahmin is the "old object" of the past. The brahmin is one and the same; yet, the ruddy...
The essence of their purity differs; thus, while they appear similar, they are not truly identical. The *Zhuangzi*, in the "Tian Zifang" chapter, briefly states:
"Zhongni said to Yan Hui: 'Although you have forgotten your former self, there remains within me that which does not forget.'"

Commentary: From the words "Master Yuan" downward, "fu" (負) means to carry on one's back; it means to bear. By the power of the great transformation of impermanence, one carries heaven and earth as one hastens, and bears the myriad dharmas as one runs.
Truly, this is the greatest of those possessing strength.

Commentary: Regarding the initial phrase "and so forth," the meaning is this: one who is a "vessel of full capacity" receives the Dharma; by examining its diverse expressions, they understand that its principle is the same.
This is worlds apart from those who "wait for a rabbit by a stump" or "seek an elephant by its tracks. Below, regarding "faculties and practices":

"faculties" (根) refers to the spiritual capacity, namely the superior, middling, and inferior types. "Practices" (行) refers to conduct based on faith. "Delight" (樂) means preference; "desire" (欲) means aspiration. Thus it arises.

Xìn (信) says: Because the faculties and practices of sentient beings are unequal, and their conditions for receiving and understanding [the Dharma] differ, [the teachings] rely upon the One True [Dharmadhātu].

This is the purport of the Liáng dynasty’s *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya), which generally holds that there is nothing that does not flow from this Dharmadhātu; many schools cite this, so I shall not elaborate further here. Regarding the "eighty thousand" [dharmas] below:
this number is cited provisionally based on the antidotes to the eighty-four thousand afflictions, though in reality they are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. (*Abhidharmakośa*)
The *Samayabhedoparacanacakra* states: "The Muni taught eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*). The *Qixin lun* (Awakening of Faith) states:
"Thus, he is fully endowed with inconceivable Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges," and so forth. At the end of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, that scripture briefly says:

"At that time, the Buddha observed the net-canopy banners of the Great Brahma Heaven Kings, and because of this, he explained that immeasurable worlds are like the mesh of a net, each being distinct."

The distinctions are immeasurable. The gateways of the Buddha’s teaching are likewise so. Although their purport is profound and the teachings differ, they all lead to the Middle Way and the true mark (*dharmatā*).
As stated in the *Lotus Sūtra*: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time, through various parables and expressions, expound all dharmas;
these dharmas are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle. Therefore, those who study the teachings should not engage in partial understanding.

When considering the teaching in relation to the capacities [of sentient beings], whether it be the doctrine of permanence or impermanence, both are teachings intended to guard against emotional attachments.

From the perspective of the Sage, the teaching should only serve as a means to abandon expedient means and enter into the ultimate reality, because it is beneficial for ordinary beings. As stated at the beginning of the *Lotus Sūtra* (the first chapter):
"The Tathāgata appears in the world solely for the sake of the one great causal matter. This "one matter" refers to the realization and vision of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Furthermore, he expounds all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings; by this measure, it can be seen that what is taught as impermanent is fundamentally permanent.
If one infers this through principle, then all dharmas must necessarily possess both meanings. This is like the *śāla-śa* bird and others.
If one turns back from delusion to awakening, then [the teaching] merely demonstrates non-transmigration; therefore, the title is called "The Non-transmigration of Things" (*Wu Bu Qian*).

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "following the sounds," this is a critique of those scholars who cling to the literal text while obstructing the underlying principle. "Sounds" refers to names and expressions.
However, there are five faults in grasping the meaning by following the sounds alone, as explained in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

To briefly indicate what is meant by "perfect sound": it means that within a single voice of the Tathāgata, all voices are fully contained; he preaches various dharmas, reaching universally across all classes of beings, just as described in detail in the *Prādurbhāva-parivarta*.
This is shown here: by taking this meaning, one is led to a comprehensive understanding of many meanings within a single dharma, such that these many meanings return to a single reality.
One must not merely hear of "change" and understand it only as "impermanence" and so forth.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "ancient and modern," it means that one cannot point to the ancient as being the modern, and so forth.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "first there are," etc., it means that based on "immovable" and "not coming," three propositions are stated for each respectively. This is very easy [to understand].

Commentary: Regarding the first two phrases and so forth: because the various scriptures are manifold, they are called "numerous texts" (*qúnjí*); because the thousand gateways present divergent doctrines, they are called "the hundred schools" (*bǎi jiā*).
Furthermore, "the aforementioned" refers generally to the preceding treatises. "By way of analogy" refers to [doctrines such as] suffering, emptiness, and selflessness;
for instance, those discussed under "suffering" mostly pertain to the Hīnayāna, while those discussed under "permanence" mostly pertain to the Mahāyāna. However, the Mahāyāna...
Among these, there is also one sutra that illustrates both [aspects] simultaneously. For example, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks of medicinal ingredients categorized into a thousand varieties;

while the metaphors for the teachings differ, their efficacy in curing illness is no different—the underlying principle is one. Regarding the phrase "the ocean of teachings is equal," this takes the awakening of the mind as primary.

"Sealing" means to guard or preserve. Formerly, there was a man traveling by river who lost his sword; he carved a mark on the boat's hull to record its location. Even as he traveled to distant lands, he still pointed to it [in search of the sword].

"To lose it by marking the boat on the riverbank is to be utterly deluded. Marking the boat is a metaphor for clinging to the literal text; losing the sword is an analogy for being lost to the essential meaning.
Just as one cannot recover the sword by marking the boat, how can one realize the Truth by adhering to the letter?

Those who suffer from 'ulcers' are those who cannot set aside words to seek the meaning, but instead incur the affliction of mere textualism; they merely exhaust their minds and weary their thoughts in vain labor."

Commentary: The phrase "from this point onward" marks the division of the sections. Although the preceding discussion treated the times of the past, present, and future, it did so by correlating them with specific objects;
therefore, they constitute a distinct category.

The *shū* (commentary) states: "This refers to the commoners and those below; the distinction between delusion and awakening can be understood through contrast. Regarding "clouds and mud": Confucianists use this term to describe a vast disparity in status, like that between clouds and mud.
The *shū* says, "That which appears to be contrary" means they are mutually opposed; this is also a phrase from Laozi, as previously indicated regarding departing and staying.
Although they differ, their ultimate aim is one.

Regarding the commentary’s mention of "those who cling to [the view of] transmigration" and so forth: "seeking" (qiú) means to investigate; that is, to seek the past within the present. The following section merely reverses this.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the text encompasses both," the commentary explains it through the dual aspects of the ancient and the modern.

However, as for the section beginning with "those who cling," the common sentiments of deluded people merely reckon that the present departs from the past as a process of transition. As an ancient poem says: "I saw the spring branches green yesterday; Who would have known the autumn leaves would turn yellow?
The sound of cicadas has not yet ceased, Yet the cold geese have already formed their ranks. It further says: "Counting on one's fingers, ten million generations pass."

The passage of time is as urgent as a thunderclap; all say that worldly conditions shift and pass away with great rapidity. As these shifts persist for a long duration, they become what is called "antiquity.
Yet, if one seeks this through reason, it is simply the accumulation of time that constitutes antiquity; antiquity is never formed by the shifting of time itself.

Moreover, as for time, it perishes in every moment (*kṣaṇa*), and its nature likewise has no location. It is only through deluded conceptualization and discrimination that one reckons the existence of the three periods of time.
Thus, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: "It is not said that bodhi has past, future, or present."

The "Treatise" (Lun) refers to the understanding and penetration [of the meaning]. The "Commentary" (Shu) summarizes and demonstrates this. The Commentary states: "The Four Images (Sìxiàng) are the four seasons.
Below this, the *Appended Statements* (*Xici*) of the *Book of Changes* (*Yijing*) says: "In the Changes there is the Great Ultimate (*Taiji*), which gives birth to the Two Forms (*Liángyí*).
The Two Forms give birth to the Four Images," and so forth. The explanation says: "The Four Images are wood, fire, metal, and water. Now, regarding the "four seasons," it is because...
The treatise says, "the wind rushes," hence it is called *shí* (time). This is likely derived by taking [the seasons] according to the four symbols (*sìxiàng*):
Wood reigns in spring, Fire in summer, Metal in autumn, and Water in winter. Regarding the *xuánjī* and so forth, the *Yáo shū* states: first, Tiānshū; second, Xuán; third, Jǐ;
fourth, Quán; fifth, Héng; sixth, Kāiyáng; seventh, Yáoguāng. *Chén* refers to the star *Chénxīng*.

A single point. Viewed from this region, it lies to the north; this is what the *Lunyu* (Analects) means when it says, "It is like the North Star, which dwells in its place while the myriad stars encircle it.

This refers to how the Three Terraces, the Seven Stars, and others all revolve around it, completing one circuit of the heavens in a single day and night, as swift as a flash of lightning—this speaks of its rapid movement. Master Yuan [Dongping] followed this because the principle he understood was correct.

He took it by its name. "Master Yuan" refers to Dharma Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu. His response to Master Kumārajīva’s verse runs roughly as follows: "Where does the original beginning ultimately come from? Arising and ceasing exist at the limits of being and non-being. If even a single hair stirs within the realm of movement, It creates the momentum of this collapsing mountain. The commentary explains: When one exhaustively investigates the two phenomena of birth and death, they have no original beginning. As stated in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*: "Is birth prior? No. It continues: "Is death prior? No. "Are they simultaneous? No. "Are they sequential? No. Thus, these dharmas are devoid of an origin. Furthermore, the verse states: "Arising and ceasing exist at the limits of being and non-being. This means that if one seeks the source of arising and ceasing, they are found neither within existence nor within non-existence; they are merely provisional designations. If one allows even a slight movement toward the realm of conditioned phenomena, it results in the formation of this "collapsing mountain"—the vast and continuous cycle of birth and death. This is because the mind, once stirred, gives rise to all manner of afflictions and karmic obstructions. Therefore, one must remain in a state of quiescence, free from the movement of thought, so as not to give rise to such calamities. This is the meaning. It is said: "The mind is the master of the body; the body is the servant of the mind. If the mind is agitated, the body suffers; if the mind is tranquil, the body is at ease. One must therefore guard the mind with utmost care. As the verse says: "The mind is like a monkey; it leaps about in the forest of objects. If one can restrain it and prevent it from wandering, one will attain liberation. This is why the verse concludes: "One hair stirs within the realm of movement / And it creates the momentum of this collapsing mountain. This is the essential point. One must strive to maintain a state of non-action and stillness. This is the profound intent of the verse. It is said: "To seek the Way while remaining amidst worldly affairs is like trying to find water in a mirage. If one abandons the world and dwells in seclusion, practicing meditation and contemplation, one may gradually realize the truth. This is the path of the sages. One must not allow the mind to be distracted by external conditions. As the verse says: "If even a single hair stirs within the realm of movement," it immediately leads to the ruin of the great mountain of the Dharma. Therefore, one must be vigilant. This is the instruction. It is said: "The mind is the root of all dharmas. If the mind is pure, all dharmas are pure; if the mind is defiled, all dharmas are defiled. One must purify the mind. This is the ultimate teaching. One must not harbor even a trace of doubt or hesitation. As the verse says: "Arising and ceasing exist at the limits of being and non-being. This indicates that the nature of the mind is originally empty and quiescent. If one realizes this, one transcends birth and death. This is the fruit of the Path. One must not be deluded by appearances. As the verse says: "If even a single hair stirs within the realm of movement," it immediately creates the momentum for the mountain to collapse. This is a warning against the slightest negligence. One must be steadfast. This is the final exhortation. It is said: "The Buddha-dharma is vast and deep; it cannot be fathomed by the intellect alone. One must rely on the guidance of a true teacher and practice with diligence. Only then can one attain the realization of the ultimate truth. This is the core of the teaching. One must not be complacent. As the verse says: "One hair stirs within the realm of movement / And it creates the momentum of this collapsing mountain. This is a vivid description of the perilous nature of the conditioned world. One must awaken to this and exert oneself in cultivation. This is the way to escape suffering. One must not waste time. As the verse says: "Arising and ceasing exist at the limits of being and non-being. This means that the cycle of birth and death has no fixed duration. One must seize the opportunity to cultivate while one is healthy and strong. This is the urgent call to action. One must not be negligent. As the verse says: "If even a single hair stirs within the realm of movement," it immediately leads to the ruin of the great mountain of the Dharma. This is a reminder of the fragility of life. One must cherish every moment. This is the heart of the teaching. One must not be distracted. As the verse says: "One hair stirs within the realm of movement / And it creates the momentum of this collapsing mountain. This is a description of the power of karma. One must be mindful of one's actions. This is the foundation of morality. One must not be arrogant. As the verse says: "Arising and ceasing exist at the limits of being and non-being. This means that all things are subject to change. One must remain humble and respectful. This is the mark of a true practitioner. One must not be stubborn. As the verse says: "If even a single hair stirs within the realm of movement," it immediately creates the momentum for the mountain to collapse. This is a warning against the pride of self-conceit. One must be open-minded. This is the quality of a wise person. One must not be narrow-minded. As the verse says: "One hair stirs within the realm of movement / And it creates the momentum of this collapsing mountain. This is a description of the consequences of ignorance. One must cultivate wisdom. This is the means to liberation. One must not be lazy. As the verse says: "Arising and ceasing exist at the limits of being and non-being. This means that the path to enlightenment is long and difficult. One must persevere with vigor. This is the spirit of a bodhisattva. One must not be discouraged. As the verse says: "If even a single hair stirs within the realm of movement," it immediately creates the momentum for the mountain to collapse. This is a reminder that even a small fault can lead to great disaster. One must be careful. This is the principle of heedfulness. One must not be reckless. As the verse says: "One hair stirs within the realm of movement / And it creates the momentum of this collapsing mountain. This is a description of the power of mindfulness. One must maintain constant awareness. This is the essence of concentration. One must not be forgetful. As the verse says: "Arising and ceasing exist at the limits of being and non-being. This means that the nature of reality is beyond conceptualization. One must transcend all views. This is the realization of emptiness. One must not cling to views. As the verse says: "If even a single hair stirs within the realm of movement," it immediately creates the momentum for the mountain to collapse. This is a warning against the attachment to self. One must be selfless. This is the mark of a saint. One must not be selfish. As the verse says: "One hair stirs within the realm of movement / And it creates the momentum of this collapsing mountain. This is a description of the suffering of saṃsāra. One must seek the cessation of suffering. This is the goal of the Path. One must not be attached to pleasure. As the verse says: "Arising and ceasing exist at the limits of being and non-being. This means that all pleasures are impermanent. One must let go of all attachments. This is the practice of renunciation. One must not be greedy. As the verse says: "If even a single hair stirs within the realm of movement," it immediately creates the momentum for the mountain to collapse. This is a warning against the fire of desire. One must be cool and calm. This is the nature of nirvāṇa. One must not be hot-tempered. As the verse says: "One hair stirs within the realm of movement / And it creates the momentum of this collapsing mountain. This is a description of the power of anger. One must cultivate patience. This is the virtue of a noble one. One must not be impatient. As the verse says: "Arising and ceasing exist at the limits of being and non-being. This means that the nature of the mind is originally pure. One must realize this purity. This is the attainment of Buddhahood. One must not be deluded. As the verse says: "If even a single hair stirs within the realm of movement," it immediately creates the momentum for the mountain to collapse. This is a warning against the darkness of ignorance. One must cultivate wisdom. This is the light of the Path. One must not be ignorant. As the verse says: "One hair stirs within the realm of movement / And it creates the momentum of this collapsing mountain. This is a description of the power of karma. One must understand the law of cause and effect. This is the foundation of ethics. One must not be careless. As the verse says: "Arising and ceasing exist at the limits of being and non-being. This means that all phenomena are interdependent. One must understand dependent origination. This is the insight of a sage. One must not be confused. As the verse says: "If even a single hair stirs within the realm

If death must precede birth, then what gives rise to death? If there is no birth, how can there be death? Thus, when one investigates it, there is no beginning or end. Arising and ceasing are themselves birth and death.

As for the limits of existence and non-existence, these two dharmas exist through the convergence of conditions; existence is not true existence, for when conditions depart, it becomes non-existent, as stated at the beginning of the treatise.
Regarding "a single hair" and so forth, this refers to being deluded regarding the principle of the emptiness of this nature. Being deluded...
When a single hair’s breadth of emotion first arises, one immediately enters the realm of the turbulent movement of birth and death. "The mountain collapses" refers to the term *tái* (to topple);

it means that once birth and death have begun, their momentum is difficult to halt, just as once a mountain has collapsed. This is explained from the perspective of delusion; through analogy, the state of awakening can be understood.

Commentary: Regarding the first phrase, "benefiting others," this is explained according to the Dharma-character (Faxiang) school. The practice of the two benefits (self-benefit and benefiting others) fulfills the stage of the cause only after three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;
the treatise’s mention of "ten thousand ages" or "a hundred kalpas" merely cites these numbers for the sake of correspondence.
"Cultivation and refinement" refers to the process of practicing, advancing, tempering, and polishing. "Question" refers to a hypothetical inquiry used to introduce the subsequent text.
Commentary: Regarding the first phrase, it conveys the meaning of the *Analects* to encourage people to advance in their studies. It says in full: "It is like building a mountain;

though one basketful has been placed, I shall continue to advance. The explanation states: To build a mountain nine fathoms high, the work begins with a single basketful; by advancing without ceasing, [the goal is reached].
When the nine fathoms are finally completed, the advancement lies within oneself; thus it is said, "I advance. The Master Lao also said, "A nine-storied tower begins with piling up earth.
Accumulating earth below clarifies this through metaphor; the movement and operation below clarify it through the application of the law.

This means that the fruit is summoned by the cause, and without the cause there is no fruit. Since the fruit is manifest, one knows that the cause does not undergo transformation. [The subsequent phrase follows. That...

The sixty-four chapters are in Chinese. "Relying" (*zhàng*) is also a metaphor for entrusting. From the first "downward," it is also a metaphorical manifestation. "A thousand" refers to a thousand *li*;
according to its grammatical structure, it simply says "a thousand. From the second "by practice," it also manifests the principle through the dharma, which is no different from what preceded.

It universally illustrates the two types of practice; although there are two practices, because the fruit of the dharma is one, it serves as a universal proof. From the phrase "merely raising," [it refers to] the middle.

The intervening examples are identical to the initial cause; in all cases, they are not extinguished. The *Great Commentary* (Dàshū) refers to the *Avataṃsaka Great Commentary*, which explains the ten kinds of non-obstruction of the Buddha-body;

this is precisely the non-obstruction of cause and effect. That school takes the mutual penetration of cause and effect such that they do not obstruct one another as the meaning of the "mysterious gate" of non-obstruction. Here, we take a single portion of the cause as it is perceived within the fruit.

Regarding the phrase "The meaning is that because causes and practices are realized, there is no transformation," and so forth: the Sūtra states, "All functional activities are like a single thought-moment," which means they do not shift.
Guifeng’s commentary says: "Now, within a single thought-moment, all things are fully known and vividly manifest together, like many mustard seeds contained within a crystal jar.
The meaning is essentially the same as before. Following the previous question, the sub-commentary points out that the three periods of time act as mutual causes for one another.
Wait and then arise. If thought does not arise, the characteristics of the three periods of time vanish, and the single nature is revealed. Regarding the phrase "the treatise refers to the lower":
whether it be causes or time, they are all termed "phenomena" (*vastu*). Since the essence of phenomenal dharmas is empty, they are identical with the Truth (*tathatā*).

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the flow of the True" (*zhēnliú*) and so forth, this is also from the *Xuántán* (Hanging Discourse). It says: "Without the practice that flows from the True, there is no way to accord with the True.

Therefore, within this school, one first realizes the Dharma-realm of Vairocana and subsequently cultivates the ocean of Samantabhadra’s practices. Realizing the principle and giving rise to practice is called 'the flow of the True.
This practice is signless and non-abiding; each and every aspect accords with the True. Because it accords with the True, for this reason..."
It does not shift. If one dwells in the lower [stages], I shall employ Chan Master Yongjia’s *Song of Realizing the Way*. It says:

"To practice giving while dwelling on signs produces heavenly merit; it is like an upward-pointing arrow shot into the void. When its momentum is exhausted, the arrow falls back down, bringing about an unfavorable rebirth in the next life."
Commentary: Regarding "the three calamities" and so forth, according to the verses of the *Kalpa Chapter*, one cycle of increase and decrease constitutes one kalpa.

After eighty such cycles of increase and decrease have passed, the fire calamity first arises to destroy the trichiliocosm. This continues until, following eight fire calamities reaching the First Dhyāna Heaven, the water calamity arises;
and after seven water calamities, the wind calamity begins to stir. This is explained in detail therein. "Ku" means cruel; "lü" means to submerge or extinguish. The rest [is as follows].
It may be omitted.

Regarding the phrase "among the middle [sections]" in the commentary: according to the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, within the causal stage, buddha-nature is termed "that which is to be attained" (*prāpya*), while within the resultant stage, it is termed "that which has been attained" (*prāpta*).
These two stages are far removed from one another because the cause does not reach the result. If the cause were to reach the result, the result would necessarily be the cause.

Furthermore, if cause and effect were to occupy the same temporal position, there would be the fallacy of infinite regress. To say that "the cause of the cause leads to the effect" clarifies that the effect is summoned by its own cause.

If the effect were not summoned by the cause, it would have to be spontaneous, which would likewise entail the fallacy of infinite regress. Moreover, the fact that the effect does not coexist with the cause demonstrates that the cause is not permanent.

By stating that "the cause of the cause leads to the effect," one knows that the cause is not interrupted. Although the effect is mentioned last, I fear people might misunderstand; [it should be understood] as relying solely upon the cause.
In discussing the principle of non-transmigration from the perspective of phenomenal results, one returns to the fundamental truth of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*).
The questioner employs this as a means to clarify the purport of the treatise. As for the former point, it is as stated in the preceding discussion: "All phenomena come from nowhere," and so forth;

one should know that this is but one aspect of the various phenomena produced by causes. What need is there to labor over a redundant analysis? The meaning of the response can be understood accordingly. Thus, one may discern the thematic thread of the treatise.
"It exists from beginning to end. Regarding "in vain" (*tángjuān*): *táng* means empty; *juān* means to discard. Below, the section on the youth uses a metaphor to distinguish the cause.

Reading the book is the metaphor for the cause; reaching proficiency is the metaphor for the result. If one were to say that the merit of the reading perishes along with it, then proficiency would not be reached.

Since proficiency is indeed reached, we know that the prior effort does not vanish. "Similarity to the characteristics" refers to the characteristics of the youth reading the book, which are perceived by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

The mental faculty (*manas*) functions together with visual consciousness and the other sensory cognitions. The preceding moment perfumes (*vāsana*) the succeeding moment, and the succeeding moment draws forth the preceding;

this continues until it reaches maturity. Such is the meaning of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). This refers merely to the perfuming and drawing-forth within the continuity of moments, extending sequentially to subsequent states.

In reality, however, the preceding perishes and the succeeding arises; the cause transforms and the effect emerges. This differs from the practice of the Nature School (*Faxiang*), which claims that the practice accords with the principle (*li*) from beginning to end, and that the principle does not [change].
If phenomena were to contradict [the principle], then causes and characteristics would be distinct; yet phenomena do not contradict the principle, meaning that causes do not undergo transformation.

Therefore, although the preceding treatise uses the term "Tathāgata," it merely cites the fruit to reveal the cause. Since the principle of the cause is clarified, the nature of the fruit is naturally revealed. The commentary cites the meaning of the Buddha-fruit according to Master Qingliang:
the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), while the *dharmakāya* (dharma body) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This is because they are neither identical nor different.
"Moving and yet not moving. I shall now cite the text from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "This body is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*); the eternal body is the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

[In the] commentary, regarding the phrase "without saying," etc., there are two meanings here: first, it is a hypothetical expression; that is to say, even if heaven were to collapse and the earth were to sink...

Nor is there anything called "non-quiescence" and so forth; these two are spoken of according to actual reality. Heaven and earth are also phenomena produced by dependent origination; they have their formation and their destruction.
When the heavens and earth overturn, this is among the greatest of transformations. However, if one realizes that the nature of consciousness is empty, there is no transformation.
That which is like a great flood, such as a water disaster, extends up to the second dhyāna heaven. As stated in the "Tang Wen" chapter of the *Liezi*: "In that case..."
Heaven and earth are also things. As things, they have deficiencies. Thus, in antiquity, Nüwa melted stones of five colors to patch the heavens;
she used the severed legs of a giant turtle to establish the four poles. Later, Gonggong contended with Zhuanxu for the title of Emperor.
In his rage, he struck Mount Buzhou, breaking a pillar of heaven and severing a cord of earth. Consequently, heaven slanted toward the northwest, and the sun...
The moon and stars find their place therein. The earth does not fill the southeast; the hundred rivers and floods flow back into it.
This also speaks of destruction, yet we do not know the principle by which there is a great destruction. Furthermore, the *Tian Rui* chapter briefly states:

A man of Qi worried that heaven and earth would collapse and he would have nowhere to dwell. Someone enlightened him, saying: "Heaven is formed from the accumulation of qi; the earth is formed from the accumulation of clods."
"It is established. One goes about and dwells within it all day long; how can one worry about its collapsing or falling? When Changlu Zi heard this, he laughed and said:
"Rainbows, halos, clouds, mists, winds, and rains—the four seasons' accumulated vapors form Heaven. Mountains, rivers, seas, metal, stone, water, and fire—accumulated forms form Earth.
Since they are formed through accumulation, how can you say they do not decay? Now, Heaven and Earth are within the void."
Among all minute things, there is one that is vast within; for one to worry about its destruction is truly far-fetched. To say it does not perish is likewise incorrect.
Nevertheless, the treatise implicitly employs the meaning of Zhuangzi. As the "Xiaoyao" chapter says: "Even when a great flood reaches the heavens, one is not drowned.
*Ji* (稽) means "to reach" (*zhì*). The essential point is no different from what preceded; the words of the commentary are clear enough. As for "Qingning" (Pure Tranquility):
Laozi said: "Of those who attained the One in the past: Heaven attained the One and became clear; Earth attained the One and became tranquil," and so forth.

Now, by means of clarity and tranquility, the eyes do not shift. Under the heading "A Thousand Doors," it is because within the fundamental source, conditions meet and their nature is empty—this is simply the single meaning.

The style of the discourse is like the transformation of wind and clouds, with the colors of the sunset interlacing; in a hundred moods and a thousand forms, they suddenly appear and suddenly vanish. However...
If one seeks [the truth] through the principles of our school’s tenets, there is nothing that is not understood.
Regarding the phrase "revealing by contrast" (*fanxian*) in the Commentary: within the Xianshou school, to speak of emptiness apart from phenomena is considered nihilism (*duan*);

to clarify existence apart from emptiness is considered eternalism (*chang*). To be empty while being existent, and existent while being empty, is the insight of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). Below, under Qingliang, he cites scriptural evidence. Next...
It is said that words and images are not the immediate reality; one must embody them with an empty mind to perceive them through direct observation (*mujik*).

A Zen text records that when the Lord of Qin read this treatise, he threw his cup to the ground and asked the Dharma Master, "Is this not [the work of] Xian? The Master remained silent. [The Lord of Qin remarked,] "What kind of vulgar and uncultivated talk is this?
It is utterly inconsistent with reason. Given the Lord of Qin’s understanding of the Dharma, such a question should not have been made."
Given the master’s brilliant insight, he likewise should not have remained silent. Had he been questioned, he would certainly have replied: "The conditions of the cup give rise to a single object.
When confronted with a mind of arising and ceasing, there is wholeness and breakage; yet when sealed by the wisdom of the emptiness of nature, there is neither arising nor ceasing.
Because essence and function are fundamentally quiescent, wholeness and breakage occupy distinct positions; thus, when conditions assemble—

[End. When conditions separate, it breaks. Whether it is whole or broken depends on conditions, not on the cup itself. If this wholeness does not come from the breaking, then the breaking likewise does not proceed from the wholeness.
Since the two do not reach one another, their natures each abide in their own single moment. My humble understanding is shallow, yet even this may serve as a point of entry;
how much more so for the profound realization of the Master of the Treatise! This treatise also takes the various Prajñāpāramitās as its primary authority.
...and composed [treatises] such as the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "all," etc.: excluding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it refers to all worldly phenomena within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)—namely, the five aggregates (*skandha*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and eighteen elements (*dhātu*)—up to and including the supramundane dharmas, such as the ten powers (*bala*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the eighteen [unique qualities of a Buddha].
It is not shared with the *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge). All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) produced from conditions are not real.

Because they are not real, they are empty. As stated in the seventh fascicle of the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*: "The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are empty because they are not real. Furthermore, there is no difference between the five aggregates and the Bodhisattva.
The six *pāramitās*, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmas*), and even the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) are all without end.

[End of section. The dharmas of the Buddhas are empty; the dharmas of the Buddhas are quiescent; the dharmas of the Buddhas are not real. Regarding the phrase "equal to illusions and so forth," the sūtra contains ten similes:
like a dream, like a light, like a shadow, like an echo, like a mirage, like a transformation, like a reflection in a mirror, like the moon in water, and like a city of the Gandharvas.
Therefore, their intrinsic nature is empty. One should know that all phenomena exist only as [conventional designations].

Names—what substantial reality could they possess? They are not true in their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), yet they are fundamentally empty in their nature (*svabhāva*). Although characteristics are not true, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is not non-existent;
although nature is fundamentally empty, it does not exist apart from conditions. That which is neither existent nor non-existent is the primary truth. As the subsequent treatise states:
"The myriad things have a reason why they do not exist, and they have a reason why they are not non-existent," and so forth. It further says: "Contact..."
All things are of one and the same nature. I shall not cite further sources for fear of prolixity. The *Prabhāsa-sūtra*, chapter seven, states:
Subhūti said to Śāriputra, "All dharmas neither aggregate nor disperse. Śāriputra asked, "What does it mean that they do not aggregate? What does it mean that they do not disperse?"

Subhūti said: "The five aggregates, up to and including wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, and outflowing and non-outflowing dharmas, neither aggregate nor disperse. Why? Because their intrinsic nature is such.
For this reason, these various dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent; such passages occur more than once."
Commentary: Regarding the first phrase, "citing according to the sūtra," this is also an interpretive citation; it distinguishes the principle of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Within all Mahāyāna teachings, this principle is shown as the defining characteristic of the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*), and it appears most frequently in the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* takes this as its primary tenet and explains it; the present commentary follows that approach. As for the phrase "in terms of the mind," this refers to the *Prajñācitta* (the Mind of Wisdom). By means of the non-arising *prajñā*...

If one illuminates the wondrous principle of non-arising, it is neither having illumination nor lacking illumination; thus the treatise says: "It is the wondrous function of profound discernment. Regarding the "essence of the school":
this principle of the emptiness of nature is the essence that serves as the foundation for all phenomena. Under the section on "Ultimate Truth" (paramārtha-satya):
it means that while all dharmas are termed conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) in terms of their characteristics, they are termed ultimate truth in terms of their nature. This truth transcends...
It transcends the mundane world; therefore, the commentary (*śāstra*) calls it "unsurpassed. A detailed explanation of the distinct characteristics of the various truths is as found elsewhere.
Regarding existence and non-existence, the subsequent treatise states: "Because of dependent origination, it is not non-existent; because it arises from conditions, it is not existent," and so forth.

Regarding identity and difference, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* elucidates the Middle Way as being free from the eight [extremes]. Thus, the beginning of that treatise says: "Neither arising nor ceasing, neither permanent nor..."

"Cessation. Neither identical nor different; neither coming nor going," and so forth. Now, for brevity, we speak only of "identity" and "difference. The treatise further states: "If they were identical, there would be no conditions;

if they were different, there would be no continuity," and so on. The term "and so forth" (etc. includes other [concepts] such as arising and ceasing, annihilation and permanence, and coming and going. As the text is voluminous, I have not cited it all. This is not a matter of personal interpretation below; rather, it is from the verse in the "Refutation of Causes and Conditions" chapter:

[Verse: ... (as cited above) ... ...and so forth. The phrase "and so forth" refers to the remaining [categories]: arising and ceasing, annihilation and permanence, and coming and going. Much of the text has not been quoted here. This is not my own sub-commentary; it is the meaning of the treatise itself. The verse from the "Chapter Refuting Causes and Conditions" says: [The verse continues...]
All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another; they do not arise from both, nor without a cause. Therefore, one knows that there is no arising.
Now, while the root verses of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* were composed by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, the prose commentary (*bhāṣya*) was the explanation provided by the Brahmin Candrakīrti.

Herein, I shall briefly rely upon that prose commentary to explain the preceding verses. Regarding "not arising from themselves," this means that among all things, there is nothing that arises from its own essence.

Arising necessarily depends upon a multitude of causes and conditions before it occurs; furthermore, it does not arise from another. This means that because the "self" (sva) does not exist, the "other" (para) likewise does not exist.
Why? Because it is by virtue of the existence of the self that there is an other. Since the self does not arise, how could the other possibly exist? The commentary explains:
this principle takes all phenomena (*dharmas*) as the "self" and causes and conditions as the "other. Therefore, it was previously stated that all things do not exist.
Arising from its own essence necessarily depends upon a multitude of causes and conditions.

Even if other schools maintain that the cause is "self" and the conditions are "other," this position is also subject to extensive refutation as found in the *Great Commentary* (*Mahā-śāstra*). Regarding the "unshared" [position], it refutes the doctrine that arising occurs through the combination of self and other.
Within the treatise, the theory of co-arising (co-production) entails two faults: first, the fault of arising from self; second, the fault of arising from other. Not...
Regarding "no cause": if things exist without a cause, they would be eternal; consequently, the retribution of good and evil deeds would not be summoned by causes.
