Thus, those who practice giving and uphold the precepts would fall into hell, while those who commit the ten non-virtues and the five heinous crimes would be reborn in the heavens.

Regarding the statement "nor a creator": the non-Buddhist outsiders of the Western Regions (India) calculate that the arising and ceasing of all phenomena must have a creator. According to the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, some calculate...
It is held that all things arise from Īśvara, arise from Viṣṇu, arise from time, arise from the world, arise from transformation, or arise spontaneously (*svabhāva*), and so forth.
Yet, in this region as well, it is reckoned that there is a creator with a master. As the ancients said: "The Creator-child has many clever skills.
Furthermore, a Chinese poem states: "How laughable is the work of Nature, lacking any fixed standard; it turns things red and plays with purple."
It is simply due to human beings. All see that the birth, extinction, transformation, and transition of the myriad things are brought about by the workings of the Great Transformation (*huagong*).
Thus, they reckon that there exists a creator in the Western Regions; this is the doctrine of spontaneity (*ziran*) which also exists here in this land.

Even this has been briefly indicated below, yet they have not yet mastered the principle of phenomena arising through causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*), let alone understand the principle that what arises through conditions is illusory and its nature is fundamentally empty. There is none.

Having given birth [to this understanding], one can explain the ultimate truth of the Middle Way. Because the two truths are mutually identical, it is said that "there is no arising, yet there is arising," and so forth.
The rest may be understood accordingly.
Commentary: As for "revealing by contrast," it means that only the sage’s wisdom of non-arising illuminates the principle of non-arising prior [to manifestation].
Commentary: The phrase "the ultimate fruit" is explained based on the stage of Buddhahood. The phrase "manifesting transformation" refers to assuming a name according to the class of beings;
as stated below: "being celestial among celestials, being human among humans," and so forth. "The Unsurpassed One" (Anuttara) refers to the convergence of the ten titles of the Tathāgata.

First: "Internal penetration" (*neitong*) means that illuminating principle is called "internal. "Emergence" (*chu*) means transcendence. This explains the divine mind. The passage beginning with "fully awakening" (*xijue*) is from the sixtieth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

"External response" (*waingying*) means that illuminating phenomena is called "external. The passage beginning with "reaching the limit of vision" (*jishi*) refers to the provisional wisdom (*quan-zhi*) which casts its gaze to observe forms and extends its hearing to listen to sounds, being present within the realms of the five desires;
here, "sound and form" (*shengse*) are mentioned as representative examples. [The text continues with] "realizing the source" (*liaoben*).
Because they are empty, form cannot glue one to it, nor can sound restrain one. Nanda loved Sundarī and returned home; this was being glued by form.
Kāśyapa heard a *vīṇā* lute and rose to dance; this was being restrained by sound.
Thus we know that when objects are not understood as empty, they immediately burden one's spiritual intelligence. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 17, mentions a certain upāsaka.
He went far away with a group of merchants to pursue his livelihood. At that time, there was cold snow; traveling by night, he lost his companions and stayed within a mountain cave.
Then, a mountain spirit transformed into a woman and came, wishing to test him, and spoke this verse: "The white snow covers the mountains and the earth;
Birds and beasts have all hidden away. I alone have no one to rely upon; I only pray that you will take pity on me. The Upāsaka...
Covering his ears with both hands, he replied with this verse: "Shameless and wicked man, you utter such impure words;

may water wash them away and fire burn them away, for I do not wish to hear such sounds. Even a wife’s heart has no desire for this, let alone committing sexual misconduct—even at the cost of one's own body and life, like a moth rushing into a lamp-flame. Having heard this verse, the mountain deity immediately lifted up this man.

He was sent back among his companions. Regarding "those who are attached to sound": it is like five hundred sages dwelling in the mountains who heard the singing voices of Kinnarī women bathing in a pond in the Snowy Mountains (*Himavat*).
Upon hearing their songs, they immediately lost their meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); their minds became intoxicated and wild, and they could not restrain themselves.
It was as if a great wind were blowing through the forest trees; hearing this subtle, exquisite, soft, and pure [sound], they gave rise to wrong views.
Such are their thoughts; therefore, they do not realize that their minds have gone mad. In this life, they lose all merit, and in future lives, they shall fall into the evil realms.
As for those attached to perfumes: it is like an Arhat who frequently enters the dragon palace; having finished his meal, he hands his bowl to a śrāmaṇera and tells him to wash it.
In the bowl were a few grains of leftover rice. The śrāmaṇera smelled it and found it exceedingly delicious. He then employed a stratagem by crawling under his teacher’s rope bed;
grasping the legs of the bed with both hands, they entered the dragon palace together. The dragon said, "This man has not yet attained the Way;
why have you brought him here? The teacher replied, "I was unaware. The śrāmaṇera then ate the food and also saw that the dragon girl’s body was upright, graceful, and exquisitely fragrant.
He was peerless. His mind became deeply attached, and he made a solemn vow: "I shall perform meritorious deeds to seize this dragon's place and dwell in his palace.

The dragon said, "Henceforth, do not bring this śrāmaṇera here. After the śrāmaṇera had returned, he single-mindedly practiced giving and observed the precepts, focusing exclusively on his aspiration to become a dragon as soon as possible.
At that time, water gushed from beneath his feet as he circumambulated the temple; he knew for certain that [his wish would be fulfilled].
He was reborn as a dragon. He went directly to the edge of the great pond where his former teacher used to enter, covered his head with his *kāṣāya*, and entered;
he died immediately and transformed into a great dragon. Because his merit was so vast, he killed that [other] dragon, turning the entire pond a deep red.

Before this had occurred, the various teachers and the monks had rebuked him, but the śrāmaṇera said, "My mind is already settled; the signs of my state have already appeared. At that time, the teacher...

The assembly of monks was led to the pond to observe this. Such causes and conditions arise from attachment to fragrance; as for attachment to flavor, it is like the case of a certain novice who constantly craved curd.
When a donor sent curd to the monastic community, the novice always received the leftovers. His mind became attached to them with constant delight and could not let go.
After his life ended, he was reborn inside that jar of leftover curd. The novice’s teacher obtained [him].
The path of Arhatship. While the curd was being divided, he spoke, saying: "Be gentle; do not harm this novice who loves curd.
The others said: "This is a worm. Why do you call it 'the novice who loves curd'? He replied: "This worm was originally my novice."
It was solely because he sat craving the leftover curd that he was born within this jar. When the teacher received his portion of the curd, the insect came out from within it.
The teacher said, "O you who craved the curd, why have you come here? He then gave the curd to it. Regarding those who touch [impure things]:
for example, there was a rishi on a mountain in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī who urinated into a washbasin during the second month of spring. He saw a deer copulating...

As soon as lustful thoughts arose, his vital essence flowed into the basin. A deer drank it and became pregnant; she gave birth to a child who resembled a human, though with the feet of a deer and a single horn.

He was born beside the hermitage of the immortal. Seeing that the child was human, the deer entrusted him to the immortal and departed. The immortal, knowing the child was his own son, raised him. When he grew up, he mastered the scriptures and treatises.
He further studied seated meditation, practiced the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), and attained the five supernormal powers (*pañca-abhijñā*).
While climbing a mountain, he encountered rain. Because his feet were unsteady, he slipped on the muddy ground, breaking his *kuṇḍikā* (water flask) and injuring his foot.
He became greatly incensed and, filling the *kuṇḍikā* with water, performed a spell to stop the rain. Crops and fruits failed to grow, and the people fell into poverty.
The king was distressed and commanded his ministers to convene a council to discuss the matter of the rain. A wise man among them proposed: "I have heard that within the mountains there is..."
The seer Ekaśṛṅga, because his feet were infirm, stumbled and injured his foot. In anger, he cast a spell upon this rain, causing it not to fall for twelve years.
The king reflected, "If it does not rain for twelve years, there will be no people remaining. The king immediately issued a proclamation:
"To whoever can cause this seer to lose his supernatural powers and become my subject, I shall grant half the kingdom to rule. At that time... [text ends]
In the kingdom there was a courtesan named Śāntā, peerless in her beauty. She came forward in response to a public call and asked the people, "Is this man a human or a non-human?
The crowd replied, "He is merely a human, born of a rishi. The woman said, "If he is a human, I am able to overcome him.
Having spoken, she took a golden tray filled with fine jewels and presented it to the king, saying, "I shall ride upon this rishi."
When he arrived, he immediately sought out five hundred beautiful women and prepared "joy-pills" by mixing them with medicinal herbs; they were colored to resemble various fruits.

He also brought potent wine that appeared like water in color and taste. Clad in garments made of tree bark and grass, resembling a sage of the elephant-hermit type, he reached the hermitage and stayed in a separate hut.
When the sage went out and saw him, the women came forth to welcome him, offering flowers and incense.

He nourished him. The immortal was greatly delighted. The woman addressed the immortal with polite and respectful words of greeting. She led him into the chamber and seated him upon a fine couch and bedding.
She served clear wine as his drink and gave him *mṛdvīkā* (grape) cakes as fruit. Having finished eating, she spoke to her daughters, saying:
"Since my birth, I have never before obtained this fruit-water. The woman said, "Because I have practiced virtue, the devas have granted me this wish, and thus I have obtained this fruit-water.
He asked again, "Why is your complexion so full and radiant? She replied, "It is because we eat this fruit-water.
The woman addressed the seer, saying, "Why do you not stay here? The seer said, "I could indeed stay. The woman said, "Then let us go together."

He washed himself and agreed to it as well. As the woman’s hands were soft and supple, his heart stirred upon touching them. While washing with her, they engaged in sexual intercourse, and he immediately lost his supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
Heaven sent down a great rain for seven days and seven nights. After seven days, the wine and fruit were all exhausted;
the water from the mountain streams and the fruits of the trees that followed were no longer delicious. When he asked for the former [wine and fruit], she replied, "They are already gone. Now...
"We shall go together; there is a place where we may find something. The seer said, "As you wish," and they immediately set out together.
Not far from the city, the woman lay down on the road and said, "I am utterly exhausted and can go no further. The seer said, "Ride upon my head.
The woman first sent a messenger to inform the king, saying, "Please observe my capability. When the king came out to see her, he asked, "By what means was this possible?"
He replied, "By means of skillful expedients, I have caused him to dwell within the city so that he may receive offerings and respect, and I have appointed him as a high minister.
However, his body has gradually become emaciated. The King asked the seer, "Why are you not happy? He answered, "Although I have obtained the five objects of desire, I constantly long for quietude;
I am unable to go to the places where the various seers roam. The King reflected to himself, "The calamity of drought has already been removed; for what reason should I forcibly seize [him] again?"
As for his resolve, he was immediately released and returned to the mountains. Through diligent practice, before long he regained the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

Regarding the phrase "both emerge," etc., this explains the reason why the two wisdoms emerge without stagnation. Regarding the phrase "the above," etc., this distinguishes that the substance of the two wisdoms is one;

they are merely established as two according to their functions. As the *Ratnaketu-śrī-sūtra* (Renwang jing) says: "Regarding the truths, they are always inherently two; regarding their realization, they are always..."
"From one": the meaning of the commentary is that it cites the two truths as being mutually identical as a single source; that the Real (zhen) and the Responsive (ying) are fused as a single mind.
In the commentary, the character "ying" (responsive) refers to provisional wisdom (quanzhi), not to the [Buddha] body.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "further explaining," this means that the preceding text is once again investigated, scrutinized, and clarified to elucidate its underlying principle.

This passage is extremely obscure; therefore, the commentary provides a full exposition of it. Below, it will be explained in accordance with specific difficulties. Regarding the phrase "conforming to dharmas" (*anuloma-dharma*), this explains the term "conforming" (*anuloma*).

It refers merely to conforming to the inherent emptiness of dharmas themselves, rather than making them empty through analytical disintegration as is done in the Hīnayāna. If one relies upon the dharmas...
It is analyzed and deconstructed; therefore, it does not reach the subtlety of the infinite. That which does not stagnate in quiescence does not depart from phenomena.
That which does not stagnate in phenomena realizes that phenomena are empty. Regarding the phrase "the single qi": as the Master of Lao says, "One gives birth to two," where "One" refers to qi.

"Regarding the phrase 'The mind says' below: it means that one contemplates all phenomena through the principle of the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*); there is not a single phenomenon that is not empty by nature.

Regarding the phrase 'Whatever' below: the objects confronted by the six sense faculties, the contacts produced by the six consciousnesses, and the various desires such as form that taint those contacts—all these are empty by nature.
'Turning the hearing back to hear one's own nature' refers to the secret application of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* method of contemplation."
Regarding the meaning of the perfect penetration of sound, it is fully stated: "Reverse-hearing to hear one's own nature; as hearing is restored, the obstructing faculty is eliminated," and so forth.
"Reverse-hearing" means not following external sounds. "Hearing one's own nature" means that the nature of hearing does not arise from sound itself, but is solely one's own nature.
Once the nature of hearing is restored, one hears clearly throughout the ten directions, and the obstructing dust and the veiling faculty naturally vanish and cease. This faculty...
Since this is so, it is the same for all the sense-faculties. Thus the Sūtra says: "When one faculty returns to its source, the functions of the six become still.
The distinction between the preceding and following sections can be understood from the text below.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "contact" (*sparśa*), it means that the mind is defiled by its object; this is termed contact. To explain it in detail, contact arises from the conjunction of the three—sense organ, object, and consciousness.
Contact is defiled by various objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth. What is here called "touching things" refers generally to all objects encountered by the six consciousnesses.
Below the section on Qingliang, he cites a passage from the *Dacāo* (Great Commentary). The term "manifestly" (*jùrán*) means clearly or evidently. This refers to the two truths (*satyadvaya*).
The mutual penetration [of the two truths] is clearly manifest within the Middle Way. Furthermore, one may simply state that the purport of the argument is that they are profound and unified.

If one were to synthesize this through the mutual penetration of the two truths, it would likewise be appropriate to say that they are mixed yet eternally one, and differentiated from the one yet eternally mixed.
Now, it is simply stated that they are brought to a state of purity and unity; therefore, we rely on this assembly.

[In the] *Sūtra Commentary* (Shu), under the section "Yun'an," these two phrases are missing from the current edition, but they are present in the Tang edition. They are highly sufficient from the perspective of the underlying principle.

The sub-commentary (*shu*) states: "Regarding 'about to refute' below, the purport of the treatise can be understood. From "the mind and objects mutually encompass" down to "one should know," Master Daosheng’s [view] is cited in the *Dacāo* (Great Commentary).
He maintains that the ultimate (*zhen*) is correct and the conventional (*su*) is incorrect; both arise through mutual dependence (*xiangdai*). If they depend on one another, they arise together;

if they do not depend on one another, they perish together. Therefore, there is only the single truth of non-arising (*wushengdi*). The "four words" refer to the Four Noble Truths (*sidi*). — *Zhuang* [End].
The "Zi Qi Wu" (Discourse on Equalizing All Things) chapter states: "That [side] has its own standard of right and wrong; this [side] also has its own standard of right and wrong.

When that 'is' finds no counterpart, it is called the Pivot of the Dao. Regarding the "Three Houses," as recorded in the *Analects*: "The Three Houses used the *Yong* [psalm] for the ritual of clearing away the remains.
These were the descendants of Duke Huan of Lu: first, the Jisun; second, the Zhongsun; and third, the Mengsun. *Yong* is the title of a poem from the *Shijing*.

Furthermore, the world has long adhered to the administration of Lu and usurped the rituals of the Son of Heaven. Now, regarding those who disparage the three masters below, this refers to those who err in their understanding of time.

Those who are called "students of the Dharma" have not yet realized the principle of the emptiness and existence of dependent origination; thus, their deluded views are in chaotic confusion, as seen in the cases of Daoheng and others mentioned below.
The phrase "by means of correct principle" (zhènglǐ) below points back to the preceding passage concerning the common root of self and others. [This concludes] the Seven Sects.

Regarding this, that commentary states: "The Liang dynasty monk Baochang composed the *Xùfǎlùn* (Continued Treatise on the Dharma), which describes the *Qīzōnglùn* (Treatise on the Seven Schools) composed by the Song dynasty monk Tánqīng.

These are: first, the School of No-Principle; second, the School of the Profound Principle; third, the School of Suchness-as-Form (*jísè zōng*), and so on, up to the seventh, the School of Realization of Essence (*tǐhuì zōng*)."

However, as the world is distant and there is no [reliable] practice, one need not be overly pedantic. Regarding the fact that the nature of principles varies according to different regions: the explanations and meanings differ in accordance with what each respective author has set forth.

As for the reference to the *Liang zhuan* (Biographies of the Liang Dynasty) and other sources, some claim it was composed by Zhi Mindu; this is likely incorrect. According to my examination of the *Liang zhuan*, Master Du...

There is no other account of this whatsoever. However, the *Biography of Zhu Fatai* records that Daoheng possessed considerable talent and ability and constantly adhered to the doctrine of "Mind-lessness" (*xīn wú*).

He propagated it extensively throughout the region of Jing. Since he is described as having such talent and ability, it is likely that this master himself composed [the treatise] and propagated his own views.
Fatai said, "This is a heterodox teaching; it must be refuted. He then assembled eminent monks and ordered his younger brother...

Zi Tan-yi challenged him on this point. Daoheng was eloquent and resourceful, remaining unyielding. The following day, Huiyuan gathered again to attack him; his interrogations were sharp and piercing.
Daoheng felt a sense of unease and, striking the table with his fly-whisk (*zhuchi*), failed to provide an immediate answer.

Those present all laughed, and the doctrine of *xinwu* (mindlessness) ceased at that point. Regarding the phrase "the mind is without the various dharmas," Yao’s commentary states: "This refers to my..."
The fundamental mind is originally devoid of all phenomena; all phenomena exist of themselves and do not exist within my mind.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "arising from the mind" and so forth: the mind does not give birth to all phenomena, for the mind itself has no objective referents. Because one maintains this state, the spirit and mind are tranquil;
taking this as attainment, however, the correct teaching of the Mahāyāna holds that the myriad dharmas have no intrinsic substance and are all merely manifestations of the mind alone.

Arising through the convergence of conditions, their nature is fundamentally empty. Failing to reach this principle, one claims that all phenomena exist inherently and that one's own mind is devoid of phenomena;
this is why such a view errs by a vast margin. Furthermore, it accords with the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which clings to the notion that phenomena exist as real entities external to the mind.
Commentary: "The Later Eastern Jin" refers to the eminent monk Zhi Dun, whose courtesy name was Daolin. According to the *Yaoshu*, Master Lin held that "form is not produced by itself;
it still exists as provisional form. This commentary follows the account in the *Beishan lu*; the general meaning is the same. Regarding the phrase "That which is called... and so forth:
names such as blue, yellow, large, small, long, short, and so on, are all merely the false conceptualizations of human sentiment applied as names.

It is not that form itself is so called. Thus, Master Lin said: "Form is not form by itself. If the mind descends [into realization], one penetrates that the nature of false conceptualization is empty.
If one does not grasp it as being truly blue or other such things, then all characteristics will naturally fail to establish themselves. Therefore, it is said: "Although it is form, it is not form."
Commentary: "To align with this" means that the Master of the Treatise, wishing to refute their doctrine, first demonstrates the correct principle (*nyāya*).

Once the correct principle is realized, biased views will naturally perish. Regarding the second phrase below: all those previously designated as "blue" and so forth—substantial, obstructive forms—are produced through conditions.
As for dharmas produced by conditions, they fundamentally lack names such as "blue," "yellow," "long," or "short. Since these nameless dharmas are substantial and obstructive...
It is precisely form (*rūpa*). How could it wait for a person’s name before false views arise regarding phenomena such as "blue" and so forth?

From sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) downwards, the teachings that employ various *prajñā* to dismantle existence begin with the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of the mundane world and extend, finally, to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*) of the supramundane.
All are empty; it is not only form that is so. Because all dharmas arise from false conceptualization, they all possess names and marks.
However, as they are produced by causes and conditions, they lack any substantial nature, and are therefore all empty. Regarding "blue and so forth":
the names "blue," "yellow," and so on, arise from false conceptualization, while the marks of blue, yellow, and so on, are produced by causes and conditions.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the first clause," etc., this explains the first clause of the *Śāstra*. "Not yet having attained" below explains the latter clause of the *Śāstra*.

However, the section beginning with "yet dependent origination" below implicitly cites the *Awakening of Faith* to explain it. The *Śāstra* states that *ālayavijñāna* has two meanings: first, the meaning of awakening; second, the meaning of non-awakening.
Based on the meaning of non-awakening, three further characteristics arise: the first is the characteristic of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*).

In the Dharma-characteristics school (Faxiang), the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) corresponds to the second, the evolving aspect; the seeing portion (*darśanabhāga*) corresponds to the third, the seen aspect (*nimittabhāga*);
and thus it is said that [the mind] also has the seen aspect as its object. That which is the "mind capable of seeing" refers to the continuity of the cognitive aspect (*jñānanimitta*).

"Evolving in accordance with aspects" means evolving in accordance with the dharmas—such as the sense organs, the body, the environmental world, and the five sensory objects—that appear within that *ālayavijñāna*.
"Arising attachment" refers to grasping and calculating the characteristics of names (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, the commentary on the *Jñāna-lakṣaṇa* (Wisdom Characteristic) briefly states:

"Depending upon objects, the mind gives rise to discrimination that continues without interruption; because the mind gives rise to attachment while contemplating objects, it falsely clings to and discriminates conventional designations such as names and characteristics.
The phrase "is named" belongs to the following section, which explains [the three natures] based on the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*). Here, "name" refers to the *parikalpita* (imagined nature).
"Characteristics (lakṣaṇa) are dependent (paratantra)," according to the meaning of the *Śrīmaladevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* (Mi-yen jing), which will be fully cited and explained below.
The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "Regarding Zhu Fatai, according to tradition, he was a close friend of Master Dao’an. The fourth fascicle of Guifeng’s *Lüechao* says:
"From 'Originally non-existent' down to 'non-existence is itself non-existence,' the commentary states: 'The above all constitutes a prior narration of what was conceptualized. [End of] Guest.
They are guests. Guests all turn toward the host. Now, by establishing a person who fundamentally does not exist, it is said that all things tend toward non-existence (*wu*).

Furthermore, it cites the *Erya*, which states: "A guest (*bin*) is one who submits. This means that the inner sentiments submit to non-existence. Consider how the composition of this text descends even to the point of the actual nature of things.

A brief commentary on the *Shichao* says: It does not say they are "not existent" (*fei you*); rather, "non-existence" (*wu*) negates this existence. It is not "not non-existent" (*fei wu*); rather, "non-existence" negates [that].
"That [view] does not exist.

[In the] Commentary, under the first two phrases, "斥" (chì) means to refute or critique what is visible. Regarding the phrase "Now examining," etc., this is done by contrasting and distinguishing the three schools:

"Mind-Non-existence" (Weixin) holds that all dharmas truly exist, while "Fundamental Non-existence" (Benwu) holds that the grasping at dharmas is fundamentally empty; both cling to one-sided extremes.
Therefore, Master Lin regards the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) as empty while not engaging with the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature);

he relies on the dependent nature while not identifying it as empty. Thus, each remains stuck in one-sidedness. As for our Master [Candrakīrti], he explains this solely in relation to all phenomena arising through conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna*).

Because conditions assemble, they are not non-existent; because they arise from conditions, they are not existent. The wondrous principle of the Middle Way is thus brilliantly and spontaneously resolved. By means of the Middle, he refutes...

Because they are partial, the three schools were all unable to establish [the truth]. Question: I have already heard your instruction regarding how the dharma of dependent origination is neither existent nor non-existent.
But what is the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)? Answer: The two views of existence and non-existence arise fundamentally from emotional delusion;
therefore, one uses "neither existent nor non-existent" to refute them. If these views are dispelled, then all dharmas are ultimately ineffable. Thus it is said:

The path of speech is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases, as is extensively explained in the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* regarding the Gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Nevertheless, the works of Master Hui-tai truly accord with the principle of the eighteen kinds of emptiness (*aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā*) in the *Prajñāpāramitā*; however, they must not be described as a mere partial emptiness (*ekānta-śūnyatā*).

If one were to categorize them according to the principles of the Five Teachings, Master Heng largely entered into the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), while Master Zhi [largely entered into the Great Vehicle].

Both [the Master] and the Dharma-characteristics school agree that emptiness is the beginning. However, while the Master [Zhiyi] teaches the principle of the Middle Way—the non-obstruction of emptiness and existence—within the Final Teaching, the former is shallow and the latter is profound.
Thus, it is far easier to achieve excellence by using the profound to refute the shallow. As for those who advocate "adhering to emptiness" and the like:
emptiness is originally a medicine to treat the disease of existence; once the illness has departed, the medicine may well be discarded. To continue taking it...
Once it has returned, it becomes his illness; there is no way to cure it. "Not merely equal" refers to the fact that even when seeing evil, [the consequences] are still more severe.
This refers to the evil of committing evil deeds. Regarding "those who eat salt," the eighteenth fascicle of that treatise states briefly:
"For example, a rustic countryman who previously did not know salt saw someone putting salt on meat and vegetables and asked, 'Why do you do this? The other person said:"
Because this salt can make the flavors of various things delicious, the man thought to himself, "This salt can make things taste good; its own flavor must be abundant.
He then scooped up some empty salt, filled his mouth with it, and ate it. It was salty and bitter, burning his mouth, so he asked, "Why did you say that salt could make things delicious?
The other man said, "Fool! This should be measured in proper proportions and mixed [with other ingredients] to make it delicious."

What is meant by "eating salt exclusively"? It refers to an ignorant person who, upon hearing of the gate of liberation through emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*), fails to practice various meritorious virtues and merely desires to attain emptiness itself;
this constitutes wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and severs all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). Such people existed in the world below, though not in every generation.
Although the Buddha-dharma arose during the Eastern Han dynasty, its practice remained scarce. From the Two Jin dynasties onwards, the sūtras and śāstras...
It has not been widely disseminated. Truly, those with a comprehensive understanding as clear and wise as Master Kumārajīva are rare indeed.

I fear that upon seeing the Master of the Treatise (Sthiramati) refute those [opponents], people might dismiss both masters as being merely casual or superficial. This must not be so; I entreat you to consult the original biography, for it will naturally inspire the utmost respect.

From "As for those of inferior capacity" onwards, the author describes the thematic structure (*zhimai*) of the treatise. However, the thematic structure of this treatise is subtle and hidden, and various masters have attempted to differentiate it.

It is also because they differ. Through my repeated investigation and scrutiny over time, I have gradually attained this understanding; the principle seems to have a basis, as can be seen in detail from the commentaries on each section, so I shall not provide an extensive exposition here.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Initially, the principle is severed" (*chū lǐ jué xià*): "name" (*míng*) refers to the expressive terminology (*nèi-míng-yán*), and "characteristic" (*xiàng*) refers to the characterized meaning (*suǒ-quán yì-xiàng*).

Regarding "comprehending the dharmas, etc. (*liǎo fǎ děng zhě*): this is a passage from the "Ten Endurances" chapter (*Shí rěn pǐn*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Regarding the passage beginning with "Second, relying on expression" (*èr jì quán xià*): if one does not rely on...
Regarding the characteristics of these words: they likewise cannot recognize the nature of the Middle Way. "Without departing from words" refers to the text of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
"The three [aspects]" refers to the text of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. "The nature of words is empty" is also text from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
Regarding "the twelve divisions of the teaching," this refers to the meaning of the *Vajrasamādhi-sūtra*. The remainder is easily understood.

Commentary: "If one relies upon," etc., means that if one speaks according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), names are established in accordance with characteristics, and one grasps characteristics based on names.
Regarding the phrase "all such [things]" (and so forth), the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When a thing is related to another thing, name and characteristic are presented as distinct."

The "Mountains and Trees" chapter of the *Zhuangzi* states: "To drift freely among the progenitors of all things, to perceive all things without being perceived by them—how could one then be burdened?
This treatise on literature is likewise based upon this principle.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "that which is named," the general meaning is as follows: names exist in dependence upon phenomena (*dharma*); yet since phenomena themselves are empty and quiescent, names are all the more illusory and provisional.
The citation from the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* uses the first two lines to prove the emptiness of objects and the latter two lines to prove the emptiness of names. As the subsequent treatise also states:
"When one does not perceive objects as [substantial] objects, then objects are immediately the True."

Commentary: Regarding the statement "there are two types [of explanations] for this," the *shu* (commentary) is easy to understand; I shall therefore explain only the difficult points. As for "their natures are each distinct":

the name (*nāman*) is the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), while the appearance (*nimitta*) is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Under the first phrase, the general meaning is that although the object is identical to the name, the name is not identical to the object;
this reveals their mutual difference. "Seeing the object but not knowing the name" refers to seeing an object that one has not yet recognized.

Although one may perceive its appearance, one does not know its name; thus, this object is not the name. As for "conventional designations" (*saṃvṛti*), in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) these two are not identical;

their nature is fundamentally empty. Regarding the section on "restriction": it refers to the names that express and the meanings expressed within a single treatise, all of which are provisionally arranged and established as skillful means (*upāya*) to lead future beings to awakening.

Commentary: Regarding "the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*): since both names and characteristics are empty as stated above, this causes the true ultimate to stand alone beyond the realm of names and characteristics.
Because names are empty, they transcend verbal expression; because characteristics are empty, they transcend the objects of mental cognition.
Thus, the *Ratnagotravibhāga* states that the ultimate truth is such that even the mind’s cognitive objects cannot know it, let alone names, phrases, or sentences.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "First, citing [the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*]," the *Mahāyāna* refers to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Because the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (the *Dapin*) extensively explains the meaning of the Mahāyāna, that treatise fully expounds the meaning of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). Here, however, only the single proposition currently in use is cited. Furthermore, it cites the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, which likewise states:

"The turning explanation" (*parivarta-vyākhyāna*) refers to the Master of the Treatise’s further explanation by means of the first truth, the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*). By means of the first...

Both the *Ekasatya-śāstra* and the *Dvividha-śāstra* contain this; therefore, it is cited as the fundamental tenet (*siddhānta*) upon which the subsequent categories of phenomena—such as form and emptiness, and the ultimate and conventional—rely.

The phrase "all [of them]" refers to the two aforementioned treatises. The term "subsequent" and so forth refers to the six sections of the treatise that follow this point, beginning with the section on form and emptiness and concluding with the citation of the two treatises regarding the seeds of phenomena based on existence and non-existence.

These various expositions all rely on that which is neither existent nor non-existent to demonstrate the ultimate truth. If one carefully examines the intent of the commentary (*śāstra*), one will naturally recognize the purport of the treatise.
If one is confused regarding the underlying thread of the purport, how can one know the author’s intention? In my view, any interpretation of sūtras and śāstras must be proficient in three aspects:
first, the value of identifying its primary tenet; second, skill in understanding the underlying thread of the purport; and third, a profound mastery of the literal meaning of the text. These three.
To fail to fully embody these titles would be to impair the holy teaching. It is not "both" true and conventional, because it exists within the state of being both;
nor is it "neither" true nor conventional, because it exists within the state of being neither.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the two treatises, etc.," *bō* (to negate) is explained as *sàng* (to lose/eradicate), and *shì* (to explain) as *díchú* (to cleanse away).

*Dù* means "to shut off. To extinguish sound is called *jì* (quiescence); to sever form is called *liáo* (vast emptiness). The place where there is no obstruction of form is termed *xūhuò* (vacant openness);
it refers to the void where the eye’s range ends. *Hùnmáng* (chaotic vastness) refers to a state of continuous and boundless expanse; it refers to the empty space of dull, solidified stillness.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "as for the objects and so forth," it means that the inherent emptiness of the nature of things does not depend on washing them away to reveal their nature;
rather, it is within the very falsity that there is truth.

Commentary: Regarding "the first four lines," etc., this refers to following the traces to explain and establish the lines concerning mutual existence and mutual non-existence. The rest is easily understood. Commentary:
"In the *Ghanavyūha*," etc., refers to the second fascicle of that [text], which concerns names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*).

Due to names and characteristics, the various consciousnesses, such as the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), arise through discrimination. The next line reveals the emptiness of names. "From here on," etc., is also a general division of the text.
This indicates the general meaning of the following text.

Regarding the commentary’s initial section on "relying upon," etc.: the principle of emptiness and form is the defining characteristic of the Dharma; it is present in all Prajñāpāramitā sūtras and the like.

Therefore, this is shown at the outset. As that scripture’s "Chapter on Non-duality" states: "Form is itself emptiness; it is not that form ceases for there to be emptiness. The nature of form is itself empty," and so forth. Commentary: Regarding the phrase "Emptiness is not...
and below: "Form" refers to the physical object. It is like water being no different from its waves; the waves are themselves the water. Gold is no different from the vessel [it forms].

Externally, the entire vessel is gold; yet that which is not one is divided into both emptiness and form, and distinguished into both phenomenon and principle, as in the *Dharmadhātudarśana* (Contemplation of the Dharma Realm), which has two gates:
"Phenomenon and Principle Are Not Two. The newly translated *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* also contains the passage: "Form is not other than emptiness, and emptiness is not other than form.
"Analysis and destruction" (*khaṇḍana*) refers to the dissection of the treatise’s discourse, such as when one sees [the earth] by digging a well or boring a hole.

Regarding the category of emptiness (*śūnyatā*): however, the meaning of emptiness is profound. As for those with nihilistic views (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*): non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) regard the cessation of the aggregates (*skandha*) without continuity as annihilation;
the Mahāyāna regards the analytical destruction [of the aggregates] by the Hīnayāna as annihilation, as explained in the *Xuantan chao*. Regarding those with distracted minds:

the *Yicheng jiujing shixing lun* states that a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment (*prathamacittotpādaka*) has not yet fully understood emptiness and possesses three kinds of doubt.
As shown below: [The] Commentary on the "Inquiry into the Illness" (*Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*) chapter explains that illness, too, is a phenomenon produced through conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna*).

If it were truly existent, then whether coming or going, it would not arise from conditions; since it arises and ceases according to conditions, it is neither true nor existent. Regarding "surpassing the sun," etc.: the recipients are five.
The aggregates are one; the life-principle is one among the formations dissociated from mind. Because all are dependently originated, all phenomena are empty.
Regarding the commentary’s phrase "the texts are equal": while the teachings vary according to the capacities of sentient beings, their fundamental principle is originally uniform.
Commentary: Regarding the second point, "relying on [the two truths]," the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Fàngguāng jīng) states:
Śāriputra asked the Venerable Subhūti, "Do you wish to cause those who have attained realization to do so from that which is unarisen? Or do you wish to cause them to do so from that which is arisen?
Subhūti replied, "I do not cause them to attain realization from that which is unarisen, nor do I cause them to attain realization from that which is arisen. Śāriputra... [text continues]
Śāriputra said, "Is it as you have said—that there is nothing attained and nothing acquired? Subhūti replied, "There is something attained and something acquired;
yet it is not through two worldly matters that there is attainment or acquisition.
It is only by way of worldly convention that there are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas. [He] wished to discuss this.
"The foremost [state] is without attainment. There is no attainment. From the stage of *srotāpanna* up to the Buddha, there is neither reaching nor attaining.

The commentary states: Śāriputra asked, "Is there attainment through the truth of non-arising (*anutpāda-satya*), or is there attainment through the conventional truth of arising (*utpāda-saṃvṛti-satya*)?
Subhūti replied by using the non-apprehensibility (*anupalabdhi*) of *prajñā* to simultaneously negate both.
Śāriputra believed that neither existence nor non-existence could be apprehended;

therefore, Subhūti replied again that while there is both apprehension and non-apprehension, these are not different from what is attained within conventional reality (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), attainment and non-attainment are both transcended.
This meaning is understood through the *Wuming lun* (Treatise on Namelessness). Thus, the subsequent commentary points to the profound attainment (*xuande*).
Commentary: From "The ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-satya*) onwards, [the text] follows the treatise to converge upon the Middle Way.
Commentary: Regarding "citing the meaning," the twenty-fourth [fascicle] states: "World-Honored One, are the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth distinct?"

Subhūti, the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) are not different. Why is this? Because the suchness (*tathatā*) of the conventional truth is equal to the suchness of the ultimate truth.
Although they were previously distinguished as being separate, it can be understood that each is distinct within its own respective category.
Commentary: Under the Two Truths, they appear distinctly different. Thus, the *Ratnaketuparivarta Sūtra* (Renwang jing) says: "The truths are eternally two, like the two horns of an ox.
Yet, the ultimate takes the conventional as its characteristic, and the conventional takes the ultimate as its nature; how could there be any great difference between them?

Commentary: Regarding the first two phrases, etc., it means that all phenomena possess both the sense of being existent and the sense of being non-existent, as well as the sense of being non-non-existent.
The next four phrases may be understood from the commentary. Regarding the subsequent four phrases, those who transcend [the extremes of] annihilation and permanence do not sever the void;

thus they escape annihilation because [phenomena] are not truly existent, and they escape permanence for the same reason. Below the final two phrases, "if there were existence" refers to depending upon this...
To perceive the existence of dharmas is likewise not the ultimate truth. It should also be said that if they were non-existent, there would be no trace to be leveled.
This is even more clearly explained by the commentary, which bypasses the text to provide a direct interpretation.

Commentary: Regarding "the ancients," it is traditionally transmitted that they were Master Jingfa Yuan; however, this remains uncertain. "Qi" (齊) means "together" (並); "together" implies duality, yet it is not "twofold" (雙).
Because the ultimate and the conventional are mutually exclusive, it is said they are "perpetually at variance" (恒乖). "Never separate" (未曾各) also implies they are "perpetually one" (恒一).
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "successively citing," this is the intention of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*. It clarifies that verbal expression is itself suchness (*tathatā*);
within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is neither speech nor non-speech. The subsequent phrase does not destroy the characteristics of verbal expression;

within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), through the convergence of causes and conditions between teacher and disciple, verbal expression arises within the unborn. As for the subsequent sutra, it is as explained in the commentary: "not turning downward," and so forth.

This discourse concerns the approximately three hundred assemblies in which the Tathāgata preached the Dharma throughout his lifetime to benefit sentient beings. Regarding the phrase "without abandoning," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 26, states:
"For example, there was an elder whose eyesight had grown dim; while he was sewing his saṃghāṭī robe by himself, the needle’s thread came loose."
He said to the people, "Who among you delights in merit? Sew for me. At that time, the Buddha appeared before him and said, "I am one who delights in merit and is never satiated.
[The man] brought his needle to him. The bhikṣu, knowing this was the Buddha, addressed him:
"O Buddha, ocean of immeasurable merit, how can you be insatiable? The Buddha said, "Although I have reached the very limit of merit..."
[The Buddha] remained thus, yet was never satiated. Eventually, when the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, his fleshly eye immediately became clear and his wisdom-eye was perfected, and so forth.
Descending further, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Taishō No. 220), fascicle 425, states: "Since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have not spoken a single word;
you likewise have heard nothing. The *Prabhāsa-sūtra* (Taishō No. 222), fascicle 17, states: "The Tathāgata remains serene and does not speak."

Regarding the Dharma: [The passage] "the tongue covers below" refers to how many sutras state that when the Tathāgata is about to preach the Dharma, he manifests the mark of the broad and long tongue, which completely covers the trichiliocosm, signifying that what he speaks is truthful and authentic.
Regarding the body being silent: this concerns the matter in the "Non-duality" chapter of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
The intent here is that Vimalakīrti’s remaining in silence is also the preaching of the Dharma, enabling people to realize the ineffability of phenomena and enter into them.
There is no limit to speech. Thus, the Great Commentary states: "Speech, silence, gazing, and blinking are all preaching; seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are all listening.
To attain the Dharma and harmonize with the spirit is itself the meaning of preaching. As the fourth fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"There are Buddha-lands where one simply gazes without blinking and speaks no words, yet this is called preaching the Dharma," and so forth.

The commentary states: "Regarding 'the texts are equal,' etc., 'to investigate' means to examine and interrogate. Although the objects are equal, this is because it merely distinguishes the meaning of the two sūtras cited previously."

Commentary: The passage beginning with "In accordance with what follows" clarifies that false views grasp at non-existence; such grasping is therefore an affliction (*kleśa*). Now, by stating that it is "not non-existent," one transforms this view, whereby the subsequent phrase becomes applicable.

Commentary: Regarding "the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-satya*) and so forth: because both meanings—transformation and non-transformation—are transcended, it is said to be neither existent nor non-existent.
Commentary: Regarding the *tathāgatagarbha*, as explained at length in the root sūtra, to state it in brief: it is the Middle Way of True Suchness (*tathatā*) that accords with conditions.

Regarding the mind of wondrous existence, there are likewise two kinds of manifestations according to words: first, the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, because it is devoid of the twenty-five states of existence;
second, the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*, because it is fully endowed with immeasurable inherent merits.
Because it contains these merits, it is called a "treasury" (*garbha*). A detailed explanation is provided in the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*.

Regarding the phrase "the commentary cites the meaning," since the sutra merely states that the mind is neither existent nor non-existent, the commentary further explains this by citing the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, saying:
"Things arise from... Although "things" (*vastu*) is a general term, it follows the sense of the preceding sutra and specifically refers to the mind, while also encompassing all phenomena.
The term "yi" (義) means "to lead.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "investigating and seeking," etc.: it is because the sutra possesses the meaning of a carpenter's line, serving to measure and determine the deviant and the correct. "Heng" (衡) refers to a scale or balance.
This is also "leveling. It levels by balancing through reasoning and measurement; the meaning is self-evident. [Commentary: First, regarding the interrogative term:
"How" means "for what reason. Regarding the restatement: this refers to the preceding Madhyamaka position that things are neither existent nor non-existent.
How is this known to be so? Therefore, it is now restated: "The reason why it is so. Here, "so" (ran) has the sense of "thus" (ru-shi). This is because...

This refers back to the preceding [discussion on] neither existence nor non-existence. Below, the text provides a counter-explanation, stating: "Now, as for 'existence' being equal [to its opposite], there are similarities and differences in the subsequent metaphors.
Herein lies their difference, which is entirely distinct from the previous meaning; yet it is also revealed by way of analogy. By means of this, one illuminates that."
The principle is established to the utmost.

Regarding the phrase "the first two phrases, etc. in the *Sūtra*, this explains [the meaning of] "non-existence" (*abhāva*). These phrases have been extracted individually; there is no further separate commentary.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "The first sentence, etc.," here the treatise merely compiles the meanings from the upper and lower sections of the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* to serve as a citation for the explanation;
it is not without purpose. Commentary:
Regarding "Universally accomplishing, etc.," the general purport of the first pair is no different from what preceded; it simply adds the term "all" (*sarva*). This...

This concludes the final citation of texts to distinguish the Dharma. Therefore, it clarifies the existence or non-existence of all phenomena, as well as the existence or non-existence of the two types of causes and conditions for those phenomena;
all of these have been fully cited and elucidated. Beyond what has been cited here, there is not a single further phenomenon that can be cited.

The commentary (*shu*) explains the preceding and following sections, which may be understood accordingly. Regarding the subsequent "confrontation" (*dui*), the preceding section analyzed existence and non-existence based upon all phenomena; existence and non-existence are...
Meaning. This distinguishes existence and non-existence; existence and non-existence are dharmas. These two dharmas also exist by way of causes and conditions, and so forth.

At the end of the "Eighteen Emptinesses" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it says: "The emptiness of non-existent dharmas and existent dharmas. The commentary explains this very extensively; I have cited it here only briefly.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is also brief. To quote it fully: "In all worlds there are four kinds of non-existence. The first is that which has not yet arisen, called..."
1. Non-existence as that which has not yet arisen: for example, when a lump of clay exists, the function of a jar has not yet occurred. 2. Non-existence as that which has already ceased:

for example, once a jar has been destroyed, it is said to be non-existent. 3. Non-existence through mutual difference: for example, there is no horse within a cow, and no cow within a horse. The commentary states:
If we speak in terms of human affairs, it is like Rāhula having no Sunakṣatra, and Sunakṣatra having no Rāhula;
or like Yǎnzǐ having no Dàozhí, and Dàozhí having no Yǎnzǐ. In these cases, they are ultimately non-existent by name, like the horns of a rabbit or the hair of a tortoise.

As for the statement that "conditions are also innumerable," this is because each follows the specific differences among the causes and conditions of various phenomena. For example, with a grain seed as the cause, it must necessarily...
Earth, water, and so forth serve as conditions; the seed of consciousness serves as the cause. This refers to the statement that "the objects of perception and so forth serve as conditions.

Regarding the commentary on the first phrase, "and so forth" (*ādi*): because the preceding cited treatises demonstrate that whether phenomena exist or do not exist, both modes of existence and non-existence do not transcend the two categories of being and non-being.
"Mutually opposed" (*vipakṣa*) means that existence and non-existence are diametrically opposed in their essential natures. This summarizes what was previously stated.

Regarding "the first three," etc.: the first phrase clarifies that because all phenomena have causes and conditions, they ought to exist; the [next] three phrases clarify that because non-existent phenomena have causes and conditions, they ought to exist.
This is why they are subsumed. One should not say they are non-existent, as this would manifest a contradiction. Regarding "subsuming the preceding two and four," etc.:
the second phrase of the preceding [set] clarifies that because all phenomena have causes and conditions, they ought not to exist; the fourth phrase...

Because it is explained that [the effect] should not exist due to the causes and conditions of existing phenomena, it is therefore subsumed [under the category of "non-existence"]. The latter three [categories] below are merely illustrated by the preceding explanation;
the rest may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the phrase "the first two lines," etc., "should exist" also encompasses the first and third [of the four alternatives], and "should not exist" likewise encompasses [them].

The first two correspond to the fourth. The explanation of their meaning is as in the commentary (*śū*). Regarding "the same in terms of phenomena" (*dharma*): all phenomena, as well as phenomena that exist or do not exist, are "phenomena.
"Same" refers to the Middle Way, which is neither existence nor non-existence.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "initially [asserting] existence, etc.," to dogmatically cling to existence or non-existence constitutes the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). "Mental speech" (*manojalpa*) means, to state the essential point:

it refers to the conceptualization of mind and thought that has not yet been manifested through the mouth. "The title indicates" means that the single title "Not Truly Empty" (*asatyatā-śūnya*) reveals its meaning.
"What was already explained in general previously" refers to the commentary following the refutation of the three schools mentioned earlier.

This is so. To know that [the former] is to comprehend the meaning of this [latter]. The phrase "if below" implies that the aforementioned principle of "Non-Emptiness of the Unreal" has now been fully expounded;

therefore, it is concluded here. "To push" (*tui*) means to investigate. "To unravel" (*yi*) refers to the manner of carefully unraveling, contemplating, and examining. This means that through thorough reflection and investigation from beginning to end, the meaning can be understood.

Commentary: In the passage "In that sutra," below, it is shown that by relying on the names and characteristics of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one reveals the non-arising of the names and characteristics of the supreme true truth (*paramārtha-satya*);

this is precisely the true truth. The phrase "as already seen in the preceding text" refers to the commentary provided below that very section. As stated in [the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*] chapter twenty-four:
"A bodhisattva practices the Prajñāpāramitā by means of names and characteristics, yet should not enter into those names and characteristics. This is because the Master of the Treatise...

Relying on the path of skillful means (*upāyamārga*), one employs names and signs (*nāmanimitta*) to explain dharmas that are themselves devoid of names and signs. Now, the scripture is further cited to demonstrate that names and signs are fundamentally empty, so that one does not become attached to them.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 89, states: "By means of the path of skillful means, one explains [dharmas] as being without names or signs," and so forth.
The phrase "For example, like... is also from the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*. The phrase "It is not that... and following are the words of the treatise (*śāstra*). "Illusion" (*māyā*) is like a knot.

A headcloth became a hare; a thrown bamboo became a dragon. Meng Qin drew lines on the ground to create moats for a level plain, and Luan Ba spat wine that turned into rain over the Shu River—such were their transformations.
For example, the nun Liánsè (Lotus-Colored) manifested as a Wheel-Turning King, leading the way with precious steps to welcome the Buddha.
Devadatta transformed himself into a small child and deluded King Ajātaśatru within the inner garden, and so forth.

Regarding the commentary on the phrase "this is equal to": the previous statement that "things do not coincide with their names but accord with reality" and this current statement that "things lack a reality corresponding to their names" are in fact no different in meaning;
they differ only slightly in phrasing. As for the phrase "names arise from one's own conceptualization," this refers to the nature of pervasive imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Therefore, as for likes and dislikes: emotional consciousness is deceptive and false. If one arbitrarily deems an object beautiful, one establishes the name "good" for it;
if one arbitrarily deems an object ugly, one establishes the name "bad" for it. Thus, how can they be fixed? Regarding one object being given many names:

for example, the moon is also called the "toad-wheel," the "cinnamon-tree wheel," the "golden wave," and the "hare's essence. Regarding one name summoning many objects: for example, the *sūtra* uses the term "well-rope" (a rope used for drawing water from a well) [to refer to various things].
Regarding the *Xi jing* and other such texts: as explained below, the *Bencao* (Classic of Materia Medica) names the earthworm "Earth Dragon" (*dìlóng*).

How could there be any reality to being a "dragon"? *Muzé* (Equisetum) is not a thief; it simply flows downward. From the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it exists; from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it does not exist.

All phenomena are merely what they are in themselves when one discusses their names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*); because they arise dependently (*pratītyasamutpāda*), they are provisional (*prajñapti*).
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "all things, etc.," within the context of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), every individual thing possesses a name and a characteristic (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*).

Since the essence of these names and characteristics is empty and has never been established from the beginning, all phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely empty and quiescent. The phrase "the aforementioned" refers to the period from the *Prabhāsa* (Emanation of Light) chapter downward.
Commentary: The first phrase is from the treatise itself, meaning that things have no "this" or "that. The section beginning with "but people," etc., is the Master of the Treatise’s own explanation.
Regarding the phrase "such as these" and so forth: this is not intended to illustrate the point through an analogy; rather, it cites these among all phenomena to demonstrate their emptiness.
Thus, the *Pao-tsang lun* (Treasure Store Treatise) says: "Taking heaven and earth as above and below; taking the sun and moon as east and west; taking the body as self and other;
and taking emotions as right and wrong, and so forth."
The *shū* (commentary) states: "Regarding 'properly citing,' etc., the explanation in the *shū* is clear. 'Original emptiness' (*yuánkōng*) takes 'original' (*yuán*) to mean 'initial.
'Also may,' etc., likewise takes 'initial' to mean 'beginning. 'There is no beginning even for a moment' means there is no beginning in the form of a sprouting omen.

'There is no non-existence even for a moment' means that deluded sentiments do not cease from moment to moment, continuing in an uninterrupted succession of *kṣaṇas*. The other metaphors can be understood accordingly."
Commentary: Regarding the first phrase and so forth: when one realizes that there is no fixed characteristic of "this" or "that," then the phenomena grasped as such are also quiescent.

The characteristics of "this" and "that" manifest in dependence upon phenomena, just as a snake manifests in dependence upon a rope. That both the subject (the grasper) and the object (the grasped) are false is the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).
The rope upon which the snake relies is called the *paratantra* (dependent nature); the hemp that the rope depends upon constitutes the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature).

The *Biography of Yue Guang* in the *Book of Jin* relates: A guest came to the home of Yue Guang. As Guang raised his cup to pour wine, the reflection of a bow from a jade screen entered the guest’s cup.

The guest thought he had mistakenly swallowed a snake; shortly thereafter, illness arose, and it did not subside for a year. Later, when he saw Yue Guang, Guang explained the matter to him and analyzed the illusion for him.

The guest suddenly attained realization, and his illness was immediately cured. There are truly many such cases like this; one should recognize that pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) arises and ceases.
According to the intent of this treatise, all phenomena of the dependent nature (*paratantra*) are neither existent nor empty.

Yet, through false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), one grasps them as being either existent or non-existent, distinguishing between self and other, right and wrong, things and the self, and so forth. These arise in a chaotic jumble, and one remains unaware of their origin. If...
When one realizes that emotions are empty, then every phenomenon (dharma) is neither existent nor non-existent. Thus, the *Treatise* says: "Since one has realized... and so forth.

Therefore, the *Verses on Consciousness-Only* (*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-kārikā*) states: "This nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is non-existent; it is merely the false attachment [of those who] rely upon it.

According to the teaching of the Nature School (*Xingzong*), this lack of awakening exists within the six coarse levels of phenomenal consciousness (*shishi*). However, according to the Dharma-characteristics school (*Faxiang*), it refers strictly to the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, as described therein.

(As stated above). In the *Laṅkāvatāra* and other sutras, this is termed "erroneous conceptualization" (*parikalpita*). Alternatively, it is called "discriminating the essence. Thus, the afflictions such as the five views and the four graspings are all instances of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*).
Commentary: Regarding "The Accomplished and Complete" (*Chengju*) below, the full text states: "This dharma is non-existent; because the dharma does not exist, one forcibly designates it with a name.
Regarding "Garden and Grove" (*Yuanlin*) below, according to Lin Xiyi’s preface to the *Zhuangzi*: "Zhuang Zhou was a man of the Song state, styled Zihou. He served as an official;

he once served as the Magistrate of Lacquer Garden (*Qiyuan*), hence the term 'Garden and Grove. The citations in the commentary are entirely from that text, and the explanations of the terms are likewise from it."
The meaning of the *shu* (commentary): This distinguishes between right and wrong; since there is no fixed substance, it is also empty.

It is no different from this. The *shu* continues: "The next two phrases, etc. refers to the fact that dharmas such as names and characteristics arise and perish and are not permanent; thus, the sage’s emotions and thoughts have already perished.
That is, by transforming [the phenomenal], one perceives the unchanging permanence. "Permanence" extends downward;

this means that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have chaotic delusions, perceiving all phenomena as having fixed characteristics with a dense array of distinctions between self and other, never for a single moment attaining penetration. The Sage reverses this: within delusion itself, there is wisdom.

Therefore, the Great Commentary (*Da shu*) explains the causal nature (*hetu-svabhāva*), saying: "Precisely because sentient beings take the inclusion of the virtues of nature (*xingde*) as their essence, they rely upon..."
The ocean of wisdom is taken as the source. Yet, as appearances shift and essences diverge, emotions arise and wisdom becomes obstructed.

Someone asked me about the principle of mutual inclusion within the Huayan school. Pointing to a pillar, he asked, "Do you mean for this pillar to enter that pillar, or for that pillar to contain this pillar?
I replied, "What you have asked precisely commits the greatest taboo of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong). That [teaching] must transcend emotion and leave behind views."

You seek [the Dharma] through emotional views (*qingjian*). Since emotional views constitute an obstruction, how could the Dharma be compatible with them? You should set aside such emotions and contemplate this. [Commentary:

Below the passage on the *Prabhāsa* [Sūtra], it is cited according to the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. The twenty-ninth fascicle of that Sūtra states: "The unmoving reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) establishes the locus for all dharmas.
This means that not destroying conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is called "establishing a locus. This is because the ultimate (*paramārtha*) is precisely the conventional.
Commentary: "The Sage is wisdom" means that one who has attained the non-conceptual mind is called a sage;

those from the first bhūmi upward are all termed sages. Regarding "the divine mind," the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* states: "The profound and real spiritual understanding is called the mind.

"Divine" (shen) means numinous (ling). This refers to the numinous and wondrous awakened mind. As the Preface by Guifeng says: "Profound, empty, wondrous, and pure; brilliantly radiant, numinous, and luminous," and so forth. "Ren" (benevolence) [is as follows].
The *Rājanirdeśa-sūtra* intends to demonstrate that the nature of delusion and the nature of wisdom are non-dual; there is merely a reversal between confusion and awakening.
Now, examining the following section, it comprehensively synthesizes the preceding text. The previous commentary, following the structure of the treatise, has also gradually unfolded its meaning.

The purport of the text is radiant and clearly established as being free from error. One who reflects carefully will understand it with clarity. The first phrase of the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* establishes its name based on its causal characteristics (*nimitta*), just as one might refer to "this" or "that."
The second phrase states that various characteristics arise based on dependent causes and conditions. These two phrases distinguish the arising of names and characteristics.
Furthermore, these two give rise to deluded conceptualization based upon the two dharmas of name and characteristic. Therefore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:

"Characteristics and names always follow one another, able to produce all deluded conceptualizations. Thus, these three dharmas merely arise through mutual conditioning; their intrinsic nature [is empty].

Fundamentally empty. Emptiness is the suchness (*tathatā*) of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). Below this, if one realizes the principle that these three natures are empty of intrinsic nature, this is precisely right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*).

Regarding the identification of the three natures: as for "characteristics" (*nimitta*) being the dependent-arising (*paratantra-svabhāva*), if we carefully examine the intent of the sūtras, "characteristics" contains two meanings.
First, the imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), such as seeing a snake based on a rope, or seeing a ghost based on a tree stump. This...

Names and characteristics are all *parikalpita* (imagined). Second, the mind and mental factors of the *paratantra* (dependent) nature—such as a rope or a tree stump—are the names and characteristics.
Regarding "profoundly seeking": "profound" (*ming*) means quiescent; "seeking" (*sou*) means to investigate. This means that by seeking with a tranquil mind, one may finally perceive the principle.
"Pointing at the palm" means seeing the principle with such clarity as if looking at an object within one's own palm. The text employs the *Analects*.
