Let us assume this as a metaphor. However, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* speaks of the two wheels of wind and gold rubbing against each other, whereby fire is seen within the ocean;

Zhuangzi says that there is fire within water that can burn the great mass of earth. If one seeks their actual reality, such things do indeed exist, yet they are not what is being taken here as the primary point.
Regarding the statement that "the cause of illness arises from medicine," the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* says: "It is like having an illness that must be treated by taking medicine. If the medicine..."
Furthermore, if it becomes diseased, it is incurable; this too is a hypothetical illustration.

However, in the world, there are many instances where medicine and tonics cause disease, such as the Tang Emperor Xianzong, who took excessive amounts of elixirs and contracted a disease of acute dryness, and others like him. These examples are all cited as metaphors for what is difficult to cure.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "as for the states," the general meaning is that if one grasps at them, the two views will arise accordingly; if one abandons them, both virtues will be discarded.
Only by neither grasping nor abandoning does one begin the practice of non-abiding. This can be understood with precision in the *Nirvāṇa-śāstra* below.
Commentary. Regarding the phrase "this refers to," the general purport first definitively establishes that the intent of Laozi is not to compete with things, but to harmonize and blend with them.
"To be the same as dust" means to be the same as things. The *Lun* (Treatise) speaks of "dust and toil" (*chen lao*), which refers precisely to the realm of birth and death.

The commentary explains the meaning of "coming and going" by following the interpretation in the *Da chao* (Great Commentary) regarding the expression "repeated cycles without limit," as well as the discussion of stillness and movement in the *Bujian lun* (Treatise on Non-Transmigration).
The principle of non-contradiction is explained as follows. Regarding the passage "To understand fully" and below, the third fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"Nirvāṇa does not exist apart from saṃsāra, nor does saṃsāra exist apart from nirvāṇa. There is no characteristic of contradiction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa."
Commentary: Regarding this objection and so forth: as the Treatise states, "Although the Sage’s mind has no cognition, if one takes it from a distance, it is pervasive;
if one takes it from nearby, it simply has no dwelling. What is now called "no cognition" is the same as saying "no dwelling. Regarding "the faculties having matured," etc.:
The *Śāsanāntara-sūtra* states: "Those who were to be delivered—whether in the heavens or among humans—have all already been delivered.

As for those not yet delivered, the conditions for their deliverance have also already been established. Therefore, it is said that those who cultivated their practice in past lives will be delivered in this life;

while for those who have newly conceived faith in this life, whether they hear the name, listen to the Dharma, prostrate, make offerings, praise, or repent, these acts shall all result in their attainment [of liberation] in the future."
Regarding the conditions for delivering [sentient beings]: even if they do not believe, those who hold wrong views likewise all become remote causes [for their eventual deliverance].
As stated in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. In the commentary (*śāstra*), the "objection" and so forth refers to the doubt that expedient wisdom arises and ceases in accordance with conditions.

Commentary: Regarding the two preceding lines, it means that mental phenomena arise from four conditions and cease when those conditions are absent. For example, for visual consciousness to arise, four conditions must be present:
first, the seed of consciousness as the direct substantial cause (*hetu-pratyaya*); second, the eye faculty as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*);
third, the visible object as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); and fourth, the uninterrupted succession of moments as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

The same applies to the remaining consciousnesses. Regarding "the mind of the noble ones is inferior": this means that the noble ones exhaustively reach the ultimate limit of the moment (*kṣaṇa*), realizing and witnessing the non-arising of the characteristic of birth (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*).
In a single thought-moment, all traces are severed; the three periods of time are suddenly shattered. Thus, the *Thirteenth Chapter on the Emission of Light* states:

"In Prajñā, there is no dharma that can arise, nor is there any dharma that can cease. As for the "four characteristics," they are birth, abiding, change, and cessation (*utpāda, sthiti, anyathātva, nirodha*).

Furthermore, these four characteristics arise in mutual dependence, revolving in each moment (*kṣaṇa*). If one is deluded regarding their phenomenal aspects (*lakṣaṇa*), they appear distinct and vivid in every division;
yet if one realizes their fundamental nature (*dharmatā*), they are extinguished at every stage. Thus, the "Momentary Chapter" (*Kṣaṇika-parivarta*) of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

"That which arises in the very first moment is simultaneously subject to cessation; this is not taught for the sake of ordinary people. Since the characteristic of arising itself does not even come into being, how could the characteristics of duration and change possibly emerge?"
This can be clearly understood through careful reflection.

Regarding the *Avataṃsaka* and other sutras mentioned in the commentary: this refers to the eightieth verse, which says, "The Buddha’s wisdom is as vast and equal as space, pervading the minds of all sentient beings," and so forth.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is as previously cited. As for "having no mind," it means that not even a single deluded thought arises.
The mind that extinguishes the mind: one is the tranquil, signless mind capable of illumination; the rest may be understood accordingly. Regarding "absence of partiality" (*wusi*):

"partiality" refers to the partiality of emotional attachment. For example, to rescue those who are kin while abandoning those who are distant—because such guidance is neither equitable nor universal, it constitutes partiality.
According to the commentary of Qingliang (Zongmi), because [the Buddha] is free from partiality, he is also said to be "without thought" (*wusi*), like a *maṇi* jewel.

It rains jewels in response to those who seek them; the celestial drum produces sound to warn of thieves. These serve as metaphors for the subsequently attained awakening (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), which manifests in response to conditions.
Since this response does not originate from a self, it is said to be "without thought. As the aforementioned treatise states: "The spirit has no deliberation," and so forth.
However, when one reflects privately upon the application of these meanings, they are fully comprehensive and sublime.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "This is only," the "Discourse on Equalizing All Things" (*Qi wu pian*) in the *Zhuangzi* speaks of the "Tianlai" (the windpipe of Heaven), saying: "This is only non-action; were there action, then ten thousand apertures would clamor together.
"Is wei" (is only) is equivalent to the colloquial expression "only except for" (zhi chu). This means that [the response] should not depend on an external stimulus;

yet where there is a stimulus, there is nothing that does not respond—like an echo in a valley answering a call, or the reflection of the moon imprinting upon clarity. Below the words "xu wu" (void and non-being), Zhuangzi and Laozi both speak of the Dao...

The school [of the *Awakening of Faith*] takes emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as its fundamental principle. It maintains that the Way of spontaneity (*svabhāva*) is the ultimate non-existence. Thus, the Master Lao said: "It is empty yet never exhausted";
he also said: "Empty the mind"; he further said: "It is in its emptiness that the utility of the cart lies"; and he also said: "Returning once more to non-being," and so forth.

This commentary explains these points based on the authentic teachings, which is precisely the intent of the treatise. The section beginning with "Xianxiu" (Worthy Head) refers to the Preface to the *Awakening of Faith*.

The general meaning is as follows: Birth and extinction reside within the capacity of the sentient being; for the Sage, there is no coming or going. Based on this, beneath the Ashvattha tree, he came yet was not born;
at the side of the City of the Mallas, he departed yet did not perish. This is simply due to the varying intensity of the conditions and responses of our own minds.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "this distinguishes," the intent of the commentary is as follows: Noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) is void and non-existent; it is neither arising nor ceasing. There are explicit texts on this point.
While it is said that delusion and wisdom merely lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), they have never been said to be without arising and ceasing.

Therefore, the commentary reconciles the meaning by stating that "arising and ceasing" are spoken of here in the sense that both [delusion and wisdom] are equally non-existent. The arising of delusion and wisdom exists through conditions; they do not arise from an intrinsic nature. They do not...
"Self-nature is cessation.

Regarding the commentary's phrase "it is also like," etc.: this cites an example. Both terms for the two truths are called *satya* (truth/reality). They are called *satya* because they are real and because they are thoroughly examined (*saty-ālocana*).
When divided into the ultimate and the conventional, they differ according to their respective divisions.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the noble mind and so forth," the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-kārikā* states: "By means of this or that pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*), one conceptually constructs various things.
This refers to the universal conceptualization and deliberation regarding non-existent selves and phenomena, whereby one clings to them as real selves and phenomena.

Based on this, both types of clinging to self and phenomena are termed "pervasive conceptualization" (*parikalpa*). According to the *Awakening of Faith*, this extends from the three stages of worthiness prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh ground.

When the mind is fulfilled, the two attachments are finally exhausted. Regarding the phrase "the characteristics of consciousness" (*vijñāna-lakṣaṇa*) below: this refers to the three subtle aspects of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), which are eliminated from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward through to the Buddha-stage.
This merely extinguishes one portion—the aspect of non-awakening (*abodha*)—within consciousness, while not extinguishing the other portion, which is the nature of awakening (*bodhi-svabhāva*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "Yongjia": it states in full that "one does not use knowledge to know stillness, nor does one know it for oneself."
It is known. It cannot be said that it lacks knowledge, for its nature is luminously clear and thus differs from wood or stone.
It is like a hand that does not grasp an object and likewise does not form a fist; yet it cannot be said that it lacks hands, for the hand remains at ease. Thus it differs from a rabbit’s horns.
Now, this verse first eliminates the delusion of having knowledge and subsequently eliminates the error of lacking knowledge; its nature is luminously clear.
However, it reveals that the essence is perfectly illuminating and not subject to cessation. How wondrous! How ultimate!
That awakening and realization are such as this causes people even a thousand years later to accept them with reverence. Guifeng’s *Brief Extracts* from the lineage of Heze quotes this;

thus the preface says: "The mind is quiescent yet cognizant; this is termed Perfect Enlightenment," and so forth. These are the gates of all wonders, quoting entirely from the text of Laozi. There he says: "Mysterious within the mysterious..."
"Profound" (*xuan*) is the gateway to all wonders. Below the *Avataṃsaka* [section], it refers to ten individuals, such as Vasumitra, who questioned Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
Each, according to their wisdom and knowledge, offered a single verse in response. The verse responding with wisdom says: "The wisdom of all Buddhas is sovereign;

throughout the three periods of time, there is no obstruction. Such is the realm of insight—equal and pervasive like empty space. The response regarding knowledge states: "It is not something that can be apprehended by consciousness."

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is likewise not the domain of the mind; its nature is fundamentally pure. This is revealed to all sentient beings. A brief explanation is provided as in the commentary (*śāstra*).

In the latter part of this treatise, the meaning of "non-cognition" (*ajñāna*) is used to manifest true wisdom (*jñāna*). However, wisdom is indeed cognition, and cognition is also wisdom; therefore, they are not differentiated.
This is not a case of distinguishing essence and function based on the three types of *prajñā*. A detailed exposition would be too prolix.

Commentary: Regarding "delusive objects": objects such as the five sense-fields are called delusive objects. From "Now, below" onwards, it is shown that both the delusive mind and delusive objects are empty by nature through dependent origination;
both are the realm of the True Truth (satyārtha) illumined by Prajñā. From "One Mind, below" onwards, they are provisionally divided according to different perspectives.
From "How, below" onwards, the previous objection is refuted and concluded.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "among these," "hidden" (*yin*) means profound and steep. "Manifest" (*jian*; pronounced *xian*) means difficult to manifest within the mind. Below the first phrase:

if the essence of the dharma (*dharmatā*) were not indicated, toward what would meanings such as quiescence and function be distinguished? As for the meaning of "quiescence and function": if one spoke merely of "quiescence and function," it would also be a phenomenon (*dharma*).
However, because it is contrasted here with "mind and object," it is termed a "meaning" (*artha*). "That is wisdom," etc., indicates the two.

The Dharma has no separate essence. [In the] *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on Dedication" (*Parīndanā-parivarta*), since Suchness and Wisdom do not exist externally to one another, they are two yet non-dual.
Now, regarding the subsequent discussion: Quiescent Suchness is the realm of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*); the function of Wisdom is the mind of Prajñā.
Regarding the phrase "using the lower [categories]," etc.: what has preceded is a general exposition of the Great Principle; from here on, the text is analyzed in detail.

"That which is the essence" and below refers to the twofold division of mind and object. "This and that" and below takes the mind as "this" and the object as "that. "Grasping both together" and below: the first two lines present two differing explanations regarding sequence.
That is to say, while the essence and its function are identical in substance, they differ in time; it is merely a difference of timing, not a difference in nature.
They are identical. In this third [case], it means that they are correctly identical yet occur at different times; thus, while they appear different, they are fundamentally identical.

It is not a matter of before and after. Therefore, it is said that they are "doubly grasped. Consequently, below, he poses a hypothetical question: "If they are identical, they are merely identical; if they are different, they are merely different."
What is meant by "different yet identical" and "identical yet different"? The *Lun* (Treatise) answers this by stating: "Therefore, to distinguish that which is different yet identical...
and so forth; this may be illustrated by referring to the commentary below.

The fourth phrase also derives from the third, because it is "identical yet different," and not merely "different yet identical. As for the phrase "this is then [the case] below," etc., it can be understood through reflection. Within this...

The four propositions do not involve a mutual comparison of meanings or characteristics; rather, because the Dharma of the single source of quiescence and function inherently possesses these four principles, one should apply the mind to illuminate them, so that their patterns and principles appear clearly.
Commentary: Regarding the explanation of the preceding "etcetera": as for "one wisdom," because it is one, it is said to be "non-dual"; this refers to the wisdom of suchness (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).

"Reality" refers to the realm of the aforementioned ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). "Citing the myriad dharmas" means that dependent origination is itself emptiness, for this is what is illuminated by *prajñā*.
As the Heart Sutra says: "Practicing profound *prajñā*, he clearly perceives that the five aggregates are all empty; he does not [perceive] the aggregates..."
One perceives emptiness outside of all such phenomena. As the preceding treatise states: "To perceive the true mark of phenomena is called prajñā," and so forth.
The phrase "internal and external" is an explanation of the term "and" (ca).
Commentary: Regarding the explanation of the preceding terms: however, the two names "quiescence" (*jì*) and "function" (*yòng*) are established through the mutual dependence of mind and object.

Function arises based on quiescence; thus, function is permitted to differ from quiescence, and so the two names are established. Now, it is clarified that there is no function external to the essence, and function is subsumed within quiescence.

At the moment function ceases, quiescence likewise does not stand. One should know that although quiescence and function are briefly indicated here, they are also spoken of in accordance with conventional usage. First...
Within a single meaning, there is nothing at all upon which to rely. The other meanings are as explained in the commentary (*śāstra*).

Regarding the phrase "the crane is too tall," etc.: this refers to mountains and peaks being too high, ravines and gullies being too deep, creatures such as the *kūṇapata* and the *garuḍa* being too large, and those like the *jiao-ming* (gnat) being too small, and so forth.
However, although their natures are inferior, they differ when viewed through their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); yet, from the perspective of their nature (*svabhāva*)...
If one draws from them, they are the same; being the same, they are fundamentally identical. How could they require being extended, cut short, leveled, or filled before they become equal?
This refers to the "Pianmu" (Webbed Toes) chapter of the *Zhuangzi*, for which the commentary cites the full text of that passage.
Commentary: Regarding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and others, the wording differs slightly. The hundredth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"All dharmas, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, within the Prajñā [Pāramitā] are neither of one characteristic nor of different characteristics. The *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (Renwang jing) also says:
"Prajñā is neither identical to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) nor separate from the five aggregates," and so forth.
Commentary: Regarding the first two phrases and so forth, this means that quiescence and function are but a single mind. It is like a mani jewel: its perfectly formed substance is quiescence;
its crystal-clear transparency is function. If separated, the two aspects appear different; if united, internal and external are one and the same.
One may reflect back upon oneself to seek it within; do not follow words to look elsewhere. As for the phrase "borrowing from below," it refers to that [which follows].
The first chapter states: "These two emerge from the same source but have different names. This is borrowed merely to form an expression and to embody the subtlety of the underlying thesis;

it is not intended to exclude alternative interpretations. I fear that if one sees that stillness (*jì*) and function (*yòng*) emerge together, one might further seek a root or source for them within stillness and function.

As the following response regarding stillness and illumination (*jìzhào*) says: "When principle reaches its ultimate, it is equally non-existent (*tóngwú*). Since it is said they are "the same," this sameness must be an ultimate non-existence.
Furthermore, it says: "If one refers to 'arising' as being the same as external phenomena, and refers to it as 'not-self,' then one should likewise say 'below.

To infer this by way of its meaning, the principle is necessarily so. When one corner is presented, the other three can be inferred. If one clings to the literal text to define the meaning, the meaning will be harmed.
Regarding the passage 'in terms of substance,' since substance is weighty, it may be called the 'host'; since function is light, it may be addressed as the 'guest.'"

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the function of the mind" and so forth: here, the mention of "mind" refers to the entirety of the single mind of the true aspect (*dharmatā*). In this state, nature and characteristics are fused;

the object and the mind are one; the provisional and the real are identical; and self and other are interpenetrating. Nevertheless, when analyzing the principle according to the text, the provisional and the real are clearly distinguished; yet when synthesizing the intent to accord with the fundamental source, stillness and function are unified as one.
Commentary: "Exhausting that which is beyond phenomena" (*xiàngwài*): "Phenomena" (*xiàng*) refers to the myriad phenomena, which is to say, the myriad things.

Because the Buddha’s principle lies beyond the mundane world, it is called "beyond phenomena. "Pure discourse" (*qīngtán*): this refers to the preceding discussion on Prajñā, which transcends existence and non-existence and deeply surpasses emotional consciousness;

it is the elegant discourse on true purity and formlessness. However, the general narrative of the preceding text can be understood by examining both the preceding and following sections. The initial translation also consists of two parts.

The first answer speaks of both [wisdoms]. The second also contains both wisdoms. The third, by taking "seeking wisdom" (*paryeṣaṇājñāna*) as its object, speaks only of ultimate wisdom (*tattvajñāna*).
The fourth answer, regarding "non-appropriation," also applies to both wisdoms. The fifth answer, regarding "this shall be," also discusses both wisdoms.

The sixth answer, regarding "abiding in non-existence," is only ultimate wisdom. The seventh answer, regarding "arising and ceasing," pertains only to conventional wisdom (*vyavahārajñāna*). The eighth answer [applies] to both.
It is not that [the term] "only" (*mātra*) applies solely to actual wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*); therefore, the Commentary says so.

Alternatively, regarding the section on "object and wisdom" (*viṣaya-jñāna*) below—such as in the responses concerning "being thus," "abiding in non-existence," and so forth—one can understand that these all contain the detailed analysis of the similarities and differences between object and wisdom. However, the beginning and end of this treatise certainly cannot be gauged by shallow or deep standards.
Nevertheless, the subtle points of its establishment are also briefly indicated in the Commentary. Now, if I were to provide a detailed exposition, I fear it would become too prolix.
"Tired of the profusion. One may examine it through inquiry to realize its own subtle ingenuity.

Regarding the "Commentary on the Explanation of Characters" (*Shuowen*) and so forth: "yi" (詣) also means "to arrive at. "The various commentaries" refers to the commentaries by [Liu] Yao, Jingyuan, and others.
"Han Chu" and below refers to Liu Jiao, the younger brother of the High Ancestor (Gaozu), who was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Chu and posthumously titled Yuan. His "remnant people" were...
"Descendants. "Externally, he was good at being humble," referring to the Six Classics of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, as well as the books of the various philosophers (*zhǐzǐ*).

"Internally, he researched... "Research" (*yán*) means to polish; it also refers to the process of chipping and carving [wood]. Furthermore, it signifies his ability to refine Buddhist principles with precision.
"With the Confucian scholars... The Biography of Master Yuǎn states: "Guests of pure faith arrived unexpectedly. Liu Yímin of Pénghéng, Lèi Cí..."
The group included Zong of Yanmen, Zhou Xuzhi, Xin Cai, Bi Yingzhi, Zong Bing of Nanyang, Zhang Caimin, Zhang Jishuo, and others.
They all renounced the world and its honors to follow Huiyuan’s travels and reside at Mount Lu—a mountain located in Jiangzhou.
Among the eighteen worthies, according to the "Vow of the Lotus Society" by Huiyuan (Yimin), there were one hundred and... [fellow practitioners] who had stilled their minds and possessed true faith.
There are twenty-three individuals. According to this, it is not only the eighteen worthy ones.

Only Xie Lingyun composed the "Eulogies on the Eighteen Worthy Ones of Mount Lu," which refers to nine people including Master Huiyuan, Master Daosheng, and Daojing; two foreign monks, Buddhabhadra and Guṇabhadra;
and the seven previously mentioned, such as the "Leftover Subjects" (Yimin). Because the biographies primarily discuss the eighteen worthy ones, I shall provisionally follow them here.

Xie Kangle noted this. "Refinement and concentration" (jingjie): "refinement" means single-mindedness; "concentration" means restriction. He planted lotuses to symbolize the lotus ponds of the Pure Land.
This accords with Li Gong’s preface to Li Bashi’s *Painting of the Eighteen Sages*, which describes the lotus pond at Donglin.
Xie Kangle opened the way. Kangle sought to join the community, but Master Huiyuan declined him, saying his mind was too distracted.

He once sent a letter inviting Tao Yuanming, but Yuanming declined on the pretext of being drunk and did not respond. Therefore, later generations inscribed: "Tao Liang was often drunk and could not be summoned;
Master Xie’s mind was distracted, yet he went and returned. Longguang is the name of a temple where Master Daosheng resided.
The Biography of Master Daosheng states that he traveled to Chang’an together with Huiri and Huiyan to receive instruction from Master Kumārajīva.

The monastic community in Guanzhong all regarded him as one of divine insight. At that time, he was on intimate terms with the Master of Discourse (Vasubandhu); "to be without opposition" means to be in perfect accord and harmony.
"Pingshu" refers to He Yan of the Wei dynasty; his courtesy name was Pingshu. He was skilled at pure conversation (qingtan) alongside Wang Bi and others;
thus, the Recluse (Huiyuan) compared him to this master of discourse, referring to him as "He Pingshu among the monks. Regarding the phrase "one who inspires me," the *Analects* states:
"Shang is one who inspires me; it is only with him that I can truly discuss the Odes. The general meaning is that when Confucius wished to explain the Odes, [he found that] Bo Shang...

You have rightly grasped the essential meaning and are able to revive the teachings of Confucius. To compare it now and examine it in detail through principle, it is indeed as Master Yao has pointed out.

As for the fact that the characters used in the commentary are nearly identical, this is also frequently the case in the Classics and Histories. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Chidu lun), fascicle 16, states:
"Just as one wishes to exit, the gate is already closed. Master Yao originally used the character *cai* (裁).

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "those who have left behind" (*yí*): In antiquity, there were high-minded scholars who established themselves through the Way and its Virtue (*dàodé*), forgetting their own persons and casting aside the world—such as those in the lineage of Xi Zilíng and Dài Kuī.

Neither the Son of Heaven could enslave them as subjects, nor could the feudal lords treat them as friends; they were called *chǔshì* (recluses). Yímín (the "Left-Behind Man") was also of this same class. Regarding the phrase "Yú Zhòng":
The *Lúnyǔ* speaks of seven men who acted according to their own principles; it refers to Yú Zhòng, [Zhōngní, Shēnshù, Wǎngzǐqí, Jiǎolǐ, Yǎngshēng, and Fǔshēng].
Yi Yi, Zhu Zhang, Liuma Hui, Shao Lian, and others were all recluses. Chaisang is the name of a county.
As for Huan Xuan, he was the son of Huan Wen of the Eastern Jin dynasty. "Usurper and rebel" refers to his intent to seize the Jin throne;

these events occurred during the reign of Emperor An, but I shall not recount them here for fear of prolixity. "Panshi" means a large rock. Regarding "stacking eggs," the *Biographies* (Shiji) states that when King Xian of Jin...

The Duke was building a nine-storied terrace. The common people were crying out in distress, yet none dared to remonstrate. When Grand Master Xun Xi entered, Duke Xian asked him, "Are you going to remonstrate with me regarding my building this terrace?
Xun said, "No. I have heard that Your Majesty delights in feats of skill; I wish to offer a small contribution. The Duke asked, "What skill do you possess?
He replied, "I am able to stack nine eggs one atop another. The Duke was delighted and ordered him to try. He succeeded in stacking them up to seven, and then to eight.
The structure was on the verge of collapsing. Duke [Huan] said, "How perilous! Xun Xi replied, "This is not yet perilous.
If Your Grace builds a nine-storied terrace, the realm will be exhausted and weary, and the common people will rebel; that would truly be perilous. The Duke said joyfully, "Excellent advice!
(and so forth). *Bì* refers to appointment; *mìng* refers to a summons. Regarding the Grand Marshal (*taishǒu*) and others: Liu Yu, the Taizu of Song, formerly served as the [Grand Marshal] of Jin...
To the Grand Marshal (Taishi). Regarding those who hold high principles and observe the rites of the worthy: Huiyu observed that Liu Zhi could not be subdued by force.

Together with the Minister of Education Wang Mi, the Chancellor Huan Xuan, and other eminent officials, they deliberated upon and honored the title of "Yimin" (Leftovers of the People) for him. *Chong* means profound; *miao* means distant.
"Far away. "Noble and lofty" means that one whose virtue is high and whose will is pure is worthy of honor and esteem. The character *yǎng* (仰) means to look up to with admiration.
The character *zhù* (佇) is an error. "Sunk on land" (*lùchén*): "land" (*lù*) refers to level ground; the meaning is that a man of virtue does not ascend to a prominent position.
Regarding the phrases "in Pinglu" and "secluded in mountain forests," these refer to Mount Lu.

As for the commentary’s citation of ancient precedents: although the present and the past are distant, their profound resonance remains eternally identical. How much less could a distance of several thousand li between north and south possibly create a separation?
As the *Xici* (Appended Phrases) states: "Those of the same sound respond to one another; those of the same breath seek one another out. This is...
This refers to the following. The "Tángdì" chapter of the *Máo Shī* states: "How much more so for those who sigh long and deeply.

Regarding the commentary on "Yuan duì" (Deeply facing each other): this means that the teacher and the student of profound learning face one another as a pair. As for the phrase "having already exhausted": this means that more than half has already been completed.
"Jie" (解) means to thoroughly understand. Regarding "yu yong xia" (語用下): the *Xici* says, "The wise man observes the *tuan* commentaries, and his understanding is already more than half complete.
"Guàn" (慣) means vexation; its pronunciation is *mèn*. It describes a state in which the mind and will are not at peace.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the first, their dwelling," it refers to the Sangha possessing the six harmonies: (1) harmony of body through communal residence; (2) harmony of speech through the absence of dispute;

(3) harmony of mind through the absence of opposition; (4) harmony of precepts through collective practice; (5) harmony of view through shared understanding; and (6) harmony of benefit through equal distribution.
This commentary now assigns these to the text as they appear; among these six, some may be lacking.

Commentary: Regarding the covenant text of the feudal lords, according to the *Zuozhuan* on the ninth year of Duke Xī’s reign, at the assembly of Kuíqiū, the sacrificial animals were displayed but not slaughtered;
the written documents were placed upon the animals. These "writings" refer to the five mandates. The first mandate stated: "Punish those who are unfilial; do not displace the designated heir;
do not take a concubine as a wife," and so forth. It continued: "All you people who have sworn this alliance, after the oath has been taken..."
"To return to what is good. "Inscription" (ming) means to carve. "Inscription" refers to a name; it means to record one's aspirations by name.
It is like King Tang of Yin, who had inscriptional words carved upon his basin, such as "If one makes oneself new today, one must make oneself new day after day," and so forth.
The intention of the "Leftover People" (yimin) was to take their sincere entrustment and carve it as an inscription within their hearts, making them as bright and clear as the sun and moon.
Commentary: Regarding "the first hexagram," this refers to the *xiang* (image) of the ninth third line of the Qian hexagram. Such is the image of Qian; it represents the figure of the sovereign.
"The hidden dragon does not act" (*qianliu long wuyong*) corresponds to Shun fishing at Leize. "The seen dragon is in the field;

it is advantageous to see the great man" (*jianlong zaitian, lijian daren*) means that the virtue of the great man gradually manifests, and it is advantageous for the people of the world to behold him. The ninth third line represents the sovereign...
"The son [of heaven] is active and vigilant all day long; in the evening he remains apprehensive as if facing peril, yet there is no blame.

The *Wenyan* says: "Double strength yet not in the center; above he is not in the heavens, below he is not in the fields. Therefore, he is active and vigilant, being alert according to the times; though in danger, there is no blame. A brief commentary states:
This line occupies the lower position of the upper trigram, hence it is said that "above he is not in the heavens. It resides at the beginning of the lower domain.
Therefore it is said that "the lower does not abide in the field. Because it rides upon the yang lines of the second and third positions, it is called "double strength and not central.

This image represents a sovereign initiating an undertaking; above, he has not yet attained the dignity of the fifth place, while below, there is the peril of double strength. Thus, the difficulty of proceeding correctly is evident.
Therefore, by day he was diligent and tireless; by night he was anxious and vigilant, as if facing peril, never letting this from his mind.

Yimin remarked that the Master of the Community (She-zhu) advanced in the Way and cultivated virtue, lecturing by day and practicing meditation by night with unremitting diligence; thus it is said, "diligent and tireless," and so forth.
Recently, I received instructions from my superior teacher, a man from Wusi in the Western Regions, who left home at a young age and recited the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.
He recited the Vinaya and various sections of the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, and studied treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā*, and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

In his middle years, he encountered the Imperial Preceptor Phags-pa, from whom he received the secret treasury empowerments and the bodhisattva vows. He maintained a constant practice of meditation at dawn and dusk.
He entered meditative concentration more than thirty times. He never had a moment’s leisure day by day for preaching the Dharma or distributing food.

He also once or twice questioned his teacher regarding his understanding, and [the Master] produced a brief compilation of five hundred sections from the Sūtras, Vinaya, Abhidharma, and the Secret Treasury;

his great achievements cannot be fully recounted. Regarding those who have surpassed him in accordance with the Way: the "Government" chapter of the *Analects* says, "At fifteen, I set my mind on learning; at thirty, I took my stand."
At forty, one is no longer confused; at fifty, one knows the mandate of Heaven; at sixty, one’s ears become attuned to all sounds; at seventy, one follows the dictates of the heart.
Regarding "the ears becoming attuned," Zhu Wen-gong’s commentary states: it means that when sounds enter, the mind penetrates them, such that there is nothing contrary or obstructive.

The *shū* (commentary) states: "Regarding 'the masters of the treatise,' etc. This means that the principles of the Vaipulya teachings are as profound and vast as a deep ocean. "Ming" (冥) signifies depth and obscurity. The *shū* states: "Regarding 'the principles are not [limited by],' etc.
This means that the realization of these principles is not restricted to either the extensive or the abbreviated sections [of the canon]. "Shū" (樞) refers to the pivot or hinge of a gate.
The "pivot" (jī) is the trigger of a crossbow; both are taken from the essential points. If one grasps the essence of the pivot, then all principles will become manifest.
This present treatise is precisely the pivot of the various Prajñāpāramitā sections. Regarding the "Eight Sections," the ancients enumerated eight sections:

namely, the *Fàngguāng* (Prabhāsa), *Dàpǐn* (Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā), *Xiǎopǐn* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā), *Guāngzàn* (Suvikrāntavikrāmī), *Dàoxíng* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā), *Jīngāng* (Vajracchedikā), *Shèngtiānwáng* (Śrīmaladevī-siṃhanāda), and *Wénshūwèn* (Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā). However...
Among the collections in the present canon, the Prajñāpāramitā section is particularly numerous; I have not yet ventured to provide a detailed determination of them.
Regarding the "Snow Melody" (Xuěqǔ): this is the ancient "Yangchun Snow Melody. Because its musical mode is extremely high, those who can sing it are few;
among those who do sing it, there are none who can join in the harmony. As the ancients said: "The higher the melody, the fewer those who harmonize with it."

The analogy can be understood. Regarding "inferring by way of reversal": this refers to using inverse phrasing to deduce the underlying principle; it can be understood from the *shū* (commentary) where it is explained in a direct manner.
The intended meaning is that if one were not to forget [the limitations of] words and images, a treatise such as this could not reach such profound subtlety.
If words and images were retained, its essential purport would necessarily be distorted. Regarding "indirectly" (*wǎnzhuǎn*): other texts employ the term *wǎn*.
"Zi Yu" refers to Da Yu, the King of Xia. During the era of Yao, Yu managed the floodwaters and personally exerted himself in the labor.
His thighs were free of hair, his shins were hairless, and his hands and feet were calloused from blisters. When he ascended the throne, he lived in humble palaces and ate frugal food.
Confucius sighed that his virtue was complete and without flaw, as recorded in the *Analects* and Xing Yunzhi’s commentary.
Commentary: "Composed and at ease" (*cóngróng*) refers to the leisureliness of one's movements and conduct.

Commentary: Regarding the passage beginning with "The text borrows from below," the *Tiāndào* chapter states briefly: Duke Huan of Qi was reading a book in the hall above, while Lun Bian was planing wheels in the hall below.
Setting aside his mallet and chisel, he ascended and asked, "I venture to ask, what is it that Your Highness is reading?"
[The King] said, "These are the words of the sages. [Qian] asked, "Are the sages still present? The King said, "They have already passed away.
[Qian] said, "In that case, what Your Majesty reads are but the dregs of the ancients. Duke Huan said, "When I read books, how can a wheelwright dare to offer criticism?
If you have a reason, it may be accepted; if you have no reason, you shall die. Wheelwright Bian replied, "I, your servant, by means of—"
I have observed the work of a wheelwright: if he works too slowly, the spokes are smooth but not firm; if he works too fast, they are strained and do not fit.
When he works neither too slowly nor too fast, he attains it with his mind and responds with his hands; it is something that words cannot describe (and so forth).
Commentary: Regarding the first four lines and so forth, "knowing" refers to function (*yòng*). The text appears below, specifically in the first chapter.
"Nameless" (*wú míng*) means that prior to heaven and earth, all was a chaotic, formless state; being formless, there were no names. This refers to the Way (*dào*). "Named" (*yǒu míng*) refers to...
This means that once the qualities and dispositions have taken form, things are named according to those forms, such as "Heaven" and "Earth.
Therefore, it is the Nameless that can initiate Heaven and Earth, while the Named can act as the mother of the myriad things. "Mother" carries the meaning of giving birth and nourishing.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the surviving subjects" (*yimin*) and below, [the author] does not wish to shoulder the responsibility alone.

Commentary: Regarding the various editions and so forth, if one examines the character "spiritual" (*ling*) closely, it appears there may be some discrepancy. Why? Because "spiritual wisdom" (*lingzhi*) is "spiritual" (*ling*).

Now, when we speak of "exhausting the spiritual" (*qiongling*), that which is capable of exhausting it to the ultimate is "wisdom" (*zhi*). Since that which is exhausted is also wisdom, it cannot be fully understood; this is the first point. "Ultimate" (*ji*)...
"Number" (shù) refers to the complete awakening to all dharmas; the text omits the proof of realizing the Truth. This is the second [point].

Below, the answer is given in response to the question: "Now, non-reliance resides in profound stillness (*míngjì*). Because it is profoundly still, it is made permeable through emptiness (*xū*). The subtle exhaustion [of phenomena] exists in the ultimate number (*jìshù*).

Because it is the ultimate number, number is used to respond [to phenomena]. This is sufficient as a valid proof. This is the third [point]. Therefore, according to the *Yàopǐn* (Essentials), the meaning of the question below is based on the text.

Because this is difficult, I have set forth my own interpretation to explain it. The tranquil eye refers to the realm of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); its function belongs to the mind of true knowledge.
"Exhaustively reaching the wondrous" means that wisdom is merged with [the object]. Is it not the case that tranquil wisdom and [the object] both vanish together, conforming to become one?

Indeed, it is because mind and object are not divided into two. This is not discussed below; it is explained as being spontaneous (*svabhāva*). It is not spoken of in contrast to the two truths, but is directly revealed from the perspective of the essence of wisdom itself.
This can be understood in detail from the commentary.

Regarding the phrase "if it were true wisdom" (*bhūta-jñāna*), the intended meaning is that when the mind and its objects are in profound unity (*yoga*), one should not maintain the dual designations of "quiescence" (*śamatha*) and "illumination" (*vipaśyanā*).

Since there are two—concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*)—there are likewise two: quiescence and illumination. This is because concentration and wisdom are taken to constitute quiescence and illumination; how, then, could they be in profound unity?

"Harmony. If it is permitted that there is harmony with the unseen (the noumenal), then one should not restrict it to the realm of quiescence and function. Concentration and wisdom (*samādhi* and *prajñā*) arise from conditions through cultivation;

quiescent illumination is the inherent virtue of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna*). Therefore, the question is posed by combining concentration and wisdom with quiescent illumination. The text below borrows from the *Xici* (Appended Phrases), which says:
"If heaven and earth were destroyed, there would be no means by which to perceive the *Yi* (the Changes). If the *Yi* could not be perceived, then heaven and earth would be as nothing. Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "The text is generally equal," in all cases the first clause presents the meaning of the treatise, while the second clause constitutes a challenge. This commentary largely follows the *Yaoshu*;

since this section is also extremely difficult, it is presented here in full. One should not say "below," as in the previous instance where it was said, "the Pratyekabuddhas are in profound obscurity."
Furthermore, it says: "Within, there is the clarity of solitary discernment; being empty, it does not fail to reflect," and so forth—all of this is of this nature.

The phrase "the meaning is as follows" refers back to what was previously stated: "Because the spirit has no deliberation, it is able to reign alone beyond the world," and so on. To examine the phrase "and so forth" below:

it refers to what is said later, "The subtle perfection resides in the ultimate number (*parama-saṃkhyā*); because it is the ultimate number, the numbers respond to it. The meaning is that the spirit is the subtle perfection and the ultimate number.
This is the profound essence of the transformative manifestation. Because it reaches the ultimate limit of numerical categories (*śu*), it responds through those numbers;

that is to say, only by reaching the ultimate limit of numerical categories can one respond to them. The intent of the objection is that the wisdom which illumines reality reaches the ultimate limit of numerical categories, yet it should not be subject to those numbers.

If it were to respond to numbers, it would not illumine reality; thus, the two minds would become distinct. The intent of the reply is that it is precisely because it reaches the ultimate limit of numerical categories that it is able to respond to them. It is precisely because...
If one calculates accordingly, one immediately reaches the ultimate void; what difference could there be?

Regarding the commentary on "profoundly realizing" and so forth: first is the measure of principle (*yukti-pramāṇa*), second is the measure of scripture (*āgama-pramāṇa*). The note states that "fǔ" means to soothe and settle, and it is also like receiving.
Expedient wisdom soothes and receives all things.

Commentary: "The 'prior' and so forth" refers to the signless reality (*animitta-tattva*). "Movement and change" refers to the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). "Kai" (model) means a standard; it signifies a fixed rule.

"Du" (to behold) means to observe. The intended meaning is as follows: if one perceives only movement and engages with it, harmonizing with its impulses, this is to abide in the realm of signs while losing sight of signlessness.
However, at the time of responding and meeting [the situation], if one simply observes the principle that dependently arisen phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, then...

There is no birth that can be received. "Obtaining one" refers to obtaining the principle; "losing the matter" refers to the phenomenon. If one were to cause [the mind] below to rely on the two truths within the mind—this is the commentary.
Regarding the phrase "narrating the preceding," it means first citing the questionable passage to initiate the objection.
Commentary: "To take this as an analogy" means that there is no phenomenon that is not thus; it is therefore appropriate that it is truly so.
Commentary: "This corresponds to... refers to the preceding root treatise. "Already is," etc., refers to what was previously stated: "there is no phenomenon that is not thus," and so forth.
Later, it is again stated: "Since there is nothing that is not such, it is 'such' yet without being 'such,'" and so forth. A *máo* (spear) is a lance; a *dùn* (shield) is a buckler.
Formerly, there was a man who displayed two items together for sale. Displaying the spear, he said, "It can pierce ten layers of shields.
Displaying the shield, he said, "The spear cannot penetrate it. Thus, they are metaphorically contradictory. As for glue and lacquer, although they are two distinct substances—
[The two] appear distinct, yet their nature truly accords; this refers to the fact that the metaphors used are not contradictory.

In the *Sū* (Commentary), the intention behind the phrase "fearing a rescue" [of the opponent's argument] is as follows: "that which is appropriate at the proper time" does not mean a mere, ordinary appropriateness; "that which is truly so" does not mean a mere, ordinary correctness.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "delusions are not equal," this implicitly employs the "Discourse on the Teacher" by Han Changli (Han Yu). It states:

"A teacher is one who transmits the Way, receives students, and resolves their delusions. Since people are not born with knowledge, who can be without delusion? If one’s delusions are not resolved through a teacher... (and so forth).

Commentary: Regarding the phrase “the auspicious signs were received,” Master Huiyuan expressed his admiration and did not grant his approval lightly. The *Benzhuan* (Original Biography) refers to the biography of the Master of the Treatise (*Śāstrakāra*).

The passage beginning with “as numerous as the sands of the Ganges” refers to the innate virtues (*dharmatā-guṇa*) within the mind, which are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; the teachings and their meanings, when analyzed and measured, also possess infinite distinctions.

The passage beginning with “Master Huiyuan’s school” relies on the biography of Master Huiyuan, which states that he once annotated the *Dharmatā-śāstra* to show it to Master Kumārajīva. Master Kumārajīva sighed in praise, saying: [text continues]
The people of the borderlands have not yet been extensively exposed to the sūtras and śāstras; thus, what they describe is obscure, yet it accords with principle—how marvelous!
Master Kumārajīva also translated the *Shixiang lun* (Treatise on the True Mark) in two fascicles for the Ruler of Qin, but I regret that I have not seen it.

However, both "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*) and "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) are principles found in the various Prajñāpāramitā sections; though the names differ, the principle is the same. Therefore, the commentary says so.
The commentary states: "Liaor" (聊爾) means trivial or insignificant.
Regarding "the style of writing and so forth," such things existed among the ancients, but they are not seen today. Furthermore, "kuang" (況) here carries the sense of "moreover" or "furthermore."

Commentary: Regarding the first two phrases, the underlying intention is that if one were to write at the very beginning of the title, "Although the manifestations differ, they have no point of origin," there would be no such precedent.

Commentary: Regarding "Jiadun" (Secluded Retreat), this refers to the hexagram *Tianshan Dun* (Retreat under Heaven and Mountain) in the *Yi Jing*. The image of the hexagram is as follows: the transformation of the Yin lines reaching the second position forms the image of the mountain.

Just as when the autumnal qi is at its peak, the mountains gradually grow while the heavens gradually rise higher to avoid them—hence the winter sky is called the "Upper Heaven"—this hexagram takes the mountain as its image to signify that the Way of the petty man is flourishing, and the noble man retreats from it; thus it is the fifth [hexagram].

This hexagram-line is called "the auspicious withdrawal" (jiadun). "Auspicious" (jia) means "good. Although this line has a corresponding partner within the inner trigram, it acts upon perceiving the opportune moment and waxes and wanes in accordance with the timing;
thus, it is also a form of the excellence of withdrawal. How could it ever descend? The old reading says: "How could it ever not be distant? (何嘗不遠).
Now, if one infers this by means of the principles of grammatical structure, it should be read as a long compound. The interpretation of its meaning also differs from the traditional explanation.
The old explanation states: "It is a metaphor for the refined verses beneath the grove. Regarding the term *lin* (grove), it refers to a bamboo grove.

During the Jin dynasty, the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove—Ji Kang, Shan Tao, Xiang Xiu, Ruan Ji, Ruan Xian, Wang Rong, and Liu Ling—lived in seclusion in a bamboo grove at Shanyang. They were all pure...
They spoke of morality while holding benevolence and righteousness in contempt; they abandoned themselves to wine and sensual beauty, disregarding ritual and music.
Their contemporaries called them "liberated and expansive" (kuang-da). Yet, they greatly threw human relations into chaos and were cast out by the teachings of name and instruction (ming-jiao).

Since the time Master Tang Yao established this doctrine, successive generations have inherited it. In my view, the pure assembly of the Lotus Society ought not to be compared to those who abandoned themselves in the Bamboo Grove.
The flow of waves and the chanting of the Buddha’s name should not be compared to the practice of non-action.

I have only heard that at Donglin, morning and evening, the cultivation of the mind through Chan and lecture is solemn and harmonious; I have not heard of a gathering every half-month where songs and chants resound in confusion.
Furthermore, as for the term "under the pines," it may be applied to any dwelling place of those outside the secular world; it does not refer exclusively to the Seven Sages.

This is what one should focus upon exclusively. I have also once applied this phrase to the examination of the renowned scholar Lu Zhi, the Hanlin Academician; his interpretation of the punctuation was identical to my own.
Furthermore, he stated that the word "yan" (言) in the phrase "yan ji zhi yan" (言集之言) is likewise a particle, just as in the *Shijing* it says:

"Cai cai fu yi, bo yan cai zhi" (Gathering the *fúyǐ*, now gathering it) and "Cai cai fu yi, bo yan you zhi" (Gathering the *fúyǐ*, now possessing it). The commentaries on the *Shijing* all state that these are particles. I am indeed but a minor scholar... [text ends]
In studying, if the principles are clear and evident, one should not yield when it comes to practicing benevolence; who would follow the tracks of past errors to obscure future generations?
Therefore, whenever my interpretations of the meaning differ from those of antiquity, it is all for this purpose. Nor have I compared every instance of gain or loss, nor pointed out every flaw.

"Rely on the Dharma, not on the person"—this is the excellent instruction of the Sage. The rest is as explained in the *Shu* (Commentary). [Note: The character "讀" (dú) is pronounced "dòu" in this context.]

Commentary: Regarding "Qing received [the mandate] from below," etc.: *yeng* (膺) also means the chest; *qi* (企) means to look up with expectation. "Embracing the One" refers to the chapter on the "Soul and Spirit" (*zai ying po*) in the *Laozi*:
"Can one embrace the One without being separated from it? Can one concentrate the vital energy (*qi*) to achieve pliancy, becoming like an infant? This does not refer only to what follows.
The *Mao Shi* says: "The high mountains are looked up to; the illustrious path is trodden. Regarding the phrase "one corner," it is as Fu Jian said:

"I preside over a great enterprise, and the four quarters are gradually at peace; only one corner in the southeast has not yet submitted to the royal transformation. He likewise regarded the Jin as "one corner."
Commentary: "But [if one] desires... means that for me it is insufficient, yet for you it is more than enough.
Commentary: Regarding "Cao Tang," the Biography of Master Kumārajīva states: "The Ruler of Qin dispatched over eight hundred śramaṇas, including Sengqie, Sengqian, Faqin, Daoliu, and others.
The *Book of Jin* states: "Those who practiced seated meditation at Cao Tang numbered three thousand at all times. Now it says...
Five hundred [years]. This is according to the *Benlun* (Original Treatise).

Regarding the "secular ruler" (*suzhu*): Confucianists regard a sovereign who is benevolent and sagacious as a "heroic ruler" (*yingzhu*), one who is昏暴 (obscure and tyrannical) as a "cruel ruler" (*nüezhu*), and an ordinary, mediocre sovereign as a "secular ruler.
As for the "five Hu": the first was Liu Yuanhai of Former Zhao, a person of Xiongnu origin.

It was established in the fourth year of the Daxing era of Emperor Hui of the Western Jin dynasty. It lasted for three reigns until it was destroyed by Shi Le in the fourth year of the Xianhe era of Emperor Cheng of the Eastern Jin.
Second, Shi Le of Later Zhao: a person of the Jie ethnic group from the north, he established his rule in the third year of the Xianhe era of Emperor Cheng.
He reigned for four generations until his state was extinguished in the eighth year of the Yonghe era of Emperor Mu. Third, Fu [Jian] of Former Qin...

The Hong [dynasty] was of Xiyu (Western Regions) origin. It was established in the seventh year of the Yonghe era of Emperor Mu and lasted for six generations until it was extinguished by Yao Chang in the nineteenth year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Xiaowu.
The Later Qin of the four [successive rulers], Yao Zhongyi, was also of Qiang chieftain stock.
It was established in the ninth year of the Danyuan era of Emperor Xiaowu and lasted for five generations until it was extinguished by the Jin in the thirteenth year of the Yixi era of Emperor An.

Fifth, the Wei dynasty was founded by Tuoba Gui, who was also a Xianbei. He established the state in the eleventh year of Emperor Wu’s Taiyuan era, changed the dynastic name to Wei, and designated the era as Dengguo.
There were eleven successive reigns in total, during which the state was divided into Eastern and Western Wei.
Eastern Wei ceded its mandate to Gao Huan, who founded Northern Qi; Western Wei ceded its throne to Yuwen Tai, who styled his dynasty Later Zhou. [The city walls] had moats surrounding them.

It is like a moat and ditch. "Not distant" means that even ten thousand *li* are not considered far. "Without departing" refers to the translation hall, where the Tripitaka masters translated extensively;

it refers to the propagation and protection [of the Dharma], where a single person personally presided over it. The hundred officials offered their faith and the myriad commoners took refuge. As for the monks, whether Indian or Chinese, there were approximately eight hundred of them.
They were all men of "white eyebrows" (eminent elders) who mutually promoted the teachings, and men of "blue eyes" (youthful scholars) who stimulated one another in debate. Their lips...
Her teeth shed the beauty of pearls and jade; her breast unfolds the brilliance of brocade and embroidery. Her conduct is as pure as ice and frost; her will is as firm as pine and cypress.
I pray you, before the mirror of history, recognize these noble achievements for yourself.
Commentary: Regarding "Master Ling and others," the *Biography of Master Huiyuan* states: Initially, when the sutras were circulating in Jiangdong, many were incomplete;

there was no record of the methods of dhyāna, and the Vinaya-piṭaka was fragmentary. Master Huiyuan lamented these deficiencies in the Dharma and thus ordered his disciples Fa Jing and Fa Ling to travel far to seek out various scriptures.
They traversed deserts and snows for many years before returning, having obtained Sanskrit manuscripts of all of them, which enabled their translation and transmission.

Below the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Great Commentary* (*Dàchão*) states in brief: "In the early Eastern Jin dynasty, there was a śramaṇa named Zhi Falin, who was devoted to the Mahāyāna and sacrificed his body to seek the Dharma.
Upon reaching the kingdom of Cakravāḍa, he obtained the first portion of the *Avataṃsaka*, consisting of thirty-six thousand verses, and so forth."
From this point onward, the commentary (*śū*) is abbreviated; each is explained in its respective biography. To cite further would be excessive.
Regarding the phrase "the Master of the Treatise and others": the Ruler of Qin was a time when the Three Jewels were widely propagated. Master Kumārajīva was a true and virtuous friend.

The character *cè* (廁) means "in succession," implying that he was not merely a companion in conduct. *Cǎi* (彩) refers to radiance and countenance. *Liè* (列) means "rows" or "order. As for "Śāriputra": [End of excerpt]
"Śāriputra. "Yù-yù" (郁郁) describes an appearance of flourishing literary elegance. "Chén-jì" (陳跡) refers to traces already laid down in the past;
it originates from the *Zhuangzi*, though citing it here would be too prolix. "Liú-fāng xià" (流芳下) means that one's fragrant fame is transmitted downward. Huan Wen of the Jin dynasty said:

"Men cannot cause their fragrance to flow for a hundred generations," and so forth. "Liaoliao" (rare/scant) means that although the Dharma teachings were flourishing, the "dragons and elephants" (great masters) were sparse.

Following the entry on "Shu" (Commentary/Tradition), this refers to the *Biography of Hui guan*. Master Daosheng and Master Daorong were able to resolve the doubts of others; Master Sengzhao... [text continues].
One observes that Master Guan was adept at settling their debates. However, as there were many figures at that time, various evaluations and disparagements naturally arose.

As the Biography of Master Sengsheng states: "Sengsheng and Sengrui manifested their natural genius; Huiyan and Daoquan attained the depths of the flowing stream; Huiai and Daoheng advanced with vigor;
while Kou Yuan was merely one who remained silent and stumped. The commentary explains: this means that Masters Sengsheng and Sengrui’s brilliance and insight were innate; "wa" (窪) refers to depth.
As for Master Yan and Master Guan, their profound contemplation and lingering attachment were only then able to follow in his footsteps. Peng Xiangyan spoke of striving hard just to advance.
"Guan" is a surname; his given name was Daoyuan. Regarding these three masters, this gentleman merely remained silent and speechless.
Nevertheless, his observance of the precepts was lofty and pure, and he served as the teacher to Liu Huilin. "Pian" means "together. As for the "Eight Talents," they were born during the Zhaohui era.
There were also Rong, Rui, Ying, Yan, and Heng, as well as Guan. Some accounts state that there was no Heng but rather Pínggōng;
however, since there is no biography for Pínggōng, this appears to be an error. Master Zhào of Xīhé considered [Shēng]gōng and [Héng]gōng to be one person, and some also refer to him as Heng.
The *Běishān Lù* (Record of North Mountain), when describing the ten eminent disciples of Kumārajīva, adds Dàohéng to the list above the "Eight Talents."
Daobiao: All of these have authentic transmissions. Regarding the phrase "those of the same breath" (*tóngqì*), the text of the *Xící* (Appended Statements) states in full:
"Clouds follow the dragon; wind follows the tiger. It further says: "The crane cries in the shade, and its young respond to it.
As for those who were "in perfect accord," the *Zhuāngzǐ* refers to the Grand Master Tàizōng. It briefly records that Zǐyǎn, Zǐyú, Zǐlǐ, and Zǐlái said to one another: "Who among us could..."
"Non-action (wuwei) is the head; birth is the spine; death is the tail. Who knows that life and death, existence and non-existence, are one body?
With such a person, I would befriend. The four men looked at one another and laughed; their hearts were in perfect accord, and they subsequently became friends.

Regarding the verses on the recitation of the Buddha's name (*nianfo*), the text has not yet been seen. Master Huiyuan’s preface to the verses states: "As for the Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha..."

"What is it? It refers to the focused contemplation of quiescence," and so forth. Regarding "comparison and resonance" (*bixing*): in the *Mao Shih*, many passages employ comparison and resonance by entrusting meaning to external objects;
such is the case with the chapters on the "Guanju" and "Chichao."

The commentary states: "Regarding 'Hongshi' and so forth," this refers to the Master of the Treatise himself composing the preface to his own annotated scripture. "Cū" (麤) is pronounced "cū" and means "brief" or "concise.
As for the phrase "completed words," this refers to the words already established by Master Kumārajīva, which the Master of the Treatise then annotated.
Commentary: The section beginning with "Ying" also slightly modifies the original text to make it easier to understand. That *Xu Wugui* chapter briefly states:

When Zhuangzi was escorting a funeral procession and passed by the tomb of Huizi, he looked back at his attendants and said: "A man from Ying had plastered over the bridge of his nose until it was as thin as a fly's wing.

He asked a master carpenter to chisel it away. The carpenter then wielded his adze with such force that it created a whirlwind; listening intently, he struck it, and [the plaster] was completely removed."

The plaster did not injure his nose, and the man from Ying stood without losing his composure. The commentary states: "Plaster" refers to white earth. This is also a parable. The sub-commentary (shū) states:

"From 'the sub-commentary says' below, it refers to what was previously stated in the Preface to the Treatise: 'The essence of Prajñā is neither existent nor non-existent; it is empty yet..."* *(Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated at this point.)*
"Regarding 'losing the illumination' and 'illumination not losing its emptiness,' etc.: this profound principle will remain a source of constant confusion and obscurity until later [in the text].
The Master of the Treatise raises it once more to provide an answer."
The Commentary states: "Regarding 'the question,' etc., it again raises the previous objection to clarify the intent behind that which was asked.

Regarding "the two words," Master Yao’s intention is that although each consists of four characters, they do not express the provisional and the real; therefore, they are likewise referred to as "two words.

Regarding "human sentiment," the consciousness of pervasive conceptualization is shallow, superficial, and dull; it knows one thing as dark and another as light, according to what it itself has attained.
This refers to the distinction between two types of wisdom. How could this be the case for the Sage?

[The] Commentary [states]: "Regarding the previous [point], 'exhausting the void and reaching the ultimate number'—this refers to the essence of meditative concentration and wisdom itself, once one has reached the point of transcending the middle.
'Dual negation' means that both quiescence and illumination are simultaneously absent, such that it can be compared to no image. Therefore...

The phrase "entrusting words to the same as non-being" does not refer to a non-being that is the negation of being and non-being. The subsequent reprimand below criticizes [the view] that the essence of ultimate sameness is without marks and without name;
herein, one must not further seek a fixed distinction between concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā).

However, because the Sage’s means of gathering and transforming beings do not consist of a single word of instruction, sentient beings have no way to awaken and enter [the truth]. Therefore, he points to the place of intimacy, saying: "That which is called the Dharma..."

This refers to the mind of sentient beings. Furthermore, because this mind has been pure and undefiled from the very beginning, free from the characteristics of clamor and agitation, it is called "quiescence" (*jì*).
Because it possesses numinous clarity and conscious awareness, it is called "illumination" (*zhào*). Guifeng said: "The mind is quiescent yet cognizant; this is termed Perfect Enlightenment.
To seek realization of this mind, there are two paths: first, awakening (*wù*); second, cultivation (*xiū*). Through awakening, one penetrates its fundamental nature.

Coming from the reality that has always been present, one departs from the delusion that was previously non-existent. Relying on the wisdom of thorough awakening, one cultivates the practice of dependent origination.
If this practice is cultivated through the gate of phenomena (*dharma*), then by practicing without practicing, the myriad practices are fully perfected.
If it is cultivated through the gate of principle (*tattva*), then by practicing without practicing, the single mind is tranquil and still. These two gates, moreover, are not to be [dichotomized].

Because of this sequence, one initially unifies them through *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight); thus, both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* pervade both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*).

After a long time, these develop into *samādhi* (concentration) and *prajñā* (wisdom), at which point both *samādhi* and *prajñā* each pervade *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Ultimately, the realization of this mind is called "quiescence and illumination" (*jizhao*). As for "quiescence and illumination":
Mind and phenomena are non-dual; the provisional and the ultimate are both contained within them. Essence and function are fused, and emptiness and existence are transcended.

At this point of fusion and transcendence, how could there be room to differentiate between stillness and illumination? This is indeed the essential point of the principle of nature; therefore, I have briefly set it forth.
All of this relies upon the teachings of Xianshou, Qingliang, and others, and is not merely my own personal opinion.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "dispelling delusion" and so forth, the intended meaning is that identity is the source of both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Originally identical, difference arises from it.
As for the subsequent phrase "dispelling [difference]" and so forth, this means that once difference exists, one deviates from identity.

Regarding the section on "non-attainment": among the various *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras, the teachings expounded are immeasurable; yet if they were to be summarized in a single word, they would not transcend non-attachment and non-apprehension. If...
When there is no attachment to external objects, then all phenomena are equal. When there is no attainment within, then the mind is tranquil and extinguished.

Thereafter, with the mind free from obstruction, Prajñā manifests before one. One attains Bodhi without anything being attained; this is true attainment. One realizes Nirvāṇa without anything being realized; this is true realization.
Although it is called "realization" and "attainment," how could there possibly be any sign of attaining or realizing? Thus, Master Kumārajīva attained awakening.

The Preface by Xuán states: "Those who forget their achievement harmonize with the Dao; those who maintain a vacant mind penetrate the principle; those who darken their minds attain the True One; and those who cast aside wisdom share in the state of the Sages. Regarding the commentary:

the response to the preceding [question] refers to what was previously stated: "It means that when one takes the essence of the mind as spontaneous, it extends even to the responses of the manifold phenomena."
"Or perhaps it has almost ceased," and so forth. In the commentary (*śū*), first the sentences are excerpted to determine the great meaning;

following the section on "purity," the text itself is then explained. Regarding "not form" and below: this briefly negates that it is neither existent nor non-existent, as all [categories] are insufficient.
Vaidhī is the queen of King Bimbisāra. "Kěn" means sincere; "qiè" means most urgent. This is an abridgment of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*.
It is said: At that time, in the great city of Rājagṛha, there was a crown prince named Ajātaśatru.
Following the instructions of his evil friend Devadatta, he arrested his father, King Bimbisāra, and confined him within seven layers of chambers, forbidding all ministers from approaching.
The Queen Mother, Vaidehī, who had revered the Great King, bathed [him]...
He bathed in pure water and anointed his body with parched grain flour mixed with ghee and honey. He filled various necklaces with grape juice and honey to present to the king.
After seven periods of three days had passed in this manner, the king’s countenance became serene and joyful. King Ajātaśatru took notice of this.
He immediately commanded the inner officials to confine Queen Māyā in the deep palace. At that time, having been secluded, Vaidehī turned toward Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and paid homage to the Buddha.
[The text continues] until: "The Buddha vanished from the mountain and appeared in the royal palace," and so forth.
As for "Śrīmālā" (勝鬘), she was the daughter of King Prasenajit. "Āṅ" (仰) means to look up with longing; "qí" (祈) means to pray or entreat. The *Furen jing lüeyi* (夫人經略義) states: "Āṅ..."
"O Buddha, World-Honored One, you have appeared universally for the sake of the world; you should likewise bestow your compassion and surely grant me the sight of you.
At the very moment he gave rise to this thought, the Buddha manifested in the sky. Through the sign of wisdom, his body became unimpeded.
The Dharma-body is called "True," for it has no coming or going. It responds to all others, arising in accordance with the capacities of beings.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "from this point onward," it means that the principle of being neither existent nor non-existent applies to both the essence (*tǐ*) and its function (*yòng*).

With respect to its function, it is thus neither possessing knowledge nor lacking knowledge. Therefore, what follows below—such as "the Way transcends the realm of names, for causes are non-existent"—all refers to the essence.
Furthermore, the statement "sage-wisdom is without knowing, yet there is nothing it does not know" refers to the function.
Therefore, the Commentary states that it "also comprehensively includes the aspect of cognition. Regarding the phrase "all minds and mental factors," the brief explanation is as provided above.

Regarding the phrase "conditioned by existence," this explains that existence does not exist of itself; rather, it exists by depending upon conditions. Thus, the *Śāstra* says, "Because there is the existence of existence," and the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says, "There has never been a single dharma that was not produced from causes and conditions," and so forth.
Regarding the commentary on the first phrase and so forth: this explains the True in contrast to the false. The True is not produced by conditions;
because it is not produced by conditions, the mind of the Sage does not exist as something that arises dependent upon conditions. Since it is an existence that is non-existence, there is its "True.
Because it constitutes an existence that is non-existence, it thus constitutes a phrase that is "not non-existent. This explanation in the commentary is too brief.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "desiring to clarify," etc.: previously, the distinction between the real and the delusory was briefly indicated; now, this section clarifies their mutual difference in detail to answer the preceding objection.
The preceding objection stated, "exhausting emptiness and reaching the ultimate limit of numbers," where "numbers" refers to the delusory mind and delusory objects.

Because one realizes that their nature is empty, they are able to exhaust emptiness and reach the ultimate limit of numbers, as will be shown below. Now, by taking up the delusory to indicate the real, it serves as a negation of existence for what follows.

Regarding the meaning of "not non-existent," the first two phrases below [the verse] use shadows as a metaphor for appearances (*nimitta*) and echoes as a metaphor for delusion. As for "names," both substance and sound serve as metaphors for the deluded mind.
Regarding the phrase "as for the mind" (*yì wèi xīn xià*), the commentary is also too brief. To explain it fully:

the mind that can manifest existence and non-existence is precisely the manifestation-phase (*xiànxiàng*) among the three subtle states of *ālayavijñāna*. This mind is capable of manifesting all six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
Regarding "objects" (*viṣaya*): all objects do not transcend existence and non-existence. Because these objects exist, they draw forth the internal mind.

This internal mind consists of the characteristics of the cognitive consciousness (*sattvākhya-vijñāna*) and its mental states (*nimitta*). Based on these characteristics, the aspect of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) continuously discriminates, asserting either existence or non-existence.
Depending upon these objects that act as influences, all names and appearances (*nāma-nimitta*) arise; this is what is referred to in the treatise as "reckoning names."

Once names and characteristics have been established, one relies on those names to grasp those characteristics, engaging in various forms of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). In the *Vyākhyā*, this is identified with the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*; therefore, it is explained here.

If one does not rely on this treatise, the explanation of the meaning will be incomplete. Regarding the section "The Mahāyāna" and below: this was also composed by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna. "People" is a metaphor for manifest phenomena;

"people in a city" is a metaphor for existence, non-existence, and so forth; "fear of oneself" is a metaphor for the marks of wisdom and so forth. These constitute the four coarse types of discrimination. The Great... [text ends].
The meaning is that objects arise from the mind; yet, not realizing that they are already the mind itself constitutes delusion and error.

To then follow after them with various kinds of discrimination regarding what is pleasant or unpleasant is to become doubly deluded. Therefore, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "All discrimination is the discrimination of one's own mind," and so forth.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the first sentence, etc.," this refers back to the preceding statement that "existence does not exist," which serves as the basis for what follows.

That is to say, the deluded mind exists when there is existence and ceases to exist when there is non-existence; the enlightened mind is not like this, and therefore it is said to be "abandoned" (or "set aside").

Regarding the phrase "contrasting with the preceding, etc.," this means that the enlightened mind does not arise through causal dependence on external signs. The commentary is also extremely brief; I shall now demonstrate this once more. As for "the mind has no shadow or echo," this refers to the enlightened...
