Commentary: "Fǎngfù" (vague semblance) and so forth means to approximate the principle by means of its phenomenal forms. "The characteristics are severed" explains that one entrusts oneself to a realm where emotions are extinguished.
"Words are lost" explains that when one attains the meaning, words are forgotten. As for the passage beginning with "But it can be... the intended meaning is as follows:

to conceptualize whether *nirvāṇa* is existent or non-existent is a discriminative calculation of the mind. To lead people to abandon such sentiments and realize the principle—that it is neither existent nor non-existent—is the purpose of establishing these words.

This is the fundamental intent [of the teaching]. To claim that "neither existence nor non-existence" is nirvana is likewise to mistake the finger for the moon or to develop an illness from taking medicine;
in both cases, one has not yet escaped the delusion of cognitive perception.

Commentary: Regarding "confusedly entangling" (*fēnrào*) and so forth, this refers to the state of being busily and intricately entangled; it describes the appearance of agitation and disorder. This applies equally to both delusions (*moha*) and karma (*karman*).

Regarding the "three realms of existence" (*traya-bhava*), these are the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the realm of formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*). Regarding "drawing them out," the *Lotus Sūtra*, Chapter One, states:

"Sentient beings are attached everywhere; I draw them forth to enable their escape. The phrase "merely provisional" (*dànjiǎ*) and below means that even the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is provisionally designated as such and lacks ultimate reality.

Therefore, the third chapter of that sutra explains the parable of the conjured city. This is merely the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Guide; it is explained in detail as in the *Xuántán* (Profound Discourse).

Thus, the treatise says: "One borrows the non-existent to demonstrate the void. Even if [the city] were not actually his possession, it was intended to cause those who would otherwise reject and abandon the path to cast off the cycle of birth and death within the three realms of existence (*tribhava*) and enter the realm of no-remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).
It does not mean that "non-existence" refers to annihilation or empty nothingness. [This is said] for fear that [the meaning might be confused with] Confucianism or Daoism...

Below. Because the two schools discuss existence and non-existence in a manner similar to the internal school’s terminology of "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) and "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*), there is a fear that they might cite internal scriptures as examples, asserting that *nirvāṇa* is non-existent.
Therefore, this distinction is made to demonstrate that in the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), there is no remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).

By borrowing the term "Great *Nirvāṇa*" (*Mahāparinirvāṇa*), it is shown that [the Lesser Vehicle] does not possess either of these two. The first distinction is "Great *Nirvāṇa*"; the second is the distinction...
...is a provisional designation and not non-existent.

Regarding the commentary on the first phrase and so forth: the preceding treatise asks, "How could one say that there is a separate 'existence' outside of existence and non-existence that can be so named?

Based on this, it does not transcend existence and non-existence. Regarding the second phrase and below, the preceding treatise states: "Precisely because of [the nature of] existence and non-existence..."

The enumeration stops within the six sense objects. Since the interior of the six sense objects is not the abode of nirvāṇa, and so forth—based on this, it does not reside in existence or non-existence.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the two objects," etc., only the latter clause is selected for explanation; the first two are easy to understand, and thus are not commented upon.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "First, it clarifies," etc., this explains the first three lines. As stated previously: "Neither emerging nor remaining; there is no place to seek awakening.
Furthermore, it is not permitted that this is a mere empty void without substance. Since the Way exists, the subtle and wondrous path can be sought;
thus, thousands and tens of thousands of sages follow the same tracks to return to Nirvana—it is not a vain return.

Commentary: As for "if it were a Vaipulya [sūtra]," this means that it would lack an essential substance. If one asks, "Who is there that does not emerge?"—since its Way exists, it neither emerges from nor is it within existence and non-existence.
If it must be within existence and non-existence, how could it both not emerge and not be therein?
Commentary: Regarding the first three phrases and so forth: "Name" (*nāman*) is that which can give rise to verbal expression; "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is that which can produce names;

and "mind" (*citta*) is that which can manifest existence and non-existence. If the various characteristics are manifested in accordance with reality, it is said that "the mind manifests characteristics," whereby characteristics give rise to names, and names give rise to all verbal expressions.
Nirvāṇa is not like this; it is neither a characteristic of existence nor non-existence, and therefore it possesses neither existence nor non-existence.

It is called "nameless. Because it is nameless, there are likewise no various verbal expressions such as "not emerging" or "not abiding. Since the host has nothing to speak, the guest likewise has nothing to hear.
This commentary merely provides a brief indication of one corner [of this truth].

Below the section on "Principles and Phenomena, Good and Evil, etc.," [the text] states that "normative guidance and maintenance constitute the Dharma. This implicitly employs the Great Commentary (*Mahā-ṭīkā*) to explain the purport of the Great Sūtra regarding both "Dharma" and "non-Dharma.

As for "unconditioned dharmas," each likewise maintains its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), serving as a normative guide for persons to give rise to the understanding of existence or non-existence.
Regarding the phrase "without verbal expression," the twenty-first sūtra states: "That which is not heard is called Great Nirvāṇa."
[The text says: "It is not a name," and so forth, up to "because it is not sound" and "because it is ineffable.

The Commentary states: This causes one to forget names. Because [the ultimate] neither emerges nor resides [within them], they are mutually contradictory; thus, one merely relies on names to manifest the Sublime, yet the Sublime does not reside within the name.

If one clings to the name to seek the Principle, then when the name contradicts [reality], the Principle will deviate. How, then, could one attain awakening? Therefore, the *Complete Enlightenment*...
It is said: "The teachings of the Sūtras are like a finger pointing at the moon; one must understand that what the finger points to is ultimately not the moon.

Once, when I reached this point, I mistakenly composed a verse: "To see the mind by illuminating the text, The mind is not what the text can calculate. One must know how to catch the fish beyond the hook."
It is not a hook outside the fish. Commentary:
Although this is so, it establishes the preceding principle. Subhūti—also known as Śunakṣatra—does not direct his mind toward signs;
he is without mind. His ears do not follow after sounds; he does not listen. Among these, the most essential point is to understand its intent through right reflection and right contemplation.
"Listen and you shall hear; listen and you shall attain. [Commentary:
The verse below answers this. In the *Sixty Kinds of Unobstructed Functioning of the Realm* in the "Detachment from the World" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it says:
"To abide within the realm of the Buddha while not abandoning the realm of Māra is unobstructed functioning. This is also as Master Zhi said: "Māra..."
Emerging from the realm of the Buddha, the Buddha arises from the realm of Māra; the two heads cannot be distinguished, mingling within the royal city.
Regarding the first phrase and so forth: this means that although one does not depart from afflictions (*kleśa*), one is likewise not identical to them. This is truly difficult to express.
Therefore, it is said that it lies in "wondrous awakening. This means that within delusion itself there is truth; it is not a matter of abandoning delusion.

As for "viewing with equanimity," this refers to the unimpeded unity of emptiness and form, which is solely the realm of the one true reality. A detailed discussion reveals two meanings of equanimity: first, the non-duality of emptiness and existence;
second, the identity of the subjective mind and its objective objects within the suchness of reality.

Commentary: The text below resembles the "Qi Wu Lun" (On the Equality of All Things) chapter, which says: "Heaven and Earth were born together with me; the myriad things and I are of one and the same rank. Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "that which is identical to me," this clarifies that to hold either to identity alone or difference alone is a failure. To hold both to identity and difference, or neither to be outside nor to be within, does not transcend these errors.

It should likewise possess four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). Here, however, only the "neither emerging nor abiding" is clarified; therefore, it is distinguished solely in terms of being both identical and different.
Regarding "identical to the self," this refers back to the preceding point that [the mind] shares the same sense faculties as the self, taking only the meaning of identity.
As for "phenomena and principle being in contradiction," this refers to the ninth and tenth points concerning the non-obstruction of phenomena and principle within the *dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*.

The "mutual negation" (*xiāngfēi*) gate: mutual negation is precisely contradiction. Regarding "not being therein": since *nirvāṇa* is the principle (*lǐ*), and the principle does not reside within the phenomena of existence or non-existence.
Now, if [the opponent] were to proceed downward, they would fall into the error of mere identity. This error is twofold: first, the failure to establish existence or non-existence;

second, the failure to establish "not being therein. By proceeding downward from the point of identity, one also encounters the seventh and eighth points regarding the mutual relationship between phenomenon and principle.

This refers to "immediacy" (*ji*). Because they are immediately identical, they are the same. Regarding "not emerging": the principle of *nirvāṇa* is immediate within both existence and non-existence; this is why it does not emerge.
As for the phrase "if now," etc., it refers to the fault of [the mind] merely emerging as something distinct. This fault is also twofold: first, it deviates from the realization of sameness.

Secondly, it is neither non-emergent nor non-existent. However, the ancient commentaries all do not interpret it in this way. I have examined the concluding passage below regarding why it is "neither emergent nor existent" and so forth;
logically, these should be explained in connection with what precedes and follows. This definitively eliminates all remaining delusions.

The *Ratnagotravibhāga*, in the first fascicle, in the Chapter on the Jewel of the Dharma (*Dharmaratna-varga*), states: "It is neither existent nor non-existent, nor is it both existent and non-existent, nor is it identical to those."
Nor is it separate from that; "that" refers to existence and non-existence.

Regarding the commentary on the first two phrases: for now, let us discuss the provisional and the ultimate as a whole. It is "mysterious" (*xuan*) because the void and the profound universally encompass all things.
Regarding the second two phrases: although they speak of "illuminating the principle," the intent is to reveal the mystery of wisdom; therefore, they simply say "spiritual discernment" (*lingjian*).
There is still more; thus, it is vast and expansive, as if there were still room remaining.

The Commentary (*Śū*) follows what preceded it: the first phrase of the treatise refers to fundamental wisdom realizing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), while the second phrase refers to subsequent wisdom illuminating the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Below "the profound root" (*xuan-gen*): Since the "root" is used as a metaphor for principle (*li*), "uprooting" is used as a metaphor for realization (*zheng*). As for "principle has no beginning": this is because it cuts off the initial limit. Regarding "is not illumination," etc.:
following the interpretation of Master Daosheng, the meaning is that when the wisdom of correspondence exhausts the marks of arising (*sheng-xiang*), it appears as if there were a beginning.
Once the marks of arising are exhausted, the beginning is identical to the fundamental source; it is originally equal, being one with awakening. Why?

What begins must end; therefore, it is said that this is not merely illuminating what exists in the present. The passage from "The Awakening of Faith" (Qixin lun) below, which serves as a scriptural proof for the "arousing of the mind," states in full:
"Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva’s merits are fully perfected, he manifests a body of supreme height and magnitude throughout all worlds in the Akaniṣṭha heaven.

This means that through the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, ignorance is suddenly exhausted; this is termed 'all-encompassing wisdom' (*sarvākārajñatā*). The remainder of the text follows.
Next, regarding the commentary:

at the point where it says "briefly reaching the lower [section]," there should logically be the two characters "zhì rén" (至人). Whether these were omitted for brevity or lost in transmission, the phrase "demonstrating both non-abiding" means that one abides precisely while not abiding.
The *Great Commentary* explains non-abiding nirvana (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*) by stating: "Because of abiding in both, one is able..."
Regarding "neither abiding in both" and so forth:

the commentary states that the first two phrases refer to the mind and its objects being discussed in opposition, while the latter reveals their identity. Being identical, they are without marks and without names;
they are vast and empty, with nothing upon which to rely. This is as extensively demonstrated in the *Wu zhi lun* (Treatise on Non-knowing) within the section "Seeking Wisdom through Conditions."

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "a general exposition," this refers to what was previously stated: "The Way of Bodhi cannot be schematized or measured," and "Within the six sensory realms lies no abode of Nirvana.
These words appear below; they are from the text of that [work] concerning the hexagrams.

That work means that one must exhaust the principles of cosmic transformation (*zhìhuà*) before one can fully realize the nature of all things. Only then can one act in accordance with the mandate of Heaven (*tiānmìng*). Now...
Commentary on the Borrowing of Their Terminology:
Regarding the first four phrases and so forth, it means that one contradicts three, and those three are likewise not ultimate. The intent is that "one" is the ultimate;

as for "three," because there are distinctions between the Small and Great Vehicles, they are not ultimate. Since they are not ultimate, they belong to the realm of the impermanent and the conditioned.
"Extinction. Regarding "ascending and descending": ascending and descending refer to the discourse on a person's cultivation and progress; high and low refer to clarifying this through the Dharma.
Both convey the sense of differentiation and manifoldness.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the principle is without equality," this clarifies the matter by relying directly upon the principle itself. Since there are not even two, how much less could there be three?

This is why it is ultimate. Thus, the original sutra (the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*) states at [fascicle] twenty-two: "The nirvana attained by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is equal and without distinction."

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "there are no two superior [vehicles]," the character "two" (二) is likely a scribal error for "correct" (正). This refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, in the "Expedient Means" chapter, which states:
"In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma; there is neither a second nor a third, except as taught by the Buddha’s expedient means.
The *Zheng fahua jing* (Correct Lotus Sutra) verse says: "The Buddha-way is one; never has there been a second. The commentary cites the Parable of the Phantom City to correspond with this.
The treatise may be consulted. Regarding the "burning house," the second summary states: There was a great elder whose wealth was immeasurable.
His residence was vast, yet it had only a single gate. Five hundred people lived within it; the halls and pavilions were decayed and ancient, with beams and rafters sagging and perilous.
Suddenly, fire broke out all at once on every side. The elder’s sons were inside this dwelling.
He thought to himself: "Although I have safely escaped from here, my children have no intention of seeking their own deliverance.
The elder said to them: "This house is already burning; you should come out quickly! But the children, being attached to their play, were unwilling to believe or accept his words.
At that time, the elder employed another skillful means and addressed them, saying: "The toys for which you all have such fondness—"
"How rare and difficult to obtain! If you do not take them, you will surely feel regret later. These various goat-carts, deer-carts, and ox-carts are now outside the gate for you to play with.
At that time, the sons, hearing of the precious playthings described by their father, vied with one another to exit the burning house.
The commentary states: "The three carts correspond in sequence to the metaphors for the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*). Fire...
The house is a metaphor for the triple world (*tridhātu*). Thus, that sutra says: "They are being burned by the fire-house of the triple world," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the three vehicles (*triyāna*) and so on": it is like the differences among the sons; while their individual inclinations are distinct, there is no difference in their common avoidance of the calamity of the fire-house.
Regarding the phrase "that which is mounted" (*yāna*): this follows the explanation in the *Dàochào*. That work states that each of the three vehicles has its own teaching.

Regarding the principle, practice, and fruit: I shall now briefly explain them according to the teaching and the practice. As for the teaching, the "Expedient Means" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"Based on the single Buddha-vehicle, I have taught three [vehicles] through differentiation. That which elucidates and demonstrates the dharma of the Four Noble Truths is called the Śrāvaka-teaching;

that which elucidates and demonstrates the dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination is called the Pratyekabuddha-teaching; and that which elucidates and demonstrates the dharmas such as the Six Perfections is called the Bodhisattva-teaching. Regarding practice:

To speak briefly regarding what follows: the practice of the śrāvaka consists in contemplating the Four Noble Truths; the practice of the pratyekabuddha consists in the twelve links of dependent origination;

and the practice of the bodhisattva consists in the simultaneous application of compassion and wisdom, operating with equality between self and others. These are explained in detail as found in those respective texts.
To summarize them collectively, they converge upon the principle of the three returning to the one, which is extensively expounded in the *Xuántán* (Profound Discourse).

Commentary: Regarding "the habituation of the fetters" (*saṃyojana-vāsanā*) and so forth: "fetters" (*saṃyojana*) refers to the binding of the remainder; that is to say, they are merely subtle latencies (*vāsanā*). Regarding the "three vehicles" and below:

Śrāvakas are able to exhaust the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of afflictions, but cannot exhaust the latencies. Pratyekabuddhas partially sever the latencies. When the stage of a Bodhisattva is fulfilled, both the seeds and the latencies are entirely exhausted.

Commentary: Regarding the first phrase and so forth: it means that while the nature originally possessed by all sentient beings is singular and without difference, the conditions of prior cultivation (*pūrvābhyāsa*) truly differ in being small or great.

Because the treatise follows the principle of "new cultivation" (*navavāsanā*), it says they are not identical. That is to say, having previously cultivated within the Mahāyāna teachings, one develops a Mahāyāna nature;
the consciousness, mind, and inclinations are likewise solely Mahāyāna. The other two [vehicles] are to be understood by analogy. This is the "dual" [classification].
The "Illumination of the Lower" [section] states: Because the Mahāyāna simultaneously severs the two hindrances, its realization of the principle of the two kinds of emptiness is profound;
whereas the Two Vehicles only sever the hindrance of afflictions and realize the principle of the emptiness of the self, and are therefore shallow.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "due to consciousness, faculties, and so forth," this also follows from the preceding discussion to clarify that the distinction lies in consciousness and the faculties.

As for consciousness and the faculties, they differ in being small or great; as for wisdom and deliberation, they vary in being shallow or deep. The rest of the commentary is easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "as for power": the power of wisdom is simply small or great.
Commentary: "By the preceding" refers to the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* and other texts cited within the discussion on the difficulty of attaining [the fruit].

The three grades of light emission differ according to the depth or shallowness of the intellectual power (*jñāna-bala*) of the Three Vehicles; it is not that there are three grades within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Regarding the treatises on wisdom (*jñāna-śāstra*), they are like the human realm where the ascent and descent of principle differ, yet this does not mean that Nirvāṇa itself has differences. As for the citation below: according to the teaching, the Dharma varies according to the person, thus dividing it into one [part].
It forms three [categories]. Regarding their practice, individuals differ due to their own specific cultivation; thus, the three are brought together and returned to the one.

In the Commentary, the phrase "first establishing" means that one first distinguishes and establishes the principles of person and dharma, and only thereafter proceeds to raise objections against them.
Commentary: Regarding the first two phrases and so forth: since the Dharma follows the person, and as there are three types of persons, the Dharma is likewise fixed at three.

This is because their characteristics are identical. Furthermore, regarding the passage "If below": the wisdom of the Three Vehicles is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) can be known by implication. It transcends both existence and non-existence.
Is this not indeed a profound convergence? The commentary states:
"Regarding 'as for humans, etc.'—this explains that 'one is also without three. As for 'if they were different,' it is as the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* says:
'All exist through non-being (wuwei) yet possess distinctions. Now, since [the vehicles] are mutually identical, from where could the Three Vehicles derive their differences?"
Commentary: There is no precedent for this. It means that upon reaching the other shore of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*), one is identical to the bliss of non-action.
The text below [the passage] at [section] twenty-three states: "The Way is identical to the Way; the attainment is identical to the attainment;

the loss is identical to the loss. For one who is identical to the Way, the Way is also the joy of its attainment; for one who is identical to the attainment, the attainment is also the joy of its attainment."
Those who share in the loss also find joy in regaining it; yet, while this applies generally to those below, the capacity to truly attain it belongs solely to the wisdom of the Three Vehicles.
Since wisdom depends upon the person, the commentary refers to "the person."

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "although the principle is equal," this employs the terminology of the profound discourse on the classification of teachings. It says: "Although the principle is of a single flavor, the expressions [that convey it] have varying degrees of depth.
This is also like the three animals crossing a river; although the river is one, it does not prevent the depths reached by each of the three animals from being different.

Commentary: Regarding the first four lines and so forth: the "net" is a metaphor for the three realms (*tridhātu*). Although the three birds each escape the net, their strength and capacity vary—some being small and others large—and their soaring flight varies in distance, some being far and others near.
"Reproaching those below" refers to reproaching the preceding [section], which likewise lacks the threefold distinctions.
Commentary: Regarding "the three vehicles, etc.": the various aggregates (*skandhas*) are not one; their collective assembly is termed a "multitude. The manifestation of form is termed "birth.

When the three vehicles exist within the realms, they are subject to "segmented" [death and rebirth]; when the five aggregates exist outside the realms, they are subject to "transformational" [death and rebirth].

Although the five aggregates differ in terms of superiority or inferiority, they all constitute tainted (*sāsrava*) birth and death, and have not yet been transformed into untainted (*anāsrava*) aggregates. As for "the mind of continuity," it refers to...

Among the six coarse [consciousnesses], the second is the *samsvedaja-vijñāna* (the consciousness of the mind). "The harmonious integration" (*he-he*) below refers to the *mūla-vijñāna* (the fundamental consciousness).

One only breaks this consciousness from the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*) onward until the stages are fully perfected. As the *Awakening of Faith* says: "Breaking the characteristics of the harmonious integration consciousness;

extinguishing the characteristics of the continuous mind," and so forth. Those who have not yet reached Equal Enlightenment (*samalaṃbuddha*) are so called because Bodhisattvas at the stage of Equal Enlightenment have not yet exhausted the *utpatti-lakṣaṇa* (the characteristic of arising).
Because fundamental ignorance has not yet been extinguished, they have not yet realized the ultimate mind of the single Dharma-realm; thus, they are all termed "sentient beings.

Furthermore, as stated previously below, it is established that while the unconditioned is the same, the three vehicles are different. As for "by means of persons," this refers to viewing the person from the perspective of the Dharma.
Human beings are always three, while the Dharma is always one. When viewing human beings through the lens of the Dharma, the Dharma remains one while human beings remain three.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "following what preceded," etc.: within the objection, there were neither three in the "one" nor three in the "difference. Now, the analogy is used to clarify the Dharma.

It merely manifests the three vehicles; that there are likewise three within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) depends on the depth or shallowness of one’s subtle discernment, not upon the unconditioned itself.
[The commentary] states "because...
and so forth: because the wisdom of the three vehicles differs in its superiority and inferiority, the afflictions and hindrances they sever vary in their density and thinness.
It is the same. The principle realized is gradual and not yet profound; it is due to these stages that three distinctions arise. Who says that those of lower capacity do not have names?

They are categorized as such because they lack the name [of the higher realization]. Those who do not possess the name do not claim to be different while failing to realize [the truth]; thus there are three distinct types.
All of these [distinctions] are based on the degrees of shallowness and depth regarding the *pariśuddhi* (purity) of *upāya* (expedient means) and *nirvāṇa*;

they do not refer to *prakṛti-viśuddhi* (intrinsic purity). Regarding the term "ten thousand entanglements" (*wan lei*) in the treatise: because afflictions and karma are manifold, they are called "ten thousand. Regarding "to cause to flourish" (*zi yi*): the *Chunqiu Zhuan* (Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals) says, "Do not allow it to spread;

once it has spread, it is difficult to deal with. Now, concerning the eleven knowledges (*jñāna*) in the commentary: the sixth chapter of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that there is *dharmajñāna* (knowledge of phenomena)... [text continues].

The eleven [knowledges] are: subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), knowledge of the origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), and knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 23, explains this in great detail; here it is cited briefly.

Knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) refers to the untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) regarding the four truths of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) refers to the knowledge regarding the two higher realms.

Knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) refers to the knowledge that discerns the present minds and so forth of others in the desire realm and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) refers to all tainted knowledge (*sāsravajñāna*).
Knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) refers to the untainted knowledge obtained when contemplating the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as impermanent, suffering, empty, and so forth.

Knowledge (*jñāna*) consists of three types: those pertaining to the truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path. Each is the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) obtained by contemplating its respective fundamental truth.

Regarding the Knowledge of Exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*): when one reflects, "I have seen suffering; I have abandoned origination; I have realized cessation; I have cultivated the path," the untainted wisdom, vision, clarity, and awakening that arise at that time constitute this knowledge.

Regarding the Knowledge of Non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*): it refers to the realization, "Having seen suffering, I shall not see it again; having abandoned origination, I shall not [abandon it again]... [and so forth].
Furthermore, having abandoned [defilements] once more and having fully realized them, there is nothing further to realize; having cultivated the path once more, there is nothing further to cultivate.

When one reflects in this way, the untainted knowledge, vision, clarity, and awakening arise. One who possesses such knowledge of reality as it is realizes the general and specific characteristics of all phenomena exactly as they are, without any obstruction or impediment.
According to the treatise, the ten types of knowledge mentioned previously are common to the three vehicles; such is the knowledge of reality as it is.

Regarding "wisdom": this belongs exclusively to the Buddha alone. That it is stated thus in the present treatise is because, within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, from the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) up to the stage of the pratyekabuddha, these are traversed in common by the three vehicles (*triyāna*), and for the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), this constitutes the ultimate limit. Therefore, the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣaya-jñāna*) resides in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of the two vehicles.
The ninth stage, which transcends the three vehicles, is named the Bodhisattva stage; hence it is said that [the knowledge of non-arising] is absent [in the lower stages].
The arising of wisdom occurs at the stage of a bodhisattva. Otherwise, for what reason would there be a "Bodhisattva Ground" established outside of the Pratyekabuddha?

Since the fruit-stage is fully manifested through the single wisdom of reality (*yathābhūta-eka-jñāna*), the treatise does not mention it; please examine this in detail within the commentary, as all of it is explained according to the *Jñānaprasthāna*.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Now, below": however, there are two types of bodhisattvas: first, those who directly study the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); second, those who previously [followed] the Small Vehicle.
Regarding the "later great" [classification]: according to the scriptures, the establishment of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is mostly based on the sequence of first small and later great.

Therefore, the Master of the Treatise identifies the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) as belonging to the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) as belonging to the bodhisattvas. The knowledge of exhaustion refers to the total exhaustion of views, the total abandonment [of afflictions], the total realization, and the total cultivation.
The knowledge of non-arising refers to the sealing [of reality] such that [phenomena] do not arise again. Thus, these two knowledges are not essentially different. Hence, the *Dàocháo* [states]:...

Some say that the ten knowledges (*jñāna*) of the Hīnayāna exclude the knowledge of suchness (*yathābhūta-jñāna*). Others state that the two vehicles of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) constitute the essence of the vehicle of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Based on this, it follows that the two vehicles also possess the knowledge of non-arising; however, they differ from the Bodhisattvas in terms of their depth and shallowness.

The intent of the question here is precisely that of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*’s Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-naya*), as this teaching universally applies to all three vehicles; therefore, the Bodhisattva is also included within it.

Among the teachings, this is the greatest in its capacity for collateral transformation (*pāra-vaśa*). As the *Xuántán* (Profound Discourse) quotes the Tiantai Master Zhìzhě regarding the Four Teachings: First is the Tripitaka Teaching (*piṭaka-vinaya-śāstra*).

This teaching clarifies the principle of the four noble truths of conditioned arising and cessation; it is the primary teaching for the Śrāvaka vehicle, while it collaterally transforms Bodhisattvas and others.
Second is the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), which concerns the four noble truths of non-arising. "Shared" means commonality; the three vehicles equally receive this teaching. Therefore...

The modes of practice for the Bodhisattvas' severance and realization are largely identical to those of the Two Vehicles. Thus, the *Dàchāo* (Great Commentary), fascicle four, states: "The provisional wisdom of the six-foot [Buddha-body] is the substance of the ox-cart.

Furthermore, it distinguishes that the Three Vehicles share eight commonalities in their cultivation: namely, teaching (*jiao*), principle (*li*), wisdom (*zhi*), severance (*duan*), practice (*xing*), stages (*wei*), cause (*yin*), and fruit (*guo*).
Third is the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), which refers to the immeasurable Four Truths. Fourth is the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), which refers to the [immeasurable]... [text ends].
It establishes the Four Noble Truths; a detailed explanation is as given there. Question: If that is so, how does it differ from the Two Vehicles? Answer:

It differs because of the four great vows, the six perfections, the benefiting of self and others, and even such things as ascending to the stage of seeing [the truths], severing thirty-four mental states through the five gates in a single sitting to achieve perfect enlightenment. This is why it is distinct.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the Radiance [Sūtra] and others," while the wisdom of the three vehicles is admitted to have varying degrees of depth, the ultimate essence of wisdom is one and without distinction.

As stated in the *Avataṃsaka*, the realized wisdom of the ten stages is itself the Buddha-wisdom. Furthermore, since wisdom arises because of delusion and perishes when delusion ceases, emptiness is likewise equal.
Thus the sūtra says this. In the section beginning with "from the perspective of causes," he explains that the essence of wisdom is unarisen, thereby manifesting emptiness.
The commentary states: "As for 'it is only,' etc., this explains that if it is not the essence, then one has already finished [the discussion].

Because the wisdom that realizes [the truth] in the three vehicles does not contradict one another, and the principle realized is equal and non-dual; if it is not realized, one sets it aside and does not discuss it, but if it is realized, then delusion..."
"It can be exhausted all at once; the principle can be attained all at once" (and so forth). This is found in the *Śāstra*. Regarding the first two phrases and so on:

prior to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), practitioners of the Three Vehicles cultivate the five stabilizing concentrations (*pañca sthāpanā-citta*) and various contemplations such as suffering and impermanence.

These primarily suppress the conceptualized afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*) of the Four Truths, while concurrently suppressing the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) of the nine stages. This continues until the stage of the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
The mind emerges. It is only at the beginning of the stage of the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) that one first abandons the conceptualized [afflictions].

Upon reaching the stage of the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), one gives rise to nine paths of uninterrupted transition (ānantaryamārga) to abandon the afflictions of cultivation belonging to the nine stages. Within the nine paths of liberation (vimuktimārga), one gradually realizes the principle.

How, then, could it be sudden? This explanation follows the five stages according to the Tripiṭaka Teaching (Āgama). In the Commentary (*Śū*), the stages and positions are described according to the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna). This teaching also possesses ten stages (daśabhūmi).
The three [vehicles] share this same progression. First is the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 75, states:

"A śrāvaka, practicing with diligence and upholding the precepts for the sake of nirvāṇa alone, accumulates various wholesome dharmas; yet, although he possesses wisdom, he does not obtain the water of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and cannot attain the Path.
Therefore, it is called 'Dry Wisdom. This refers to the stages from the level of 'Heat' (*uṣmagata*) downwards. As for the bodhisattva, from the initial generation of the mind...

Even those who have not yet attained *anulomikī-kṣānti* (conformity-patience) may bear this name. Second is the stage of the nature of the ground (*gotrabhūmi*). For *śrāvakas*, this extends from the stage of *uṣmagata* (heat) up to the *laukikāgra-dharma* (supreme mundane dharma);
for *bodhisattvas*, they attain *anulomikī-kṣānti*. They cherish the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena and do not give rise to false views;

they obtain the water of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). Third is the stage of the three patiences (*tri-kṣānti-bhūmi*). For *śrāvakas*, this extends from *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* (patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering) up to *mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti* (patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path).

These are the fifteen moments of mind. The commentary states: This refers to the moment of mind that emerges from the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), which takes as its object the four truths of both the lower and upper realms, totaling sixteen moments of mind.

First, it takes the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) of the lower realm as its object, consisting of the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*) and the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñāna*).

Next, it takes the truth of suffering of the upper realm as its object, consisting of the subsequent receptivity to the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñānakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñāna*). This is because dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) takes the lower realm as its object, while subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) takes the upper realm as its object. It is also called...

The "patience regarding the subsequent category of suffering" (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*) and so forth belong to the lower stages (*adhobhūmi*). Thus, up to the "subsequent patience regarding the path" (*mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*), there are fifteen moments of mind;

among these, there are eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and seven knowledges (*jñāna*). Because they are currently designated by the name "patience," they are called the "eight patiences. For a Bodhisattva, however, it is the "patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) that constitutes entry into the Bodhisattva stage.
The commentary states: "The *Ratnarāśi-prajñāpāramitā* explains that the patience regarding non-arising consists of three [levels]: seven, eight, and nine."

The Ground attains it; that is, one realizes that phenomena are neither produced nor extinguished. As stated in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, "All phenomena do not arise from themselves," etc., as fully cited previously.

Judging by the meaning here, this is the lower grade of the non-arising patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) of the seventh ground, and not the non-arising wisdom of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

Fourth, the Ground of Vision (*darśana-bhūmi*): this is the sixteenth moment of mind, the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*), which enters the vision of the path and transcends [dualistic views].
One is born into the state of certainty and attains the fruit of *srotāpanna*. For a bodhisattva, this is *avaivartika*, which is translated here as "non-retrogression.
However, the commentary explains that the stage of *avaivartika* is broad; some say it extends from the first ground (*bhūmi*) up through the eighth ground.
Regarding the five "thin grounds," a śrāvaka—whether a *srotāpanna* or a *sakṛdāgāmin*—abandons six grades of innate afflictions of the desire realm.

Only the three lower grades [of afflictions] remain because the delusions within the desire realm are thin. From the time a Bodhisattva passes beyond the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika) until they have not yet attained Buddhahood, their remaining habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from having severed the various afflictions are likewise thin. Regarding the six stages of freedom from desire (*vairāgya-bhūmi*):

the Śrāvaka has already exhausted the three grades [of afflictions] of the desire realm and, being free from birth in the desire realm, attains the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*). The Bodhisattva, by reason of being free from desire, likewise attains it.

The five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). The seventh is the stage of those who have already accomplished [their task] (*kṛtāvibhūmi*): Śrāvakas attain the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and realize arhatship;

Bodhisattvas achieve the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*). The eighth is the stage of the Pratyekabuddhas. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, this is translated as "Awakened through Conditions" (*hetupratyeka-buddha*).

Having planted the causes and conditions for the Pratyekabuddha path in previous lives, they now encounter slight causes and conditions to leave the household life and likewise contemplate profound dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Having realized the Dharma and attained the Way, they are therefore called *pratyekabuddhas*. Regarding the nine bodhisattva stages—from the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) up to the stage of freedom from desire (*vītarāga-bhūmi*)—they are as explained above.

The commentary states: according to the *Mahā-śāstra*, within the preceding and succeeding paths of the bodhisattva’s knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārga-jñatā*), one universally cultivates the first eight stages but does not take realization;
thus, these are the "stages already completed. The stage of the *pratyekabuddha* does not refer to the bodhisattva. Furthermore, the treatise...

It says: "The Joyful Ground (Pramuditā-bhūmi) up to the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā-bhūmi) are the bodhisattva grounds," and so forth; the ten Buddha grounds are the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
The above is recorded based on the *Mahā-śāstra* (*Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*). Regarding the difficult points in between, I have likewise explained them solely by means of other texts;
however, these are merely presented in brief.

Commentary: Regarding "the ancient translations," etc., the Tripitaka Master of the Northern Liang dynasty produced eighty fascicles. All the citations within the commentary are from the preceding and succeeding sections of those treatises.

Commentary: Regarding "the causal origination," etc., the twenty-seventh sutra states: "Furthermore, one has not yet been able to cross the river of the twelve links of dependent origination; still..."
It is like the rabbit and the horse. Why? Because they do not see the Buddha-nature. As for the twelve links of dependent origination:

first, ignorance; second, volitional formations; third, consciousness; fourth, name-and-form; fifth, the six sense bases; sixth, contact; seventh, sensation; eighth, craving; ninth, grasping; tenth, becoming; eleventh, birth; twelfth, old age and death.
Each preceding factor serves as a condition for each succeeding one to arise. Thus are the twelve [links].

They are subsumed within the Dharma. That is to say, ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) are afflictions (*kleśa*); the members of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) are karma;

and the remaining seven members, beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), are suffering (*duḥkha*). As the verse from the *Pratītyasamutpāda-śāstra* states: "The afflictions are the first, eighth, and ninth;

karma is the second and the tenth; the remaining seven are said to be suffering. Thus, these three categories subsume the twelve factors. Furthermore, these twelve are mutually causes for one another, and the three [categories] likewise [interact].

The wheel of existence revolves, encompassing the three realms and pervading the four modes of birth. Herein, I shall briefly demonstrate the principle of cause and effect across the three periods of time to provide a general understanding of its vast significance.

That is to say: ignorance in the past serves as the factor that initiates karma; craving and grasping in the present serve as the factors that moisten karma, thereby summoning the fruits of the five factors beginning with consciousness.
Furthermore, through the factors of craving, grasping, and becoming in the present, one brings about future birth and old age.
Death. In the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), the two sets of cause and effect across the three time periods are the same as this. In the Mahāyāna, there may be only a single set;
thus, the first ten links are all causes, while the final two links are the results. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also clarifies the twelve links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) based on the three times.
The twenty-seventh fascicle of the sutra states: "The twelve causes and conditions are equally and universally shared by all sentient beings," and they are also internal.
It is also external. What are the twelve? Afflictions of the past are called ignorance (*avidyā*). Actions of the past are called formative forces (*saṃskāra*).

The initial conception in the present life is called consciousness (*vijñāna*) entering the womb. When the four sense-faculties are not yet complete among the five aggregates, it is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
When the four sense-faculties are complete but before the time of contact (*sparśa*), it is called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Before [the faculties] are distinguished...
Pleasure and pain are called contact (*sparśa*). The habitual cultivation of craving is called feeling (*vedanā*). The frequenting of the five desires is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Internal and external seeking is called grasping (*upādāna*). The arising of bodily, verbal, and mental karma for the sake of internal and external things is called becoming (*bhava*).
Consciousness in the present life is called future birth (*jāti*). Present form is called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and contact; feeling is called [feeling].

The aging and death of future lives—this is called the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). This has been briefly indicated in this manner. "Tín" (津) means "to descend," following the meaning of the *Unfinished* (*Majie*) and *Finished* (*Jijie*) hexagrams in the *I Ching*.
Regarding the Four Noble Truths (*catur-ārya-satya*): the nature of all contaminated (*sāsrava*) form and mind within the three realms is that of oppression;

this is named the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), which includes the three types of suffering, the eight types of suffering, and so forth. It refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*) of both the discriminative and innate types within the three realms. As for "increasing" (*zēng*):...

The long cycle of birth and death is called the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). The state of peace, which is the fruit of remaining without remainder and is manifested through the severance of hindrances, is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

The wisdom of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*)—ranging from the general and specific mindfulness and contemplation, the seven factors of awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*)—which is able to transcend and depart from the birth and death of the three realms, is called the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). Among these four, the first three are the causes and effects of the mundane world, while the latter two are...

Regarding the cause and effect of the supramundane: as for why the fruit is presented first and the cause later, it is because within the mundane world one first demonstrates suffering in order to arouse a sense of weary detachment;
one then comes to know that the fruit of the Truth of Suffering is summoned by the cause of Accumulation, so that this cause may be severed.

Within the supramundane, one first demonstrates Cessation—tranquil, eternally peaceful, free from the hardships of form, affliction, and the toil of wisdom—and endowed with the non-conditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The remaining [truths] cause the arising of a joyful mind; one knows that the reason for the truth of cessation is realized through the path, and thus causes it to be cultivated.
As the ancients said: "One who is weary of such suffering abandons such origination; one who delights in such cessation cultivates such a path.
Therefore, the Tathāgata first turned this Dharma in three ways for the group of five at Deer Park; this is precisely the intended meaning.
[The section on] Nirvāṇa also consists of twenty-seven [sections]. It states in full: "Good son, there are four kinds of wisdom that contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination.
... Even those who contemplate with inferior wisdom attain the path of the śrāvaka; those who contemplate with middling wisdom attain the path of the pratyekabuddha;
and even those who contemplate with the highest-of-the-high wisdom attain unsurpassed bodhi," and so forth. The *Lunyu* (Analects) refers to the "Eight Rows" (*Ba Yi*) chapter.
Commentary: Regarding "foremost in wisdom," this refers to how each of the ten great disciples excels in a particular field. For example: Kāśyapa is foremost in ascetic practices (*dhūta*);
Maudgalyāyana in supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*); Subhūti in understanding emptiness; Kātyāyana in expounding the meaning of doctrines;
Kapphiṇa in astronomy and calendrics; Aniruddha in the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); Rāhula in secret conduct (*guhyacaryā*), and so forth. If one follows the third fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*:
The middle fascicle states: "Among the disciples, each possessed his own particular capability. To summarize: in broad-minded benevolence and extensive learning, he was like Ājñātakauṇḍinya;
in skillful exhortation and guidance, he was like Udāyin; in constantly flying through the void, he was like the bhikṣu Subāhu;
in majestic demeanor and dignified composure, he was like the bhikṣu Aśvajit; and in diligence, ascetic practice, seated meditation, and meditative absorption, he was like the bhikṣu Revata."

They extensively established vegetarian feasts and lectures like the bhikṣu Dharoma, and constructed dwellings for the *cāturdisa-saṃgha* (the Sangha of the four quarters) like the bhikṣu Kṣudradharoma.

Thus, the Beishan lu states: "If five hundred *aśaikṣas* each seek [their goal] according to their respective capacities, they all occupy the foremost rank rather than the secondary. Even the Nirvāṇa Sūtra cited therein says: "Not at all..."

They do not even know this; how much less could they know it all? Thus, the *Bishan lu* states: "The Arhats did not understand the meaning of salt," which was a source of deep derision among the lay followers of the non-Buddhist schools.

This is because those who have merely emerged from the decaying house—the ordinary beings of birth and death—are worlds apart [from the truth]. How could they discuss external matters or worldly benefits?
It may be that the liberated wisdom of the sages is, in some respects, inferior to that of ordinary people. Yet, Confucius was a sage within the realm of the world, and...

He was able to know much. When the King of Chu crossed the river and obtained an object that he did not recognize, he sent someone to question Confucius. The Master said, "It is the fruit of the duckweed (*ping-shi*). It may be eaten. I have heard it in a children's song: 'The King of Chu crossed the river and obtained the fruit of the duckweed; round as a peck-measure, red as the sun. When split and eaten, it is sweet as honey. Later, when the state of Wu governed Tushan, they obtained a bone large enough to fill a cart and asked about it. Confucius said, "This is the backbone of a great tortoise. It is from the time of the Xia dynasty. The King of Wu sighed, saying, "I have heard that the ancients were wise, but I never expected them to be so profoundly knowledgeable. Confucius said, "If one studies extensively and reflects deeply, one can indeed know such things. Thus, the Master’s knowledge was truly vast. He could discern the essence of things through their names and appearances, and his wisdom was truly profound. This is what is meant by "being able to know much. Furthermore, when the Duke of Lu asked about the origins of the state of Qi, the Master replied, "Qi was originally the territory of the state of Guan. Its capital was at the foot of Mount Guan. The Duke of Zhou bestowed it upon Shao Kang, the son of King Wen. After Shao Kang died, his descendants moved the capital to the east of the River and called it Qi. The Duke said, "I have heard that the state of Qi was founded by the Duke of Zhou, but I never expected it to have originated with Shao Kang. The Master said, "The Duke of Zhou is a sage, and his wisdom is profound. If one does not study extensively, how can one know such things? This is what is meant by "having broad learning. Moreover, when the Duke of Lu asked about the origins of the state of Wei, the Master replied, "Wei was originally the territory of the state of Yan. Its capital was at the foot of Mount Yan. The Duke of Zhou bestowed it upon Yu, the son of King Wen. After Yu died, his descendants moved the capital to the west of the River and called it Wei. The Duke said, "I have heard that the state of Wei was founded by the Duke of Zhou, but I never expected it to have originated with Yu. The Master said, "The Duke of Zhou is a sage, and his wisdom is profound. If one does not study extensively, how can one know such things? This is what is meant by "having broad learning.
