Confucius said, "This is the skeleton of the ancient Lord Fengfeng. When Great Yu assembled the feudal lords here, Fengfeng arrived late, and Yu executed him.
Fengfeng was forty feet tall. Even with Confucius’s many talents, there were still matters he did not know;
as the *Zhongyong* says: "The ignorance of even husband and wife can participate in understanding, yet when it comes to its ultimate profundity..."
Even sages have things they do not know. Thus, the "Tangwen" chapter of the *Liezi* states:
"When Confucius was traveling east, he saw some children debating the relative distance of the sun. One child said, 'I think the sun is closer to us when it first rises.'"
Yet at midday, the sun is far from us. How do we know this is so? One child said, "When the sun first rises, it is as large as a carriage canopy;
by midday, it is like a shallow bowl. Is this not because it appears small when distant and large when near?
Another child said, "I consider the sun to be far when it first rises and near at midday. Why? Because when the sun first rises..."
When they emerged, it was cold and chilly; yet at midday, it was as if one were plunging one's hand into hot water.
Is this not because that which is near is hot while that which is distant is cool? Confucius could not decide. The two children laughed and said, "Who, then, considers you to be more knowledgeable?"

Thus we know that even matters of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) cannot be fully known except by one possessing the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*); how much more so for those pertaining to the supramundane?

Below this, the intent of the sutra is to take conventional truth as the mundane and absolute truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as the supramundane. This citation serves to corroborate the following passage.

Commentary: Regarding "voidness" (*xū*) and so forth: the Master of Old (Laozi) said, "Attain the ultimate void and maintain stillness. He further said, "The space between heaven and earth is like a bellows:
it is empty yet never exhausted; it moves and produces all the more. He also said, "Thirty spokes converge upon a single hub;
it is in the emptiness [of the hub] that the utility of the chariot lies. "Peering" (*kuī*) means a slight glance. "Treading" (*liè*) means stepping upon. "Levels" (*děng*) refers to gradations.
One must not advance by skipping levels. Regarding "ascending by steps," the *Lunyu*, Chapter 19, "Zi Zhang," states:
"The Master cannot be reached, just as heaven cannot be ascended by means of steps."
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "citing examples," the *Laozi* (Chapter 48) states: "In the pursuit of learning, one increases daily; in the pursuit of the Way, one decreases daily.
Decrease it again and again until there is nothing left to decrease. This is as seen previously below: namely, the subduing of afflictions prior to the realization of the Way.

Regarding the abandonment of delusions after the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the stages according to the Nature School (*svabhāva-nikāya*) are, in detail, the Three Worthies (*tri-piṭaka-arya*) and the Ten Sages (*daśa-ārya*), as extensively explained in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

In brief, they are the fruits of the Faith, the Worthies, and the Sages, as explained in the *Aśrayaparivṛtti-śāstra* (Awakening of Faith), the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, and the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna* (Complete Enlightenment).

In the section on "Entrusting Stages," Xianshou’s *Yicheng fenzhi jiangshu* (Lectures on the Delineation of the One Vehicle) states briefly: "That is to say, by entrusting oneself to the four stages beginning with Faith, one eliminates the four [delusions] beginning with cessation."

Regarding the characteristics: as stated in the *Awakening of Faith*, the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) eliminates cessation; the stage of worthiness (*ārya-bhūmi*) eliminates difference; the stage of sagehood (*ārya-bhūmi*) eliminates abiding;

and the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*) eliminates arising. Furthermore, there is the manifestation of the stages through the elimination of delusions, such as the manifestation and perfection of the stage of faith by eliminating the characteristic of cessation. These are demonstrated in detail according to the boundaries of their respective meanings.
Commentary: Regarding "A-vui" (阿惟) and below, in ancient translations, *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* was rendered as these characters. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* also says:
"Do not compare the light of the sun to the glow of a firefly."

Commentary: Although the following section cites scriptures separately, its underlying intent contains the movement of severing delusions discussed previously, as seen in the passage beginning with "as follows.
The subsequent section clarifies the purpose of criticizing such movement; it merely intends to expound upon the non-obstruction between movement and stillness.

Regarding the phrase "phenomena and principle": phenomena refer to movement, while principle refers to stillness. As the *Chengguan’s Record of the Teachings of Qingliang* states: "Cultivate both phenomena and principle together."
One seeks the Buddha-wisdom by relying on fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
[Commentary: Regarding the term "Vaipulya" and so forth, this principle is common to the Mahāyāna sūtras.

As for "entering the stages," from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward up to the seventh, the characteristics of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) have already vanished; in accordance with fundamental wisdom, body and mind are without marks (*animitta*), which is termed "quiescence."

This is explained based on the realization of principle through fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); it is not discussed in terms of the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence) or the *pariṇāmi-bhava* (transformative existence).

Nevertheless, if one seeks with subtle discernment, within each stage (*bhūmi*) there is a progressive cessation of obstacles and realization of the truth, as well as a gradual, part-by-part quiescence. However, the intent of the present treatise does not adopt such a view;
rather, it takes up the state of quiescent stillness already attained from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) upward. How, then, does one arrive at this quiescence?
Does one take up the movement of relinquishment (*utsarga*) after the stillness of cessation?
[Commentary: Regarding "superior portion" (*viśeṣa-bhāga*): among the various stages, the practice belonging to its own specific stage is called the "own-portion" (*svabhāga*).

The practice that advances to the subsequent stage is called the "superior portion," in the sense of being more excellent. Since this preference is a matter of the mind, and the mind has not yet attained quiescence, it involves...
This refers to seeking this body; yet the body itself is not yet tranquil. [Commentary:

These four refer to the four aspects of taking up and discarding, or loss and gain. Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the text below," it means that there is a difference between quiescent extinction (*śānti*) and what is esteemed or pursued.
"Li" (戾) means to go against or to be discordant; it refers to the mutual opposition between the states of movement and stillness.

Commentary: Regarding the passage beginning with "The south symbolizes," etc.: the preceding section cited the *Dharmakāya* (Dharma-body) and above; in the sutra text it is described as "quiescent," whereas in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* it is described as "moving.
This may be discerned from the commentary. As for "the south being Zhu-ming" (the Red Radiance):

when the five colors are assigned to the five directions, blue is the east, red is the south, white is the west, black is the north, and yellow is the center. When correlated with the Five Elements (*pañca-dhātu*), the east corresponds to Jia-Yi and Wood.
The south is Bing and Ding, Fire; the west is Geng and Xin, Metal; the north is Ren and Gui, Water; and the center is Wu and Ji, Earth.

Therefore, the south is called Zhuming (Vivid Brightness), and the north is called Xuanyin (Mysterious Obscurity). Furthermore, the hexagram Li belongs to the south and is also the image of brightness.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "However, as for receiving [the teachings]" and below: this means that in the practice of the Nature School (Xingzong), one must never contravene movement or stillness;

one must advance simultaneously in both calming (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), cultivate both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*), and maintain the equality of compassion and wisdom. This is as stated in *The Non-Transmigration of Things* (*Wubian lun*): "One does not abandon movement in order to seek stillness," and so forth.

Commentary: "Quiescence" refers to stillness; engaging in movement is called "conditioned activity" (*saṃskṛta*). Abandoning movement is called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*). Laozi also said: "By doing nothing, there is nothing left undone.
If one says that the ultimate principle is unconditioned, it means it is not subject to transformation by the four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*); thus it is named "unconditioned.
Therefore, although the name "unconditioned" is singular, its designations differ according to their specific meanings.
Commentary: Regarding the following four phrases, because it is quiescent yet constantly moving, movement and quiescence are not one;

because it moves yet is constantly quiescent, movement is itself quiescence and is not different. Regarding the final four phrases, "darkly uniting with the Truth" refers to the principle and its practice.
The mind that engages with the mundane is the practice of phenomena; the simultaneous illumination of the ultimate and the mundane is the dual flow.

Just as the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī (Nurtured by Sages) maintains the quiescence of body and mind within each stage (*bhūmi*) without losing his own portion, yet also progresses and seeks higher stages within each stage without losing his superior portion—how could one say that stillness contradicts movement, or that one no longer progresses and seeks, or that movement contradicts stillness, such that tranquility is not achieved?
Because they are extinguished, these two modes of practice are not in conflict; only then is the cultivation of non-abiding established.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase "following the preceding," this refers to how each set of four phrases in the prior text forms a pair, through which the meaning of movement and stillness can be understood.

Commentary: According to the preceding section, the commentary reconciles the mutual presentation of body and mind; this can be verified by examining the previous text, as there is no other meaning [to be derived].

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the meaning is like..."—however, throughout the upper and lower sections of the treatise, the explanations for the names "neither existent nor non-existent" differ in their respective meanings.
Now, this interpretation of the sutra further establishes another meaning: it is not that which exists as having a mind, for it is not existence;
nor is it that which does not exist as being without a mind, for it is not non-existence.

Commentary: "The common masses" refers to those such as the "common people" mentioned in the "Chapter on the Common People" of the *Xiaojing* (Classic of Filial Piety)—that is, the multitude who are dull-witted and ignorant, belonging to the ordinary and mundane stream.

Regarding the commentary's use of the term "to exclude": since the Sage possesses no delusive appearances, it is said that he "does not have [them]"; yet because his spiritual illumination is brilliantly manifest, it is said that he "does not lack [it]."

There is none. Regarding the commentary on the first two phrases: because they have been forgotten and severed, they do not exist. Regarding the next two phrases: because wisdom remains, one accords with the principle and thus they are not non-existent.

As for the passage beginning with "as numerous as the sands of the Ganges," it is stated in the section on the "Greatness of Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇamahattva*) in the *Awakening of Faith* (Qixin lun): "That which..."
This means that its own essence possesses the meaning of the great radiance of wisdom; it possesses the meaning of universally illuminating the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu);
and so on, up to being fully endowed with inconceivable Buddha-dharmas exceeding the sands of the Ganges. Furthermore, one who follows the principle says:
although these meanings of merit truly exist, they lack any characteristics of differentiation because they are of a single flavor; thus, there is only True Suchness (tathatā). This...
The meaning is: why is it that by being non-discriminative one is free from the marks of discrimination? Therefore, there is no duality. Regarding the latter two phrases, the intention is this:
if mental conceptions have not yet been exhausted, the mark of self naturally persists; once mental conceptions have ceased, the function itself is without marks.
*Qingliang xinyao* says: "In profound stillness, it operates with boundless illumination. This clarifies that while quiescent, it is constantly active. How can it be accumulated?
Does the movement of virtue deviate from the stillness of nirvana? [The] Commentary [states]:

"Regarding the answers to the questions and so forth," the text is straightforward and need not be explained; I shall merely set forth the meaning of what precedes and follows. The twenty-first fascicle of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* (or relevant sutra) states:
"The Tathāgata’s nirvana is neither conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)," and so on.

Commentary: Regarding "the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and others," this is also a citation by way of its general meaning. The *Śāstra* merely says, "giving one's head, eyes, marrow, and brain," and does not mention "kingdoms or wealth.

This is because it cites the weightier to include the lighter, using the internal as an illustration for the external. As for "and so forth" (*nàizhì*), the full text mentions "observing the precepts, patience, and meditative concentration.
It states that while dwelling in mountain forests, his body became withered and emaciated (and so on). In the commentary, the explanation below [proceeds] as follows:

Regarding the statement that the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī (儒童) beheld Dīpaṃkara Buddha while in the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains this as follows: the phrase "those whose marks of wisdom are not yet exhausted" has already been explained in the preceding text.
As for the "three wheels" (*trimaṇḍala*): first, not being mindful of the giver; second, not being mindful of the recipient; and third, not being mindful of the karmic fruit.
The twenty-fourth fascicle of the root sūtra states briefly: "One does not perceive the giver, the recipient, or the fruit of giving," and so forth. Not...
"Or inferior" refers to those from the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) downwards, who have already severed the mind that grasps at continuity and so forth;

yet because the characteristics of their wisdom have not been fully extinguished, they have not attained the complete emptiness of the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*). Regarding "inferior abiding," the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"A bodhisattva should practice giving without dwelling on any phenomenon. One should not dwell on form while practicing giving; one should not dwell on sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or mental phenomena while practicing giving."
Generosity. It continues until it says that its merit is inconceivable, equal to the emptiness of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
This is because one who practices generosity while dwelling in signs is attached to the marks of self, person, and so forth;

such a person merely seeks the merit for rebirth in heaven and does not attain the fruit of outflowlessness. Since this applies to inferior generosity, it serves as an analogy for the other practices. That is to say, whenever one performs any practice, first—
In all cases, one must forget all marks (*lakṣaṇa*). Only when the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) are empty and quiescent does one truly establish the cause for transcending the world.

Thus, Qingliang said: "Without conduct that flows from the True [Dharma], there is no way to accord with the Truth. Although the donor was of low status, Rāhula attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);

yet it was only by giving with a mind of patience that he accorded with the Truth. Therefore, it is said that the value of a gift does not lie in its quantity, but in its accordance with the Middle Way; it is this that is considered extraordinary. Giving is not valued... [text ends]... for its own sake.
Regarding the heavy and the light, one accords with the truth to form the essential. "Shian" (尠) means few. "Ti-chen" (蹄涔): when there is water in a hoofprint, it is called *ti-chen*.
As for the "Circumstances of the Flower Offering" (*Shihuayan*), the *Taizi benqi duanying jing* (Sūtra on the Prince’s Original Arising and Initial Response) states briefly:
When the Buddha Dīpaṃkara appeared in the world, there was a noble king named Jiéshèng (Jiēshèng) who ruled the great kingdom of Pāṭaliputra. At that time, I was a bodhisattva named Rútóng (Rútóng).

Dwelling in the mountains practicing meditation, he heard that there was a Buddha in the world and his heart was filled with solitary joy. Wearing a deer-skin robe, he set out intending to enter the kingdom.
He encountered five hundred Daoist practitioners discussing the meaning of the Way; both master and disciples were delighted and each offered him a silver coin. The Bodhisattva accepted them.
Upon entering the city, he saw the people repairing the roads, sprinkling water, sweeping, and burning incense. He immediately asked the passersby, and they replied, "The Buddha."
As they entered the city, the Bodhisattva was overjoyed, thinking, "Now I shall see the Buddha; I must fulfill my vow.

There was a maidservant of the royal household named Gopī who was passing by carrying a water jar. She secretly held seven stalks of blue lotuses. The Youth immediately opened his silver purse and gave it all to her.
The woman was greedy for the silver treasure. She gave him five stalks of flowers, keeping two for herself. Her mind turned elsewhere with suspicion, wondering, "What kind of ascetic is this?

Clad in deerskin, he does not spare his silver treasure. She called out to the man and told him the truth. The Bodhisattva said, "I wish to offer these to the Buddha to seek the fulfillment of my vows.
Gopī said, "Excellent. Please entrust these two flowers to me as well; I shall also offer them to the Buddha. She then waited.
When the Buddha arrived, the king, his ministers, and the people prostrated themselves and scattered flowers; yet all the flowers fell to the ground.
When the Bodhisattva saw the Buddha, he scattered five stalks of flowers, which all remained suspended in mid-air. He then scattered two more flowers, which stayed upon the Buddha’s shoulders.

Knowing the Bodhisattva’s profound intent, the Buddha prophesied for him, saying: "Ninety-one kalpas from now, in a kalpa named Bhadra, you shall attain Buddhahood and be known by the name [Śākyamuni]."

Śākyamuni: When a bodhisattva receives the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), their doubts are resolved and their expectations cease; they then attain the pure *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena).
Regarding the emission of light below: the Bodhisattva Śūnyacaryā is so named because he practices the three kinds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
These three emptinesses, being signless (*animitta*), constitute the practice of tranquility (*śānta-caryā*). The five *pāramitās*, however, constitute movement.
Commentary: Regarding "The Worthy Kalpa" (*Bhadra-kalpa*) below, this is the third [section]. To speak fully: all dharmas have no giver, yet one attains them by oneself;
to thus encourage and assist those who are destitute is called giving (*dāna*). Regarding "The Sūtra on the Attainment of Complete Radiance" (*Sampūrṇa-prabhāsa-samādhi-sūtra*) below, the verse says:
"Not teaching, but practicing for oneself; not acting, yet performing what exceeds [the ordinary]," and so forth. Regarding "The Sūtra on Dhyāna" (*Dhyāna-sūtra*) below, it refers to sitting.
The *Dhyāna-samādhi-dharmaparyāya-sūtra*, Scroll Lower. It is fully titled: *The Samādhi of Compassion*. Briefly stated, there are three kinds of objects (*ālambana*):

the object of beings (*sattvālambana*), the object of phenomena (*dharmālambana*), and the objectless (*anālambana*). Those who have not yet attained the Path are called those with the object of beings.

Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are called those with the object of phenomena. The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are called those with the objectless. As stated in the first chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-saṃcodana-sūtra*: "By means of the objectless..."
It is attained because there is nothing to be attained; it is known because there is nothing to be known. Why is this so?
The Dharma that I have attained cannot be seen, cannot be heard, cannot be sensed, and cannot be cognized, and so forth.
Commentary: Regarding the first two phrases and so forth, this criticizes the preceding [section] for having "movement" despite being named "stillness.
Under the heading "Purity," the *Gandavyūha* (Chapter on the Buddha-land of Fragrant Accumulation) states briefly: Śāriputra thought to himself that mealtime was approaching;
where would these bodhisattvas eat? Thereupon, Vimalakīrti manifested a bodhisattva and sent him to a world-system in the zenith, across forty-two Ganges-sands of buddha-fields...
In a buddha-field named Saṃghagandha, there is a Buddha titled Gandhottama who is currently sitting and eating together with various bodhisattvas.
[Śāriputra] arrived there and said: "I pray that you will grant me the remains of the World-Honored One’s meal; I shall perform the work of a Buddha by distributing it throughout the Sahā world.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata Gandhottama took a bowl filled with fragrant food from his many bowls and gave it to the manifested bodhisattva.
Those nine million bodhisattvas arrived at the house of Subhūti in an instant, as described in the "Bodhisattva Chapter. It says:
At that time, the Bodhisattvas from the Land of Universal Fragrance joined their palms and addressed the Buddha: "When we first saw this land, we conceived inferior thoughts.
We now repent and reproach ourselves. The skillful means of the Buddhas are inconceivable; for the sake of delivering sentient beings, they manifest various differences in Buddha-lands. Indeed!"

“World-Honored One, we pray that you grant us a small portion of the Dharma so that we may return to those lands. The Buddha told the bodhisattvas: “There is a dharma of liberation called ‘the exhausted and the inexhaustible.
You should study it. What is meant by ‘the exhausted’? It refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). What is meant by ‘the inexhaustible’?

It refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*). A bodhisattva such as this does not exhaust the conditioned, nor do they dwell in the unconditioned. What is meant by ‘not exhausting the conditioned’?”

This means not being separated from great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), great equanimity (*upekṣā*), and great compassion (*karuṇā*), and never becoming weary or exhausted in the ultimate task of teaching and transforming sentient beings.
What is meant by "the bodhisattva does not dwell in the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*)? It means practicing and studying emptiness (*śūnyatā*) without taking emptiness as a realization;

practicing and studying signlessness (*animitta*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) without taking signlessness and wishlessness as realizations, and so forth. The commentary explains: this clarifies that the bodhisattva fully cultivates the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

This refers to the practice of phenomenal activity (*sāṃvṛtika-caryā*), wherein one cultivates the karma of non-action (*asaṃskṛta-karma*) without dwelling [in it]. Phenomenal activity is movement; principle-activity is stillness.
When these two practices are cultivated together, how could movement and stillness be in conflict? The passage below from that commentary consists of four notes on the words of Master Zhiyi.
"One whose wise mind is not clear" means one who does not cultivate phenomenal activity, being stilled without illumination, and thus lacking the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect wisdom).
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "taking one as the source": if Nirvana were taken as the source, there would be the fault that it is not accomplished through cultivation.
If sentient beings were taken as the source, there would be the error that Nirvana has a beginning. This will be demonstrated in detail below.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "conversely revealing," it means that a *yāna* is a vehicle. Thus, the commentary states: "To control and direct [the mind] is to clarify [the path], flowing back toward the source.
Sentient beings are the foundation of the three vehicles (*triyāna*). The three vehicles pertain to causal cultivation, while *nirvāṇa* is the realization of the fruit.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "having a beginning" and so forth, the twenty-eighth fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "Good son, nirvana has no cause and its essence is that of a fruit.
Why is this? Because it is without arising or ceasing... and so on, up to: because it has neither beginning nor end. How could this not be contradictory [to the claim that it has a beginning]?

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "there are those who do not rely on [causes]," this points out an error. To examine closely the meaning of the term "having a name," it refers to the view of the provisional and limited [vehicles] that the principle of *nirvāṇa* arises through cultivation;
this is the sense of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* that "what was originally non-existent now exists.

It is not yet understood that this principle is what is revealed by the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*) and is not something produced by the "producing cause" (*kāraka-hetu*). Therefore, the twenty-first fascicle of the original sūtra states: "The first is..."
There are two kinds of causes: the producing cause (*kāraka-hetu*) and the revealing cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*). For example, a potter, a wheel, and a string are called the producing cause;
for example, lamps and candles that illuminate objects in the dark are called the revealing cause. Son of good family, the Great Nirvāṇa does not exist by way of a producing cause.

It arises solely from the revealing cause (*vyañjanahetu*). As for the revealing cause, it refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) and the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*);

these are called the revealing cause. Thus, one knows that the cultivation of the three vehicles consists only in cultivating the wisdom of the revealing cause, thereby exhausting the delusions of the truth of accumulation (*samudayasatya*).
When delusions are exhausted, nirvana manifests of itself. How could the nature of nirvana be something produced through cultivation?

Regarding the phrase "Master Sheng said," this is cited from the *Great Commentary* (*Dà cǎo*), specifically from the Preface to the *Nirvāṇa Commentary*, which explains the meaning of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Following the passage "The Constant [Nirvāṇa] necessarily extinguishes the burdens," it continues: "It is called *parinirvāṇa*; it is quiescent illumination.

Master Jian cites the *Nirvāṇa Xīnjìng Cǎo* (Commentary on the Heart-Mirror of Nirvāṇa), stating: "Master Sheng composed a commentary on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* of over fifty sheets of paper, yet he explained only the 'solid root' (*pán gēn*)."
At this point where the knotted complexities are difficult to unravel, the essential teachings of the Sūtras fully open their profound treasury, which is known as the "Commentary of Guanzhong.

From the passage "expounding this below," it is meant that the purity of skillful means (*upāya-viśuddhi*) is the wisdom of the Three Vehicles; because this wisdom possesses the capacity to purify afflictions, it is termed "skillful means."
The nature of wisdom in *nirvāṇa* is inherently present; it is also *svabhāva-nirvāṇa*, because the principle (*li*) and wisdom (*zhi*) must necessarily be mutually integrated.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "sages" (*shengren*), this refers to the fact that the sage-wisdom of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) all possesses the merit of silent resonance with reality.

The term "perfected person" (*zhiren*) used here refers specifically to the Tathāgata, because the sages of the three vehicles have not yet reached the ultimate limit of their resonance with reality and thus cannot entirely avoid the traces of form (*xiang*). The Tathāgata, however, has reached the ultimate limit of resonance.
This refers to the absence of characteristics (*animitta*). Although the mind is inferior, it dispels the absence of characteristics to manifest as characteristics.

This means that the Sage, through the purity of skillful means (*upāya*), accords with the self-nature of pure *nirvāṇa*. This nature constitutes the entirety of all phenomena (*dharma*). Therefore, the Treatise says:
"There are no things that are not created by me."

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "realizing and attesting" (*hui zheng*): this refers to the Sage’s realization that the fundamental emptiness of all phenomena is precisely their own nature (*svabhāva*).

It is by attesting to the fact that all dharmas are thus that one becomes a Sage. As the *Brahmacarya-parivarta* of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "To know that all dharmas are the very nature of the mind," and so forth;
this perfectly accords with the present meaning. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, fascicle 25, states: The Buddha addressed the Brahmin named Jāti: [End of excerpt]
The Gatekeeper says: "This very body of mine is now nirvana. This is from the second fascicle of the *Lengyan jing*. Qingliang says:
"A single thought in accord, a Buddha in every thought; every thought in accord, a Buddha in every moment.
As for Shitou, he was Chan Master Xiqian of Mount Shitou at Nanyue during the Tang dynasty. "Wuji" means "no-self. "Mi" means "non-existent."
However, since one takes the myriad things as the mind itself, it is said that "there is nothing that is not oneself.
When it asks, "Who says... and so forth, it means there is no distinction between self and other; everything is none other than one's own Dharmakāya. As the Dharma-body Verse by Master Dushun states:

"In Huai Prefecture, an ox eats grain; in Yi Prefecture, a horse has a bloated belly. The world seeks a physician, yet he applies moxibustion to the left shoulder-blade of a pig. This too is based on the Dharmakāya.
The body is the same, for there is no distinction between self and other. "Perfect Mirror" refers to wisdom; because it is the illumination within stillness, it is called "empty illumination.
"Its essence is profound" means that it is the nature of the mind itself; it is identical with all phenomena yet is not the phenomena themselves, hence it is said that its essence is profound.

Regarding "manifesting from itself": since the myriad phenomena are fundamentally empty, the Dharmakāya manifests of its own accord. The critique states: The pointing-out and demonstrations of the various patriarchs were decided upon by those who rely on Chan;
it is not permitted to add further annotations as a precedent, for fear that one would instead fall into conceptual consciousness and blind the eye of wisdom.

It is better to realize through forgetting words and attaining awakening within; this is what constitutes true attainment. For now, I shall briefly venture my lips in this assembly where the teachings circulate, so as to lead people [to understanding].

Enter quickly. According to the *Línjiān lù* (Record of the Forest), when Master Yongming was in the assembly of National Teacher Shao of Tiantai, he was carrying firewood to the gate when a branch suddenly fell to the ground.
Upon hearing this, he attained enlightenment and spoke a verse: "Thump! It is not another thing; Transverse and vertical, it is not dust.
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth— The entire body of the Dharma King is revealed. Regarding "it is not another thing," it means that [the body] is not...

From without, it triggers the faculty of hearing within oneself; the nature of sound and the nature of hearing are of one and the same nature. "Vertical" refers to north and south; "horizontal" refers to east and west.
This means that the very appearance of sound is my own nature of hearing; it is not the external object of sound. The meaning of the final two lines is:
since this sound is thus, the mountains, rivers, and the myriad phenomena are none other than my Dharma-body.
Commentary: Regarding the first two phrases and so forth: according to the Huayan school, if one does not realize the *Mahāvaipulya*, how can one attain Buddhahood in the *Avataṃsaka*?
If it were not the *Avataṃsaka* of the Buddha, one would likewise not realize the *Mahāvaipulya*. Thus, person and dharma are mutually identical; they are a single essence without exteriority.
Commentary: Regarding the initial passage and so forth, the ninth chapter of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states in full:

"One should not seek the *prajñāpāramitā* within form (*rūpa*), nor should one seek the *prajñāpāramitā* apart from form," and so on. The ninth chapter of the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (the *Fàngguāng jīng*) says:
Subhūti addressed Kauśika, saying, "The *prajñāpāramitā* is also not to be sought within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), nor..."
Seeking nirvana as equal within the detachment from the five aggregates constitutes the twenty-seventh [point]. Next, it says: "The Buddha is precisely the Buddha-nature. Why?
Because all Buddhas take this as their nature, and because dependent origination is itself suchness (tathatā).
To see the Dharma is to see the Buddha; thus, wisdom and suchness are not different. This confirms what was stated previously: that the Sage is not distinct from principle.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the preceding citations," etc., this indicates the thematic continuity and progression of the treatise (*śāstra*). This section is extremely difficult to understand; therefore, the Commentary provides a detailed exposition of it.

From the passage beginning with "Qingliang" (Cleaer Coolness) onwards is the text of the "Profound Discourse" (*xuántán*). The principles of realization and verification (*zhèng*) within the Nature School (*xìngzōng*) are in fact distinct from those of other schools.

As the *Great Commentary* (*Dàshū*) states: "Illuminating that afflictions have no root is itself the essence of wisdom (*jīti*). It further states: "The essence of illumination having no self-nature is itself the realization of Suchness (*rú*)."

The Commentary states: "If one attempts to conjoin wisdom with suchness, it is not true suchness. The section beginning with "Mingzhen" (冥真) describes the greatness of the essence (*tathatā*) according to the traces of the teaching.
The section beginning with "Foyong" (佛用) refers to two types of language mentioned in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Song* (*Song Gaoseng Zhuan*):
first, *sāmānya*, which refers to ordinary, colloquial speech; second, *bhāṣita*, which refers to formal, canonical speech. The Buddha’s teachings mostly rely upon *sāmānya*.

It is extensive. Its intent lies in the meaning and does not rely on the literal phrasing; furthermore, it is for the sake of all beings. If it were *tīvra* (extreme), it would not be something that those of middling or inferior capacity could understand.

Thus, the Master of the Treatise established his teaching by skillful means (*upāya*) in accordance with the capacities of his audience. The people of China value literary refinement and look down upon the plain;

only when the ornate and the substantive are harmonized (*wen-zhi bin-bin*) does a work become truly admirable. Therefore, this treatise is a rare and unprecedented proclamation for a thousand ages. Exalted!

Wise men treasure and play with it. "Dòu" (逗) means "to penetrate" (tōng). Regarding "fēng wén xià" (封文下): this refers to being confined by the literal text and failing to perceive the flow of its underlying meaning;
it implies being indiscriminately equated with the principles of Confucianism and Daoism. Zàn Níng was a monk from the beginning of the Song dynasty.
He compiled the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) in thirty fascicles. In the third section of that work, the "Translators of Scriptures" (*Yijing ke*), it states:

"If one employs non-Buddhist texts, it will inevitably invite slander. Yet now we observe Fang Rong polishing the prose of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, and Sengzhao citing [non-Buddhist works] to compose his treatises."
"You ought to be subject to such reproach," and so forth. The critique states: Fang Rong was a literary man; it was inappropriate for him to embellish the scriptures using secular writings.

Master Sengzhao was a man of broad learning; what harm is there in his citing [secular works] when composing a treatise? For while the scriptures are the words of the Buddha, the treatises are his own words.
As for Huida, he was a monk of the Chen dynasty who once wrote a preface to this treatise. That preface says: "Worldly rumor has it that these were composed by Sengzhao."

These [teachings] are indeed established as the true reality and ultimate truth. The *Dilun* school takes them as its general tenet, and they provide the resources for the teachings of Zhuangzi and Laozi.

Such reckless talk is truly the speech of a great pest; it deceives and misleads the deceased, and the vulgar sounds of the streets and alleys are not worth so much as a plucked-up ear of grain. As for "reckless" (*menglang*): *Meng*...

"Great" means vast; "wave" means empty. "Foolish and trivial": "foolish" refers to ignorance, and "trivial" refers to pettiness. "Establishing the words below" refers to the fundamental intent of the Master in formulating his treatise.
"Not harming below" means that one does not allow the literal phrasing to distort the underlying meaning. "Therefore, now below... [text continues].
This means that the ancient commentators, seeing that the text resembled the style of Zhuangzi and Laozi, mostly interpreted it according to the principles of Zhuangzi and Laozi.

As for myself, I have frequently drawn upon their insights first, and only thereafter explained it based on the Inner Teachings (Buddhism). Regarding "elegant language" (*yayan*): in the *Mao Shi*, there are the *Daya* (Greater Odes) and *Xiaoya* (Lesser Odes).

"Elegant" (*ya*) means "correct. It refers to literary elegance. The phrase "to cause [them] to know" below indicates that the Master of the Treatise originally employed the terminology of Confucian scholars to demonstrate Buddhist principles;
it does not mean that he was identical to the texts of Laozi and Zhuangzi or merely imitated them.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "to clarify the preceding," this meaning has appeared frequently throughout the preceding and following sections; it will not be indicated again. The passage beginning with "In a single thought-moment" is also from the *Xinyao* (Essentials of the Mind).
For those who rely on the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), that sutra does not contain the names "ancient" or "modern," nor does it speak of the "three periods of time.

Only Master Li [Tongxuan], in his *Lun* (Discourse), states: "The ten periods of time—ancient and modern, beginning and end—do not depart from the present thought-moment. This means that ancient and modern are...

This refers to the three periods of time. As for "the mutual identity and entry [of these two]," this is the "Gate of the Ten Periods Being Separately Established Yet Interpenetrating" among the Ten Profound Gates (Shi xuán mén).
Based on this, one distinguishes the perfect interfusion of temporal periods, which also comprises two gates: "mutual identity" constitutes the Gate of the Sovereignty of All Dharmas.
The mutual inclusion [of phenomena] constitutes the gate of "the one and many being mutually inclusive yet distinct.

However, while these ten gates differ in their distinction between different entities (*bhinnasvabhāva*), the mutual identity and mutual inclusion of the ten periods of time involve only the mutual identity and mutual inclusion of a single entity (*ekasvabhāva*). Regarding "root and branch" below:

the root is the principle of *nirvāṇa*, and the branches are the phenomena of the myriad things. To exhaustively investigate the root is to find that all dharmas are *nirvāṇa*; to reach the ultimate limit of the branches...
"Nirvāṇa is identical with the myriad phenomena. Regarding "sentient and non-sentient," Master Dushun’s verse says: "Sentient and non-sentient share one and the same essence;
everywhere they are identical with the true Dharma-realm. What is called 'defilement' refers to defiled dependent origination; that which is not defiled can be known [as such]."
Commentary: Regarding the mutual implication between the two passages: the preceding passage merely states that [the mind] is not separate from all phenomena, but does not mention "boundlessness.
The subsequent passage merely mentions "boundlessness," but does not mention "not being separate. Therefore, it is said they mutually imply one another.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "such as wisdom" and so forth: when both mind and object are simultaneously extinguished, it is called "profound stillness" (xuánjì).

Since profound stillness is nameless, one provisionally relies upon the name "the Ultimate" (wújí) to manifest the principle of profound stillness. Therefore, the commentary states: "It is not something separate," and so on.

Commentary: Regarding the passage "The three vehicles... and so forth, the intent is that for those of the three vehicles, first realizing *nirvāṇa* is called "advancing," while later realizing *nirvāṇa* is called "retreating.
Therefore, there is no sequence of before and after; once realized, it is identical in its profound stillness.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "under the name 'Purity' (*viśuddhi*)," the second chapter, "Observing Sentient Beings," states: "At that time, there was a celestial maiden in the room of Vimalakīrti.
Seeing the great men and hearing the Dharma they preached, she manifested her form and immediately scattered celestial flowers over the bodhisattvas and the great disciples (*mahāśrāvaka*).
When the flowers reached the bodhisattvas, they all fell away; but when they reached the great disciples, they adhered to them."
They did not fall away. All the disciples used their supernatural powers to remove the flowers, but they were unable to make them go.

At that time, a deva asked Śāriputra, "For what reason do you remove these flowers? He replied, "These flowers are not in accordance with the Dharma; therefore, I remove them. The deva said, "Do not say that these flowers are not in accordance with the Dharma.
Why is this? These flowers have no discrimination; it is you, O Venerable One, who give rise to such distinctions."
It is merely a conceptualization. If one has conceptual distinctions regarding the Buddha-dharma upon leaving the household life, it is contrary to the Dharma;
if there are no conceptual distinctions, then it is in accordance with the Dharma. Observe that the flowers do not adhere to the bodhisattvas because they have severed all conceptualizations.
For example, when a person is afraid, non-human spirits find an opportunity to exploit them; likewise, because these disciples fear birth and death, [conceptualizations arise].
"Forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles find their opportunity [to disturb them]... (and so forth). Śāriputra said, "How long has it been since you have dwelt in this room?
He replied, "I have dwelt in this room for as long as the Elder has been in liberation. Śāriputra said, "Have you dwelt here for that long?"
The goddess said, "Venerable sir, how long has your liberation been? Śāriputra remained silent and did not answer.
The goddess said, "Why does one of such great wisdom as you remain silent? He replied, "Liberation is beyond verbal expression; therefore, I do not know what to say.
The goddess said, "Verbal expressions and written characters are all identical to the nature of liberation. [The commentary states: Regarding the goddess's...
The mind considers that time has no substantial reality; it is a manifestation of the deluded mind. That which is distant is not fixed as distant, and that which is near is not fixed as near.

It is like the passage of time in a dream—what is long and what is short? Therefore, it is shown that "time is like the liberation of an elder. Since the characteristics of time are fundamentally empty, they are themselves liberation.
Śāriputra further stated that liberation is a dharma of long duration; he grasped at the dharma to define time and thus spoke of it as being "long."
...Thus it is said of the heavenly maiden (and so forth). The commentary states: According to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*, the heavenly maiden was the household deity of the layman (*gṛhapati*).

Such deities invariably manifest according to the spiritual status of their host. Since Vimalakīrti was a holy man appearing in the world, the household deity was likewise a bodhisattva assuming a provisional form.
This sutra fundamentally aims to suppress the Lesser Vehicle and exalt the Great Vehicle; therefore, Śāriputra also manifested his defeat through her words, in order to...
Those who aspire to the lesser [vehicle] shall attain swift return.

[End of] Commentary. Regarding "the nine bends" and so forth: this is a general summary of the intent behind the bends. As for the section beginning with "therefore": this narrates the beginning and end of the entire treatise.
This means that first the essence of *nirvāṇa* is revealed; next, through successive refutations, expositions, adjudications, and discernments, people are led to realization.

Whether with remainder or without remainder, whether provisional designations or the Great Parinirvāṇa, it is nameless and formless, neither existent nor non-existent, neither emerging nor abiding—yet therein the wondrous Way resides.
Those of the Three Vehicles cultivate it together and return to it together, proceeding directly by way of...
The varying depths of intellectual capacity result in three distinct differences; it is not that there are three types of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) states within the Three Vehicles.
Next, I shall clarify the path of severance and realization for the Three Vehicles: heavy delusions cannot be removed instantaneously, and the unconditioned cannot be realized instantaneously.

One must diminish and further diminish [defilements] before they become pure, and augment and further augment [virtues] until they gradually reach perfection; thus, one must accumulate merit and pursue the goal without deviation.

Quiescence: when body and mind are extinguished in stillness yet do not conflict with movement, and movement and stillness do not conflict with wondrous practice, then existence and non-existence no longer bind the numinous spirit.
This establishes the profound cause for the realization of the Three Vehicles and attains the wondrous fruit of perfect fulfillment within the single principle.

Mind and object merge in obscurity; from beginning to end, all is *tathatā* (suchness). Advancing, one does not precede it; retreating, one does not follow after it. Reaching this ultimate point, one finally—
Question: Regarding the method for attaining [this realization], such as "preserving the aggregates" (*skandha*) and "exhausting the aggregates," I shall now refute it.
Commentary: Under the first two phrases, it is meant that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are the very substance of sentient beings; there is no sentient being apart from the aggregates.
Therefore, the Treatise says: "It reaches the limit within the five aggregates."
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "in accordance with the sūtras," etc., it is because, as previously cited from the sūtras, for those who attain nirvāṇa, the five aggregates are entirely exhausted.
"There is that which is internal" refers to that which is within the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the aggregates persist," because the aggregates persist, there is a person who can attain [nirvana]; thus, it conforms to reason.

However, it also contradicts the sūtras, for the holy teachings constitute the definitive authority. If one contradicts the sūtras while discussing principle, who would submit to it? First, it should be stated below:
This is also based on conventional designation (*prajñapti*). Apart from the aggregates (*skandha*), how could there be a nature of a sentient being?

Since the Sūtra states that one attains *nirvāṇa* when the five aggregates are completely exhausted, the present treatise says that if there were an attainment of a fruit, then the nature of a sentient being would not be limited to the five aggregates.

This [former position] conforms to reason but contradicts the teaching; the second [position] fears contradicting what follows below. "Exhausting the coarse" and so forth [refers to] conforming to the teaching and bringing forth the principle. Below this: [Text continues: ...exhausting the coarse... [etc.]

I shall also explain this in accordance with the principle. There is no separate teaching or scriptural proof [to the contrary]. That is to say, the meaning of "existence" necessarily implies a person who is capable of attaining it, as well as the *nirvāṇa* that is attained.
If the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) were to be utterly exhausted, who would there be to act as the attainer?

Therefore, the commentary says so. The following section clarifies the intent behind this refutation. The intent of the refutation is that the provisional and gradual teachings of the Three Vehicles necessarily maintain the distinction between the attainer and the attainment.
The unfolding of the intention is precisely the One Vehicle; the ultimate reality reveals the primordial state, which is the simultaneous extinction of both subject and object.

The *Śāstra* (commentary) states: "The preceding unfolding [of the intention] below clarifies how it arises based on what precedes it. 'Not retaining' means not retaining the characteristics of a grasper and that which is grasped;
only then is there profound attainment. As the subsequent treatise says: "In that case, sentient beings are not sentient beings; who is it that attains this? etc.
Commentary: Regarding "forgetting attainment" and below: since *nirvāṇa* is merely the fruit manifested through cultivation, the commentary states that it is "manifested from this.
Regarding "the Dharma is true," and so forth: "Dharma" means to emulate the Dharma. This refers to the truth of *nirvāṇa*, which is free from all marks.

When the wisdom-Dharma emulates this truth, it also forgets the mark of attainment; it wondrously accords with that truth and becomes identical to it. Regarding "relying on the false," and so forth: this refers to delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
It is the mind. The deluded mind bifurcates into subject and object. If wisdom were to possess attainment, it would be identical to delusion. Regarding the phrase "one who has attainment" below:

this refers to one whose emotional attachments and views are not yet exhausted and thus cannot achieve realization; therefore, they are said to "have attainment. Regarding the phrase "one who has no attainment" below:

this refers to one whose emotions are exhausted and views are eliminated, completely forgetting the mark of attainment so as to be in perfect accord with principle; therefore, they are said to "attain. (2)
The *Thirteen Classics* state: "If the Tathāgata were to reckon that there is a mark of attainment, then all Buddhas would not attain nirvāṇa.
Because there is no attainment, it is called 'attaining nirvāṇa,' and so forth. The lower section of the *Heart Sūtra* states in full: "There is no ignorance and also no attainment.

This refers to the simultaneous extinction of both subject and object. Because they are simultaneously extinguished, the Buddhas of the three periods rely upon the non-attainment of prajñā to attain [nirvāṇa].
Regarding "Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," etc.:

The commentary states that "following" (*anu*) and so forth means that "dharmas" refers to the essence of all phenomena; that is, all verbal expressions arise in accordance with the dharmas being expressed.

The phrase "since it speaks of the lower [realms]" explains the passage in the *Śāstra* beginning with "whether it is nirvāṇa, etc. The section beginning with "nirvāṇa" provides the further explanation.
In the treatise, who alone is not *nirvāṇa*? In the lower section of the *Awakening of Faith*, it says in full:
"All phenomena exist only through the differentiation of deluded thought. If one is separated from mental thought, then there are no signs of any objective realms.

Therefore, all phenomena have from the very beginning been free from the signs of verbal expression, free from the signs of names and words, and free from the signs of mental conditions; they are ultimately [thus]."
It is equal, without change, and indestructible; it is solely the one mind, and is therefore called *tathatā* (Suchness).
Furthermore, it is said that what is termed *tathatā* is likewise without marks (*animitta*). This refers to the ultimate limit of verbal expression: by means of words, words are dispensed with.
This essence of *tathatā* cannot be dispensed with, because all phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely *tathatā*. Nor can anything be established, because all [phenomena]...

"All phenomena remain exactly as they were. The commentary states: This is because *tathatā* (suchness) is itself *nirvāṇa*. To provide scriptural evidence for this, the "Chapter on Manifestation" (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*) says:

"O Son of the Buddha, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to know the great *nirvāṇa* of the Tathāgata, he must thoroughly understand that the fundamental self-nature is like *tathatā*-nirvāṇa; the *nirvāṇa* of the Tathāgata is also like this," and so forth. This...
This is the *svabhāva-viśuddha-nirvāṇa* (nirvana of intrinsic purity).

Regarding the commentary’s phrase “because of melting and refining,” the intent of the commentary explains it as follows: because the two polarities (Heaven and Earth) are melted and refined, Heaven and humanity share a single principle;

because all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are cleansed and purified, unity and difference originate from the same source. From the section beginning with “in terms of seeing and hearing,” it refers to form (*rūpa*).

"Nature-sound" refers to the fact that nature is itself the self-nature (*svabhāva*). "Neither seeing nor hearing" means, as stated previously, that the five eyes do not behold its form and the ears, though listening, do not hear its resonance.
Commentary: That the Tathāgata is not a sentient being is because the true and the deluded are distinct; that he is not non-sentient is because their nature is non-dual.
That the Tathāgata enters nirvāṇa is likewise the explicit text of the sūtra.
Commentary: Regarding "birth and death" and so forth, the *Vajragarbha* chapter of the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* states briefly:
"It is like a phantom film on the eye that falsely perceives flowers in the sky," and continues until it says, "Birth and death and nirvāṇa are identical to arising and ceasing. The explanation says:

This means that birth and death have no reality and arise or cease according to conditions, just as a person with cataracts sees flowers in the sky. Regarding "mirage": this refers to the manifestation of the vapors of springtime.

It arises; the thirsty deer perceives it as water. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and other scriptures all state this, or say that the reflection of water sometimes appears within the earth, yet in reality there is no water.

The commentary adopts the former treatise and explains it by saying: "The great affliction is eternally extinguished, and one transcends the four flows (*catur-ogha*), because this is the *svabhāva-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa of intrinsic purity). Birth and death are like flowers in the sky; the four flows are like a mirage."

A mirage. If one seeks purity through skillful means, then even though the flowers in the sky are illusory, one must still remove the cataract; even though the mirage is false, one must still extinguish the perception of it.
Thus Guishan said: "The Buddha-nature is originally present, yet one must diligently cultivate it; delusion is fundamentally non-existent, yet it must be severed.

This is because sentient beings dwell in a land of illusion and dreams, undergoing empty and false birth and death. Although birth and death are empty, they nevertheless continue to drift and wander. [The afflictions...]

The source of affliction is a provisional phenomenon that burns by its very nature; how could one claim to have realized the Way merely by relying on innate purity, or assert that one has returned to the source by completely forgetting further cultivation?
Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "If a person, though mindful of the precious nature, does not employ various skillful means to polish and refine it, it will never attain purity."

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "this [is] by way of meaning, etc.," I have searched throughout the *Prabhāsa* (the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*) and found no passage composed in sections such as those in this treatise.
Therefore, we know that the author of the treatise has collected the meanings of the sūtras and cited them here. *Sarvajña* is "all-knowledge.

According to the meaning of this sūtra, the treatise presents four propositions—such as "Is it attained from existence? or "Is it attained from non-existence?"—and in each case, the answer given is "no. Subsequently...
The fifth fascicle states that one does not "attain" perfect enlightenment; this might still be taken to mean that there is absolutely nothing attained, yet the answer given is "no.
While the phrasing is slightly ambiguous, the underlying intent contains no contradiction.

Commentary: Regarding "no attainment" and so forth, it refers to the forgetting of attainment through profound stillness. "Pervasive" means "identical," signifying that the purity of skillful means is identical to the self-nature.
In the *Śāstra*, who would alone not be so? If one says it is newly attained, when would it ever be lost? Thus, in the lower section of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the Wei translation states:
"Mahāmati, there are two kinds of icchantikas. The first are those who have incinerated all roots of goodness. This refers to...
They slander the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. Second, they have compassion for all sentient beings; these are the Great Compassionate Bodhisattvas.
Mahāmati asked: "Of these two, which one never enters nirvāṇa? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is the Great Compassionate Bodhisattva. Why is this?
Because they thoroughly understand that all dharmas are fundamentally in a state of nirvāṇa; therefore, they do not enter nirvāṇa."

This is not like the icchantikas who have abandoned all roots of goodness; thus [it continues] below. This refers to the words of the Tathāgata of Perfect Enlightenment (Yuanjue) rebuking Gangzang for his three questions.

Regarding the commentary’s statement, “This has,” etc.: according to the intent of the treatise, it is said that one “attains” with respect to the object, “knows” with respect to the mind, and “sees” with respect to the form.
Regarding the term "hearing," the *Sū* (Commentary) explains it according to the meaning of "attaining the profound" (*xuan*). Therefore, it says "all.
The subsequent phrase distinguishes "attainment," meaning that one attains knowledge, vision, and hearing. It is called "the realm beyond limits" because it is neither mundane nor supramundane.

How could it be said that [the Buddha] alone established [a path] outside the three realms of existence? Therefore, the previous statement, "to reject the discourse of those outside the [Confucian] square," is precisely this point.
"Non-worldly" (fei-su) refers to the non-discriminating mind; it is not an object of conceptual deliberation (*ālambana*). The "Great Elephant" and "Great Sound" are terms borrowed from the *Laozi*.
Not dwelling on appearances, one perceives directly through their nature; this seeing-seeing is the Universal Eye. Not following sounds, one hears directly through the hearing;
this hearing-hearing is universal hearing. Therefore... (as cited previously) from the "Tian Dao" chapter of Zhuangzi:
Li Zhu was an ancient master of vision who could see a single autumn hair from a hundred paces away. Regarding Avalokiteśvara... (from the *Lengyan Sūtra*)...

The fifth fascicle of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* explains the twenty-five forms of noble perfect penetration (*ārya-samyak-pariśuddhi*). Among these, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva attained it through the gateway of the ear.
The sutra states briefly: "Turning the hearing back to hear one's own nature; as hearing returns, the obstructing faculty is eliminated," and so forth. Chan Master Cijue composed a verse on this:
"When turning the hearing back, there is no hearing at the place of hearing; Limitless weary beings enter the Universal Gate. Waterfalls cascading from a precipice can never be fully heard."

this refers to the manifestation of the greatness of the function of *nirvāṇa* within the "Chapter on Manifestation," as the sutra says: "O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata abides in the immeasurable..."
The unimpeded ultimate dharma-realm and space-realm, the true suchness (tathatā) and dharma-nature (dharmatā), are without arising or ceasing;

yet, for the sake of all sentient beings, they manifest at all times through the limit of delusion. Because they are sustained by original vows, there is no rest, and they do not abandon any sentient beings, any lands, or any dharmas.
The Great Commentary explains: "Because one first abides in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), one does not abide [in saṃsāra]."
Regarding birth and death: because he does not abandon sentient beings afterwards, he does not abide in nirvāṇa. By virtue of abiding in both simultaneously, he is able to abide in neither.

The former is great wisdom (*mahājñāna*); the latter is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Because great compassion and *prajñā* constantly assist one another, it is called "non-abiding nirvāṇa" (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*).
Furthermore, it is said: "Self-nature nirvāṇa is common to all sentient beings; it may also exist in those of the two vehicles who have attained no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*)."
Regarding the first three [types of nirvāṇa], only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, uniquely declares that they possess all four [characteristics].
Therefore, they are collectively summarized under the heading of "non-abiding" (*apratisthita*), which is precisely the establishment of the great task while abiding in nirvāṇa.

In this treatise, the principles of the four kinds and two kinds of nirvāṇa are elucidated according to their respective meanings, whether preceding or following one another. Finally, based on the essence of realization, its vast function arises. Therein...

Since both the "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and "without remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa*) [nirvāṇas] are functions that ought to arise, the meaning of "non-abiding" (*apratisthita*) is likewise fully contained therein;

If one carefully examines its intent, there is indeed a profound reason for this; therefore, both the present commentary (*shù*) and sub-commentary (*chão*) cite the *Great Commentary* (*Dà shù*).

Master Seng’s fourteen sections and other works are so deeply relished that one never tires of them; they are like the playful dragon sporting with the dark pearl.
The phrase "ancient and modern" below refers to how Master Zhao stood alone and peerless, with no one succeeding him; compared to the treasury of jewels, his [later] works are truly far removed.

It is certain that these were not composed by the Master himself, but were fabricated and attributed to him by later generations. Regarding the passage on "fame and virtue," it follows the assessment of Lord Pei Xiu.
The *Qīngliáng Běi* (Qingliang Stele) describes the Dharma favored by the Great Master as follows: "Master Zhaolun’s *Sijue lun* (Treatise on the Four Excellences):

he recited one hundred thousand words daily, and nothing passed before his eyes more than once. Sengrui was humble yet internally sagacious in his learning."

Competing with his time, he was deeply appreciated by the ruler of Qin, who praised him as a preeminent leader of the four seas. If even Qingliang held him in such high regard, one can well imagine the esteem of others.
Regarding the term "enveloping" (*kuò*), the *Yī* (Book of Changes), in the fourth line of the *Kūn* hexagram, states: "Enveloping the sack; no blame and no praise.
The intent there is that when a person is cautious with their speech and does not let it out, it is like enveloping the mouth within a sack. — *Lǎo-shū* (The Book of Laozi).

Regarding the section below on the "Eight Masters," according to the translation by Zhi Qian, they are also called the "Eight Evil Friends" (*aṣṭau pāpamitrāṇi*). When the Eight Evil Friends asked the Buddha whom he served as his masters, the Buddha replied:
"Indeed, there are eight masters; namely, the five precepts beginning with non-killing, as well as old age, sickness, and death. One should observe the intent of this sutra.
The five precepts are upheld by those subject to old age, illness, and death; thus, they collectively constitute eight. This differs from the eight precepts for humans and devas.

Regarding the "ninefold analysis" and so forth in the commentary: this generally demonstrates the broad meaning. There is a method that analyzes [the teachings] according to the principles of the specific tenets of the Three Vehicles.
Wuming interprets this through the meaning of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) as his own school’s tenet. Those who hold to the existence of names [of distinct vehicles] harbor doubts and stagnate;

when these are resolved, the path of the Three Vehicles opens and the principle of the single reality is revealed. The Master of the Treatise employs the intent of the *Lotus Sūtra* to compose these words.

By speaking only of "the opening of the path of the Three Vehicles," he indirectly captures the meaning that the single reality is spontaneously revealed. As for "abandoning the Small [Vehicle]," it is intended to cause them to abandon it.

thus, even in the former Mahāyāna there was a sense of the provisional, which this present treatise encompasses, as explained at length in the Great Commentary (*Dà shǔ*).

Below the section on "dividing the text," Master Yao’s commentary explains this passage as a summary of the four treatises.

"The path of the three vehicles opens" refers to the opening of the three vehicles and three stages within this treatise. "The way between the true and the false is distinguished" refers to what he calls the "concluding the objects."

The "Treatise on Non-Transmigration" (*Bùqiānlùn*) and the "Treatise on the Non-Reality of All Things" (*Bùzhēnkōnglùn*): the former concerns the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which is thus provisional;

the latter concerns the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is thus real. Thus, the Way of the sages and worthies is preserved therein. It is said that this concludes the "Treatise on the Absence of Ignorance" (*Wúzhīlùn*);

because *prajñā* is the cause cultivated by the sages and worthies, the significance of the "Nameless" (*anāmakam*) is thereby revealed. It is said that this concludes the "Nirvana" (*nirvāṇa*). — *Yún'ān Shūsū* (Cloud Hermitage Commentary).

It is said: "The path of the Three Vehicles is opened" concludes the four chapters beginning with "Difficulties of Karmic Bonds. "The distinction between the true and the false is clarified" concludes the first seven chapters.

"The existence of sages and saints" concludes the four chapters beginning with "Gradual [Teachings]. "The ultimate significance of the Nameless is revealed" concludes the four chapters beginning with "Exhausting the Source.
According to the intent of the *Daichao*, this merely concludes the treatise itself; there is no further meaning in dividing the text into sections.
